source: cross-examiner verdicts from the research fleets (one agent per contested claim, both lenses)

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: the People's Republic of China holds the largest AIIB capital subscription and voting share, from founding to now. China's membership date in AIIB's own table is "Dec 25, 2015", the day the Articles entered into force. The record says "from": "2016", which is wrong. The percentages come from particular dates: Diplomat 30.76%/26.57% (June 2021) and FPJ 26.5% (Sept 2020). AIIB's current table (voting-power.js, "update_date = July 29, 2026") gives China 29,780.4m subscribed, 30.5026% of shares and 26.3642% of votes. China has been the largest holder across the whole window. The exact figures have drifted down as new members joined, so the percentages have to carry an as-of date.
verdicts.identityTest: The subject is the member state "China" in AIIB's table, which is a separate row from "Hong Kong, China" (0.7837% shares, 0.7863% votes). The record's s "fin:government-of-china" works as a label for the PRC as a member state. It must not absorb the Hong Kong row. The target, AIIB, is unambiguous.
verdicts.baseRate: Having the founding sponsor state as the largest shareholder is the normal pattern at multilateral development banks. The US is largest at IBRD (about 15-16% of votes). Japan and the US are joint largest at ADB (about 15.6% of shares each). This edge says nothing discriminating about AIIB or India. It is a plain structural fact. China's roughly 26% vote share is unusual in one way: it is above the 25% blocking threshold for supermajority decisions. That is a known feature of the institution, not a finding of ours.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is a neutral shareholding fact that AIIB itself publishes, so no denial is needed. None found; the party was not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: China proposed and capitalised AIIB, and subscriptions follow a GDP-based formula, so China is the largest subscriber. Its vote share is lower than its capital share because AIIB spreads basic and founding-member votes across all members. The same pattern holds for the US at the World Bank and for Japan and the US at ADB. The fact does not make AIIB a Chinese agency. FPJ says this itself: "that does not make it a Chinese agency".
verdicts.reason: Both sources say what the claim says. The Diplomat: "China's shares stand at 30.76 percent (which means 26.57 percent of the votes), and no other shareholder comes close to this." FPJ: "The first largest is China (26.5 per cent)". FPJ gives the vote share as if it were the share of capital. The claim also says AIIB's members table is "client-rendered and unread", and that is no longer true. The table data is served as plain JS at https://www.aiib.org/en/about-aiib/governance/members-of-bank/.content/voting-power.js, dated July 29, 2026: "China| Dec 25, 2015| 29,780.4 |30.5026%| 299,691 |26.3642%". Next is India at 8.5702% of shares and 7.5268% of votes. The core claim (China is the largest shareholder) holds against the primary record, which meets the upgradeIf condition. The killIf condition (materially different shares) is not met: the gap is 0.26 points of shares and 0.21 points of votes, explained by dilution since 2021. The figures in the record are stale, but that calls for a correction, not a kill.
verdicts.corrections: tier: reported -> documented. Add the primary source ["AIIB Members of the Bank, voting-power table (updated 2026-07-29)", "https://www.aiib.org/en/about-aiib/governance/members-of-bank/.content/voting-power.js"] and keep Diplomat and FPJ as secondary. d: "30.50% of subscribed capital (US$29,780.4m) and 26.36% of votes as of 2026-07-29 (AIIB members table). Historical: 30.76%/26.57% (Diplomat, 2021-06). FPJ's 26.5% (2020-09) is the vote share, not the capital share. Next largest is India at 8.57%/7.53%." from: "2016" -> "2015-12-25". Claim text: delete "AIIB's own members table is client-rendered and unread" and replace the figures with the dated 2026 figures. Make clear that "Hong Kong, China" (0.78%) is a separate member and not counted. upgradeIf is met; set killIf to "AIIB table shows another member exceeding China". Optionally note that pred "own" means capital subscription in a multilateral bank, not corporate ownership or control.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated, the claim is: India (Government of India) holds the second-largest shareholding in AIIB from 2016 to the present. The AIIB members table (voting-power.js behind aiib.org/en/about-aiib/governance/members-of-bank/, read 2026-09-26) gives India's membership date as "Jan 11, 2016", which matches from=2016. The ranking holds in 2020 (FPJ), in 2021 and today. The current table shows China first (30.5026% of subscriptions, 26.3642% of votes), India second (8.5702% of subscriptions, 7.5268% of votes) and Russia third (6.6947%, 5.9160%). The FPJ line in `d` that "India joined AIIB in 2014" is a loose statement. India signed the MoU in October 2014, but its membership took effect on 11 Jan 2016. That does not affect the edge.
verdicts.identityTest: The AIIB member is India, i.e. the Government of India. The Finance Minister is India's AIIB Governor and the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA) in the Ministry of Finance administers the holding, so using min:ministry-of-finance as the owner is an acceptable proxy. The same convention is used in c045 (ADB). Strictly, though, the owner is the Republic of India. The t=fin:aiib entity is correct.
verdicts.baseRate: Not relevant: being the second-largest shareholder is a unique ranking, not a shared trait. Among 110 AIIB members only China has a larger share, and Russia (5.9% of votes) is next after India. The symmetric control already exists as c043 (China is the largest shareholder, ≈26.4% of votes). The UPA/NDA control does not apply, because the shareholding dates from 2016 and there is no borrowing-conduct element in this claim.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none is needed. This is a neutral fact that the AIIB itself publishes, with no accusation for anyone to rebut.
verdicts.innocentReading: The claim is itself the boring reading. India's AIIB capital subscription follows the bank's GDP-based allocation formula for regional members, and that formula puts India second after China. The claim implies nothing about wrongdoing.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives, and AIIB's own members table confirms it. That table shows India second by voting power at 7.5268%, after China at 26.3642%, which meets the record's upgradeIf ("AIIB members table read"). On the sources as cited, FPJ supports the claim: "There is nothing wrong with borrowing from the bank in which India (7.6 per cent) is the second-largest shareholder. The first largest is China (26.5 per cent)" (FPJ 2020-09-16). FPJ does not say whether 7.6% refers to votes or shares; the AIIB figures show it matches voting power. The Diplomat article does NOT say India is second or give 7.6%. It only says "China's shares stand at 30.76 percent (which means 26.57 percent of the votes), and no other shareholder comes close to this." The source chain for this edge is therefore partial, but the primary AIIB table resolves it in the claim's favour.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Change tier from reported to documented.
2. Add a primary source: "AIIB Members and Prospective Members / voting power table (read 2026-09-26)", https://www.aiib.org/en/about-aiib/governance/members-of-bank/index.html (data file .content/voting-power.js).
3. Update `d` to: "India: 8.5702% of subscriptions, 7.5268% of votes; second after China (30.5026% / 26.3642%); member since 11 Jan 2016 (AIIB table, 2026). FPJ 2020 reported ≈7.6%."
4. Remove the Diplomat 2021 URL from srcs for this edge, or annotate it as supporting only China's share (it belongs with c043). It does not state India's rank or percentage.
5. Change "India joined 2014" in `d` to "signed MoU Oct 2014; membership effective 11 Jan 2016".
6. Optionally note that the owner is the Republic of India, with the MoF as proxy through the FM, who is AIIB Governor.
7. Leave killIf as is; it is not triggered.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: Subhash Chandra Garg was appointed India's Alternate Governor, ADB Board of Governors, with effect from 2017-07-12. Garg became DEA Secretary in June 2017. He was moved out of DEA to the Power Ministry in late July 2019, and Atanu Chakraborty succeeded him as DEA Secretary in July 2019. The appointment date sits inside his DEA tenure, so the dates overlap. The record's "to":"2019" fits that tenure, but no source is cited for it. The ADB side of the handover was not found.
verdicts.identityTest: This is the right person. PIB and SCC Times both name "Shri Subhash Chandra Garg, Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), Ministry of Finance". Both give the institution as "Asian Development Bank (ADB), Manila, Philippines" and the seat as Alternate Governor on the Board of Governors. Both say he replaced former DEA Secretary Shaktikanta Das. The person, office and institution all match the claim's s/t fields.
verdicts.baseRate: Close to 100% of DEA Secretaries hold this seat. India's ADB Alternate Governor is the DEA Secretary ex officio: Das before Garg, Chakraborty and later secretaries after him. So the edge tells you nothing beyond "held the office". It is a plain role fact and implies no wrongdoing. The UPA/NDA control gives the same reading, because UPA-era DEA Secretaries held the same seat.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial found, and none was sought. This is a routine official appointment the government announced itself, so no response from the party is needed.
verdicts.innocentReading: The Alternate Governor seat automatically follows the DEA Secretary post. The appointment was a procedural handover from Shaktikanta Das after Garg took over at DEA. It carries no meaning beyond the office.
verdicts.reason: The cited SCC Times page (2017-07-27) opens and says: "Shri Subhash Chandra Garg, Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs (DEA)... has been appointed as India's Alternate Governor on the Board of Governors of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Manila, Philippines with effect from 12th July, 2017. Shri Garg has been appointed in place of Former Secretary, DEA, Shri Shaktikanta Das." SCC Times credits this to the Ministry of Finance. The primary source it republishes is PIB release relid=169060 (Ministry of Finance, 26-July-2017 17:33 IST). That release opened with curl and has the identical text. A PIB release is a primary record under the CONTRACT, so the tier should go up from reported to documented. The record's upgradeIf condition ("DEA notification read") is met by the PIB release. The claim holds on person, office, institution and date.
verdicts.corrections:
1. tier: change "reported" to "documented".
2. srcs: add ["PIB (Ministry of Finance) 2017-07-26 — S.C. Garg, Secretary DEA, appointed India's Alternate Governor on ADB Board of Governors", "https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/PrintRelease.aspx?relid=169060&reg=3&lang=2"], and keep SCC Times as the secondary source.
3. d / text: remove "reported (SCC Times); ADB directory pages return 404" and write "per PIB release 26-Jul-2017; replaced Shaktikanta Das". Mention the 404 only in methodology notes.
4. to: "2019" has no source. Mark it inferred ("to 2019-07, when he left DEA; end date inferred from DEA tenure, not from an ADB notice"), or leave it null until an ADB annual report or a PIB successor notice is read.
5. Carry the tier change into narrative line 644 ("[reported]" to "[documented]") and the per:subhash-chandra-garg entity sources in /home/user/india-corporate-intelligence/research/raw/finance/adb-aiib.json.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: AIIB (actor) approved (did) India financing of US$1.95bn, 1.95bn and 1.87bn (thing) in 2020, 2021 and 2022, against US$0.82bn in 2019 (when). I downloaded the AIIB data file on 2026-09-26 (HTTP 200, 213 KB) and grouped Approved India rows by the 'date' field. The result matches the record exactly: 2017 1,074; 2018 1,145; 2019 820; 2020 1,950; 2021 1,946; 2022 1,869; 2023 1,105; 2024 1,058; 2025 1,640 (US$m). Sovereign 2020–22 = 1,750 + 1,896 + 1,719 = US$5,365m, which matches the 'd' field's US$5.36bn. The window is right: Galwan was June 2020, and the CARES approval (2020-06-16) and all other rows fall inside 2020–22. One caveat: grouping by URL-path year gives different yearly totals (2020 = 2,398; 2022 = 1,421). Two India projects, Assam Secondary Roads and HORC, have 2020 paths but 2022 approval dates. On the Assam page, concept review is 2020-12-11 and financing approval is 2022-06-29. An 18-month cycle is normal and is not evidence of a stall.
verdicts.identityTest: Every row is economy = 'India' in AIIB's own file, so the lender (fin:aiib) is correct. The target node is wrong for the full amount. The US$5.77bn ('≈US$5.8bn') includes US$400m of nonsovereign approvals that went to private borrowers, not to the Union or the states: HDFC line of credit US$200m (2020), Enel Green solar US$50m (2021), Kotak Infrastructure Investment Fund US$100m (2022) and Solar IPP equity US$50m (2022). Only the sovereign US$5.365bn can be attributed to min:ministry-of-finance and the states.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not a discriminating property. AIIB's total approvals across the bank more than doubled: US$4.08bn (2019) → 9.30bn (2020) → 9.30bn (2021) → 6.62bn (2022). India's rise, 2.38x from 2019 to 2020, matches the bank-wide 2.28x. The better test is India's share, and it did not fall: 20.1% (2019), 21.0% (2020), 20.9% (2021), 28.3% (2022). That supports the 'no slowdown' reading more strongly than raw totals do. The share then fell to 9.8% in 2023 and 13.1% in 2024, while bank-wide approvals rose to US$11.2bn. Symmetry control from the SPEC (BJP-run vs opposition-run states): the 2020–22 state-level approvals are mixed. Assam, Gujarat and Haryana (BJP) got US$1.39bn; Kerala, West Bengal, Punjab and Tamil Nadu (opposition or regional parties) got about US$0.98bn. There is no party skew in either direction.
verdicts.denialFound: No accusation is being made, so there is nothing to deny. The response on record is from an Indian official quoted by Mint in July 2020 and reproduced in The Diplomat (2021-06-14): "We are not taking money from China but from the multilateral development bank. I don't see any structural change in our engagement with AIIB because of our tensions with China." https://thediplomat.com/2021/06/amid-tensions-with-china-india-proceeding-with-aiib-funded-projects/ . The record also cites SCMP (2021-06-04): AIIB president Jin Liqun said loans to India were maintained. I did not re-open the SCMP article.
verdicts.innocentReading: The pandemic facility was open to every AIIB member, and approvals bank-wide doubled in 2020–21. India's share stayed near 20–28%, so India's totals simply tracked the bank. The record's version of this reading has two errors. First, India's COVID Crisis Recovery Facility (CRF) loans were US$2.25bn in four loans, not US$1.75bn in three: CARES US$750m (2020), Health Systems US$500m (2020), Social Protection US$500m (2021), and Vaccines US$500m (2022, tagged 'CRF-Public Health'). So 2022 is inflated by the facility as well. Second, excluding CRF, the series is 820 → 700 → 1,446 → 1,369 → 1,105 → 1,058. Non-COVID approvals in 2020 were slightly below 2019. The 2023–24 dip happened while bank-wide approvals rose, so it is India-specific in relative terms. 'India's pivot to ADB/World Bank policy loans' is not sourced anywhere in the record.
verdicts.reason: The core analytic claim survives. AIIB's own primary data file reproduces every yearly figure, and India's share of AIIB approvals held or rose in 2020–22. That makes 'no post-Galwan slowdown in approvals' a sound analytic reading. The Diplomat independently found that "I did not come across evidence of any project being halted due to government intervention." Analytic is the right tier: the numbers are documented, but the 'no slowdown' conclusion is an inference, and approval data cannot show pipeline attrition. I could not refute the claim, but its benefit clause and innocent reading have factual errors that must be fixed. The ≈US$5.8bn credited to 'the Union and states' includes US$400m of private nonsovereign deals. 'Drew' overstates what the data shows, since approvals are not disbursements. 'Bilateral ties curtailed' goes beyond the cited source, which says only 'a few' Chinese investments were halted and that 'New Delhi has done little' on imports. The CRF amount is understated.
verdicts.corrections: 1) benefit.how: change 'drew ≈US$5.8bn of AIIB approvals' to 'had ≈US$5.37bn of sovereign AIIB approvals in 2020–22 (US$5.77bn including US$0.4bn nonsovereign to HDFC, Enel, Kotak fund and a solar IPP)'. 'Drew' should become 'were approved for'. 2) benefit.amountCr: 42949 is based on 5,765; recompute on sovereign 5,365 at the same rate (~₹74.5/US$), giving ≈39,970. 3) innocentReading: change 'US$1.75bn in three loans' to 'US$2.25bn in four loans (2020 CARES 750, 2020 Health 500, 2021 Social Protection 500, 2022 Vaccines 500)'; change '2020–21 totals inflated' to '2020–22 totals inflated'. Either remove 'India's pivot to larger ADB/World Bank policy loans' or source it. Note that non-CRF approvals in 2020 (US$700m) were below 2019 (US$820m). 4) d: add India's share of AIIB approvals (20.1 / 21.0 / 20.9 / 28.3% for 2019–22; 9.8 / 13.1% for 2023–24) against bank-wide totals (4.08 / 9.30 / 9.30 / 6.62 / 11.25 / 8.09 US$bn). The share is the non-trivial comparison, and it shows the 2023–24 dip is India-specific because bank-wide lending rose. 5) Change the phrase 'bilateral economic ties with China were curtailed' to 'some Chinese investment was restricted or halted (The Diplomat: "only a few")', or add a primary source such as Press Note 3 (2020). 6) Add the Mint/Diplomat official quote as the response field. 7) Note in d that year grouping uses the file's 'date' field, not the URL path year (HORC and Assam roads carry 2020 paths but were approved in 2022).

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: AIIB took CPRR (000336) from concept review on 2020-03-17 to financing approval on 2023-01-18. The AIIB project page confirms it: "CONCEPT REVIEW March 17, 2020 APPRAISAL REVIEW / FINAL REVIEW August 27, 2020 FINANCING APPROVAL January 18, 2023". That is 34.1 months. The four comparators also check out against their own pages. Gujarat RR runs 2017-03-13 to 07-04 (3.7 mo). Bangalore R6 runs 2017-07-03 to 12-08 (5.2 mo). AP RR runs 2018-04-10 to 09-28 (5.6 mo). MUTP-III runs 2019-01-31 to 09-26 (7.9 mo). The dates are right. The problem is how the window is framed, not the timestamps.
verdicts.identityTest: Passes. AIIB project number 000336 is "India: Chennai Peripheral Ring Road (Sections 2 and 3)": sovereign, USD378m, Category A. The board Project Document (2023-01-03) names the borrower-side agencies as TNHD/TNRIDC under the Government of Tamil Nadu. The OPEC Fund co-finances USD100m. So the target energy:state-tamil-nadu is the right entity.
verdicts.baseRate:
I rebuilt the full distribution from AIIB's all-projects-data.js plus each project page, for every approved India sovereign project. Neither of the claim's two premises holds.
(1) "Only case spanning the border-tension window" is false. At least 11 India sovereign projects had concept review before or during 2020–22 and approval inside or after it:
- Chennai Metro C4: 2019-12 to 2021-09, 21 mo
- Assam Transmission: 14.5 mo
- Assam Distribution: 2019-11 to 2022-02, ~27 mo
- Second DRIP: 17.2 mo
- Assam Secondary Roads: 18.6 mo
- HORC Part A (Haryana): 30.5 mo
- Chennai Metro Balance C5: 36.4 mo
- MUTP-3A: 42.1 mo
- Mumbai Metro Line 5: 2020-04-21 to 2024-09-17, about 53 mo
Several window-spanning projects took as long as CPRR or longer. Others moved fast inside the window: Delhi-Meerut RRTS about 7 mo (2020-03 to 2020-10), Kerala SWM 4.2, Resilient Kerala 5.9, Chennai City Partnership 8.3, WB Grid about 10.
(2) "4–8 months for earlier projects" is cherry-picked. Other pre-window India projects took longer: TN Transmission 17 mo (2016–17), MP Rural Connectivity 15.1 mo, WB Irrigation 24.2 mo (2017–19). Long concept-to-approval spans for Category A urban and transport projects are common in every period. CPRR is not an outlier, and n=1 was a sampling artefact.
Symmetry: long delays hit BJP-run Haryana (HORC, 30.5 mo), Maharashtra (MUTP-3A, Metro 5) and Tamil Nadu (AIADMK, then DMK after May 2021). There is no partisan or state pattern.
verdicts.denialFound: Nothing specific to CPRR was found, and AIIB was not asked about CPRR's timing. The general response on record is from AIIB president Jin Liqun (SCMP, 2021-06-04, https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-economy/article/3136109/china-backed-aiib-maintained-loans-india-during-border). He said AIIB maintained its India lending during the border dispute. The Diplomat's project-by-project check (2021-06-14) found no halted India projects.
verdicts.innocentReading:
The CPRR board Project Document (AIIB-Chennai-Peripheral-Ring-Road-Sections-2-and-3_PD_Board_Final-20230103.pdf) puts the delay on the Indian side, in readiness.
- It says: "RPF and Entitlement Matrix approved vide G.O Ms. No.78 dated 19.05.2022". The Government of Tamil Nadu approved the resettlement framework only in May 2022.
- It says: "As of December 2022, all Government land and roughly 279 ha (66 percent) of private land have been acquired ... The land acquisition is expected to be completed by March 2023."
- The procurement log shows advance tendering from 2020, then "Contract Notice (Rejection of All Tenders) (September 10, 2021)", re-tendering, and extensions into January 2022.
This meets the claim's own killIf: GoTN records show land and resettlement readiness finished only in 2022.
verdicts.reason:
The dates are accurate, but the inference built on them is manufactured by the choice of sample. Once every AIIB India sovereign project is included, CPRR is neither the only project spanning 2020–22 nor an outlier:
- Mumbai Metro 5 (about 53 mo), MUTP-3A (42 mo), Chennai Metro C5 (36 mo) and HORC (30.5 mo) spanned the same window.
- Delhi-Meerut RRTS and the Kerala projects were approved in 4–7 months during it.
- Pre-2020 projects also ran 15–24 months.
The board document itself dates the hold-up to Tamil Nadu's resettlement framework approval (May 2022) and land acquisition that was still incomplete in December 2022. That triggers the claim's own killIf. As written, the claim implies a pattern that the full data contradict. The documented facts already sit in adb-aiib:c022.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Kill adb-aiib:c052 as currently worded. If it is kept at all, restate it as analytic: "AIIB India sovereign concept-to-approval intervals, 2016–26 (n≈30): median about 9–15 mo; the 2020–22 window includes both fast (RRTS 7, Kerala SWM 4.2) and slow (MUTP-3A 42, Chennai Metro C5 36, HORC 30.5, CPRR 34, Mumbai Metro 5 about 53) cases; no border-related pattern". Include the full list, and cite the data file and the CPRR board PD.
2. Remove "the only case spanning the border-tension window (n=1)" and "versus 4–8 months for four earlier AIIB India projects". Both are false or selective.
3. Replace the innocentReading with the sourced facts: RPF approved by G.O. Ms. No.78 on 19.05.2022; 66% of private land acquired as of December 2022; tenders rejected on 2021-09-10 and re-tendered.
4. Update narrative:1 "strongestCase". Drop CPRR as supporting evidence, or add to strongestCounter that its delay matches GoTN readiness and that peers spanning the window vary widely.
5. Add the CPRR board PD URL to srcs: https://www.aiib.org/en/projects/details/2023/_download/India/AIIB-Chennai-Peripheral-Ring-Road-Sections-2-and-3_PD_Board_Final-20230103.pdf

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: "AIIB approved and later cancelled or terminated 4 India nonsovereign loans, all approved 2019–22." The approval dates on the AIIB project pages bear this out. Hero Future Energies (P?, Rajasthan 250 MW): approved December 6, 2019. Ayana Anantapuramu (P000384): approved November 26, 2020. AGPCGPL CGD (P000318): approved May 20, 2021. GreenCell (P000540): approved September 29, 2022. The cancellations are not all from the COVID period, though. The AGPCGPL page sits under /2024/cancelled/ and its latest Project Summary is dated May 31, 2024. GreenCell's page sits under /2025/cancelled/, and its termination PSI is dated November 5, 2025 and says "Status of Financing: Terminated". In GreenCell's case the loan had been signed (Inc42 reported that GreenCell received US$55m from ADB and AIIB) and was ended after that. So "fall-away during COVID" fits at most the 2019 and 2020 entries. It fails chronologically for 2 of the 4.
verdicts.identityTest: Every name matches the data file and the project pages. Borrowers are Hero Future Energies (borrower contact @herofutureenergies.com, SPV Clean Solar Power (Jodhpur)); Ayana Ananthapuramu Solar Pvt Ltd (the page says "AASPL signed a 25-year PPA with NTPC", so NTPC is the offtaker, not the borrower); AGP City Gas Pvt Ltd (borrower contacts @agpglobal.com, i.e. AG&P, which confirms it is not an Adani entity and the claim's name-collision warning is correct); and GreenCell Express Pvt Ltd, sponsor GMPL. One problem is the edge target. "min:ministry-of-finance" is wrong for nonsovereign loans: these were private borrowers with no sovereign guarantee, and the Union was not a party.
verdicts.baseRate: I re-derived these from all-projects-data.js (481 entries, fetched 2026-09-26). India nonsovereign: 22 approved and 4 terminated/cancelled, so 4 of 26 = 15.4%. The 4 total US$195.5m (65 + 35 + 75 + 20.5), which matches the claim. India sovereign: 35 approved (US$11,745.75m), 3 proposed and 0 cancelled. That is 0 of 35, not "0 of 39"; no reading of the file gives 39. AIIB-wide nonsovereign: 11 of 175 = 6.3%. Excluding India: 7 of 149 = 4.7%. By comparison, Türkiye is 2 of 22 (9.1%), Multicountry 3 of 40 (7.5%), China 0 of 18 and Uzbekistan 0 of 10. India has the highest cancellation rate of any AIIB nonsovereign portfolio with 5 or more entries, roughly 2.4 times the bank-wide rate. So the property does discriminate. The record says a 15% rate is "unremarkable for MDB private-sector windows", but gives no source for that and AIIB's own portfolio contradicts it. The record's own killIf (other members' rates similar or higher) is not met. Symmetry: sovereign cancellations run 0 for India against 4 of 216 AIIB-wide (Russia, Uzbekistan, Philippines, Argentina), so India's sovereign book is cleaner than average. The UPA/NDA control does not apply because AIIB lending to India starts in 2017.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. Nobody was asked. The AIIB pages and the GreenCell termination PSI give no reason for cancelling or terminating. A search for reasons turned up no statement from AIIB or any of the borrowers.
verdicts.innocentReading: These are private deals: AIIB pulls out when a sponsor refinances with cheaper domestic debt, prepays, sells the asset or changes the project's scope. Examples: Hero Future Energies and Ayana were bought or restructured around 2019–22, and the city gas rollout was restructured under AG&P. GreenCell was terminated after the loan was signed, which is consistent with prepayment or refinancing. None of this implies misconduct. It does not, however, explain why India's rate is 2.4 times AIIB's bank-wide rate. It is also not "during COVID" for AGPCGPL (2024) or GreenCell (2025).
verdicts.reason: The core count holds against the primary source: 4 of 26 India nonsovereign entries are terminated/cancelled, all approved 2019–22, US$195.5m in total. The names are correct and the AG&P/Adani disambiguation is right. Analytic is the correct tier for a count taken from the lender's own portal, so I am not refuting the claim. But parts of it need fixing. The sovereign denominator is wrong: the file gives 35, not 39. The innocent reading is weaker than written: India's rate is the highest among comparable AIIB portfolios, not unremarkable, and two of the four ended in 2024–25, not during COVID. Because the record's killIf test was not met, the innocent reading has to be rewritten rather than kept as it stands.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: "ADB's top-three recipient states in 2016–21 were run by BJP, INC and JD(U)", and "AIIB's sovereign approvals for India in 2017–26 went to states run by BJP, INC, DMK, LDF, TMC, AAP and TDP/YSRCP". The ADB side mostly holds. MP: BJP Jan 2016–Dec 2018, INC Dec 2018–23 Mar 2020, BJP after that, so about 4.7 of 6 years BJP. Rajasthan: BJP (Raje) until 17 Dec 2018, INC (Gehlot) after that, so about 2.96 years BJP against 3.04 years INC. "INC-led for most of the window" is true by only about 1% and is really an even split. Bihar: JD(U)-led for the whole window, but the record's `d` field is wrong. It says "JD(U)-BJP except Aug 2022–Jan 2024" and leaves out the JD(U)-RJD-INC Mahagathbandhan government of Nov 2015–Jul 2017. The AIIB side fails the date test on three party labels, checked against approval dates on the AIIB project pages. (1) Punjab Municipal Services was approved 27 Apr 2021, when INC (Amarinder Singh) ran Punjab. AAP took over in Mar 2022, and no AIIB approval for Punjab comes after that, so "AAP" is wrong. (2) The Andhra Pradesh approvals (24x7 Power 2017, Urban Water 2018, Rural Roads 2018) all fall under TDP. YSRCP (May 2019–Jun 2024) has no AIIB approval, so "YSRCP" is wrong. (3) Maharashtra MUTP-III was approved 26 Sep 2019 under the BJP-Shiv Sena government (Fadnavis). The MVA government (Nov 2019–Jun 2022) has no AIIB approval, and the later approvals (MUTP-3A 2023, Metro Line 5 2024, MAHA RE 2025) fall under Shinde-BJP or Fadnavis, so "MVA" is wrong. DMK (Chennai approvals of 23 Sep 2021, 11 Nov 2021 and 2023), LDF (Kerala 2021 and 2024) and TMC (West Bengal 2019 and 2022) are correct. The claim leaves out INC-run Karnataka (Bangalore Metro R6, 2017) and does not name Haryana (BJP), MP (BJP, approved 11 Apr 2018) or Manipur (BJP, 2024).
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match the sources. The CPSFR (ADB IED-style final review, April 2022, para 222) names "Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Bihar" as top-three states. The AIIB data file lists India sovereign projects with state names in their titles, and I count 12 named states (AP, Gujarat, Maharashtra, TN, Kerala, WB, Assam, Punjab, Karnataka, MP, Haryana, Manipur), which fits "~12". The party labels are the analyst's own addition and appear in neither source. The actor who approves is the lender's board, and the borrower of record is the Union of India (DEA). The state government is the executing or implementing agency, not the counterparty. The record should say this so that "state run by party X" is not read as "party X borrowed".
verdicts.baseRate: The BJP or NDA held CM posts in a majority of states for most of 2017–26 (roughly 12–21 of ~30), so any spread of state-level lending would show "BJP states" heavily, and that fact does not discriminate. I summed AIIB sovereign approvals with a state in the title by the CM's party on the approval date. NDA-run states got about US$4.2bn: Assam 1,151, Maharashtra 1,885, Gujarat 579, Manipur 352, MP 140, Haryana 128. Opposition-run states got about US$3.5bn: TN-DMK 1,323 plus AIADMK 100, AP-TDP 1,015, Kerala-LDF 352, Karnataka-INC 335, WB-TMC 280, Punjab-INC 105. That is about 55:45 and roughly in line with the number of states each side ran. For ADB, two of the three top states (MP and Rajasthan) were both INC-run from Dec 2018 to Mar 2020, which is when the low-income share was at its peak (70% in 2019). The fleet control (UPA vs NDA; BJP vs opposition states) gives no partisan picture either way. Per-capita and prior-lending normalisation has not been done, which the record already flags as a gap.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable: this is a null analytic finding and nobody is accused. No party was asked. No statement from ADB, AIIB or DEA on partisan allocation was searched for or found.
verdicts.innocentReading: ADB's own CPS 2013–2017 set a target of 40–50% of lending for lower-income states, and ADB had worked in MP and Bihar since 2003 and in Rajasthan since CPS 2009–12. So income category and long-standing state relationships, not the ruling party, explain why low-income states dominate. Both lenders' sovereign loans go through DEA, which ranks state proposals largely on project readiness. Two cautions on the record's wording. First, the source's word is "added that ... would be 40-50%", which is a strategy target and not a "mandate" or "rule". Second, the target explains why low-income states dominate but not why these particular three rank at the top, so "mechanically produces MP/Rajasthan/Bihar" overstates the case.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives in its conclusion but not in its wording. I checked the ADB source verbatim. CPSFR para 222 says: "The CPS 2013-2017 added that overall ADB lending to the lower income states would be 40-50% of the total ADB lending to India during the CPS period ... Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Bihar have been the top-three states that received highest share of the ADB program in 2016-2021." I opened the AIIB data file and six approval pages. Once each approval is dated, three of the eight party labels in the AIIB list fail the date test: AAP, YSRCP and MVA had no AIIB approval while in office. Karnataka-INC is missing from the list. After correction, the approval split is still about 55:45 between NDA-run and opposition-run states, and the ADB top-three include two states that were INC-run in the peak year. So the null finding ("no partisan skew visible, unnormalised") still stands. The claim should be published only with the label corrections. Tier stays analytic: it is our own comparison, it has an innocentReading, it implies no wrongdoing, and it has not been normalised.
verdicts.corrections: 1) lab and text: replace the AIIB party list with party-at-approval: AP (TDP, 2017–18), Gujarat (BJP), Maharashtra (BJP-Shiv Sena 2019; Shinde-BJP 2023–24; BJP 2025), TN (AIADMK 2017; DMK 2021–23), Kerala (LDF), WB (TMC), Assam (BJP), Punjab (INC, Apr 2021), Karnataka (INC, 2017), MP/Haryana/Manipur (BJP). Delete "YSRCP", "AAP" and "MVA". The party set becomes BJP, INC, DMK, AIADMK, LDF, TMC, TDP. 2) Rajasthan: change "INC-led for most of the window" to "BJP to Dec 2018, INC from Dec 2018 (roughly even split)". 3) d field, Bihar: change to "JD(U)-RJD-INC Nov 2015–Jul 2017; JD(U)-BJP Jul 2017–Aug 2022; JD(U)-RJD-INC Aug 2022–Jan 2024". 4) innocentReading: change "mandated ... rule" to "set a 40–50% target (CPS 2013–2017, per CPSFR para 222)", and change "mechanically produces MP/Rajasthan/Bihar at the top" to "makes lower-income states dominant". 5) Add the approval-date sums in US$m (NDA-run ~4,235 vs opposition-run ~3,510, not normalised) to d, with the AIIB project pages as sources for the approval dates (Punjab 2021-04-27; MUTP-III 2019-09-26; Chennai Metro C4 2021-09-23; Chennai City Partnership 2021-11-11; MP Rural Connectivity 2018-04-11). 6) Note that the borrower of record is the Union (DEA), not the state government.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: ADB/AIIB financed ReNew in 2014, 2016, 2017, 2025 and 2025. All five dates check out against the sources. 47926-014 PDS: "Approval 16 May 2014", borrower "ReNew Private Limited". 50195-001 PDS: "Approval 02 Dec 2016". 51210-001 PDS: "Approval 12 Dec 2017". ADB release: "(10 November 2025) — ADB has signed a $331 million finance package with ReNew Vyoman Power Private Limited". AIIB 000967: "FINANCING APPROVAL November 7, 2025 … FINANCING APPROVED FUNDING USD100 million". The "inherited" label for the Ostro Kutch loan fails the date test, though. The PDS says "The Project was acquired by Renew Power Private Limited in March 2018". ADB's own IATI India file (https://www.adb.org/iati/iati-activities-in.xml, LN3622) records the US$100m commitment on 2018-09-25, six months after ReNew took control. ADB approved the loan while Ostro was independent but committed it to a ReNew-owned SPV, so it is not a loan ReNew merely inherited. The claim also leaves out one engagement inside the window. ADB 54165-001, the "ReNew Power COVID-19 Liquidity Support Project", has borrower "ReNew Private Limited", a debt security of "INR 3,738.00 million" and "Approval 29 Jul 2020" (PDS https://www.adb.org/projects/54165-001/main; IATI LN7639).
verdicts.identityTest: The entities hold up. ReNew Private Limited (formerly ReNew Power Pvt Ltd / ReNew Power Ventures) is the borrower on 47926-014 and 54165-001 and the sponsor on 50195-001, 51210-001 and AIIB 000967. The borrowing SPVs are ReNew Vyoman Power Pvt Ltd for ADB and "ReNew Vyoman Private Limited" for AIIB. They are the same project, and AIIB says it is "co-financed with ADB". One correction: on 51210-001 the Borrower/Company is still Ostro Kutch Wind Private Limited, and ReNew Private Limited appears as Project Sponsor, not as "Company". The energy:renew evidence line and c032 "d" both get this wrong. On Adani, ADB's IATI India file (405 activities) has no Adani entity, and AIIB's all-projects-data.js lists no Adani borrower among its India nonsovereign entries. "AGPCGPL" is AG&P City Gas, a name collision the file already notes. The absence is confirmed.
verdicts.baseRate: Denominator: the Indian private counterparties in ADB's IATI India file plus AIIB's India nonsovereign list. Repeat counterparties are common in financial intermediaries. IIFL Home Finance appears 3 times (ADB 2021, ADB 2025, AIIB 2025). Shriram appears at least 3 times (ADB 2022 and 2024, AIIB "Facility II" 2026). Cholamandalam (2018, 2025), Aavas (2020, 2025), Krsnaa (2021, 2025) and Suguna (2019, 2020) appear twice each. Counted as a group, Tata is comparable to ReNew: ADB Tata Power wind 2007, Mundra/CGPL 2008, Tata Capital Growth Fund II 2019, TPDDL 2023 and Tata Energy Access Solar 2025, plus AIIB Tata Cleantech 2019, for about 6 engagements. At single-company level ReNew is the top repeat counterparty, with 6 ADB engagements (2014, 2016, 2017/18, 2020, 2025 ADB, 2025 AIIB). So "most repeated" survives and is slightly understated. But the symmetric control (the Tata group) produces a similar picture, and roughly 10–15% of private counterparties are repeat borrowers. The property picks out ReNew but says nothing about wrongdoing, which is consistent with the analytic tier.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial exists, and none is needed: the claim is analytic and alleges no wrongdoing. Neither ADB nor ReNew was asked. The closest on-record statement is ADB VP Bhargav Dasgupta in the 2025-11-10 release: "This landmark project reflects ADB's long-standing partnership with ReNew, which has spanned multiple investments and initiatives over the years." Sumant Sinha: "Our long-standing collaboration with ADB has enabled us to continually push the boundaries…" (https://www.adb.org/news/adb-renew-sign-331-million-deal-solar-wind-bess-power-plant-generating-24-7-clean-energy-india). Both parties acknowledge the repeat relationship openly.
verdicts.innocentReading: ReNew is India's second-largest IPP ("second largest Independent Power Producer (IPP) in India, with a total portfolio of 18.2 GW" — AIIB 000967). MDB private windows concentrate on a few large, investment-grade sponsors with a known corporate ESMS. ADB's CPS explicitly aimed to scale up nonsovereign renewables. The Kutch project came out of India's first competitive wind auction (the PDS says so), and the 2025 plant sells under a 25-year SECI PPA at a fixed ₹4.69/kWh. The 2014 equity was exited in 2016 "with satisfactory returns" (CPSFR). The same pattern repeats for Tata and the NBFC borrowers. The claim's innocent-reading text goes further than the evidence in two places. First, it says pricing was "market-based OCR" as though that were sourced, but loan pricing is not on the project pages, so this is ADB's stated policy for nonsovereign lending, not a checked term. Second, "on competitively auctioned SECI PPAs" covers only Kutch and Vyoman. The 2014 equity and the 2020 working-capital debenture were corporate-level and had no PPA, and the 2016 SPVs had mixed offtakers.
verdicts.reason: The main finding survives and gets stronger: ReNew is the most repeated single Indian private counterparty of ADB and AIIB, and Adani Green has no ADB or AIIB record, which the IATI file and AIIB data confirm. The claim as written still fails on facts it can be checked against. (1) The "≈₹4,400 crore cumulative" figure matches neither the file's own components (295+669+642+2,932+886 = ₹5,424 crore, which is the benefit.amountCr in the same record) nor the corrected total. The corrected total is about ₹5,950 crore: 295 + 818 (the 50195 PDS closed/committed amounts including LEAP 8324 US$22.16m, which c031 omits: 10+29.10+22.13+12.18+25.14+22.16 = US$120.7m) + 642 + 374 (the omitted 2020 INR 3,738m COVID debenture) + 2,932 + 886. (2) The list leaves out ADB 54165-001 (2020), so there are 6 engagements (ADB 5 + AIIB 1), not 5. (3) "Inherited Ostro Kutch loan" is misleading, because ADB committed the loan on 2018-09-25, after ReNew acquired Ostro in March 2018. (4) The two 2025 items are one co-financed project, not two independent choices. With these corrections the claim stays analytic. It becomes neither kill nor documented, because "most repeated" is our own inference over the lenders' records.

Add the "2020 ADB 54165-001 COVID-19 liquidity debenture INR 3,738m (₹373.8 crore), approved 2020-07-29" engagement, source https://www.adb.org/projects/54165-001/main, and change the count from "5 engagements" to "6 (ADB 5, AIIB 1), incl. the Ostro Kutch loan". Change "inherited Ostro Kutch loan 2017" to "Ostro Kutch loan approved 2017-12-12 pre-acquisition, committed 2018-09-25 after ReNew's March 2018 takeover (ADB IATI LN3622)". Note that the 2025 ADB and AIIB items are one co-financed project, and that US$40m of the US$331m is LEAP 2 (JICA-funded, ADB-administered), not ADB OCR. c031: add LEAP 8324 US$22.16m (closed), making the total ≈US$120.7m ≈ ₹818 crore, not US$98.6m / ₹669 crore. c032 "d" and the energy:renew evidence line: ReNew Private Limited is the "Project Sponsor" on 51210-001, not the "Company"; the Borrower/Company is still Ostro Kutch Wind Pvt Ltd. Innocent reading: mark "market-based OCR pricing" as ADB policy, not a verified loan term, and limit "SECI PPA" to Kutch and Vyoman. verdicts.dateTest: Claim as a sentence: JICA signed a JPY 400bn (about ₹22,627 crore) ODA loan agreement with the Government of India for MAHSR tranche V on 2023-12-21. The comparison window runs from AIIB's first India approval in 2017 to 2026-07. I found no date problem. The JICA page says: "New Delhi, December 21, 2023: Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) has signed a loan agreement with the Government of India to provide an Official Development Assistance (ODA) loan of 400 billion Japanese Yen (approx. INR 22,627 Crore) as tranche five for the 'Project for the Construction of Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail (MAHSR).'" I re-derived AIIB India sovereign approvals from all-projects-data.js, fetched today (HTTP 200). Grouped by the file's date field they are: 2017 924, 2018 995, 2019 645, 2020 1,750, 2021 1,896, 2022 1,719, 2023 902, 2024 675, 2025 1,241, 2026 (to date) 1,000 (US$m). Grouped by the year in the project path, 2020 reaches 2,198. On either count the highest year is at most about US$2.2bn, which is about ₹19,400 crore even at today's ₹88. The tranche is about US$2.8bn at December 2023 yen rates. The claim holds on either year grouping and any plausible exchange rate. One caveat: the claim sets a single multi-year loan commitment against annual approvals, which are different measures (see innocentReading).
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. s=fin:jica is the Japan International Cooperation Agency, the signatory named on the JICA release. The release names the borrower as the Government of India; ODA loans are signed through the Department of Economic Affairs, so t=min:ministry-of-finance is acceptable. The project is MAHSR, with NHSRCL as executing agency. The AIIB rows are India with financing_type "Sovereign". There are no individual people, so name-collision risk does not apply.
verdicts.baseRate: Only one comparison in this set exceeds AIIB's annual India approvals: of 10 JICA India loan agreements checked, only the tranche V agreement is above US$2.2bn. The Embassy table shows JICA's whole-programme annual commitments to India were above AIIB's peak year in most years: 2018-19 JPY 537bn, 2022-23 567.5bn, 2023-24 893.6bn. So "Japan out-lends AIIB to India" is not a notable finding; it is the normal pattern. The discriminating content is only that one project tranche outweighs any AIIB year. The claim does not frame any family, religion or ethnicity as the actor.
verdicts.denialFound: none found — not asked. The claim alleges no wrongdoing by JICA, AIIB or the Ministry of Finance, so there is nothing to deny.
verdicts.innocentReading: MAHSR is one very large flagship project, and the yen loan is a multi-year commitment signed in a single agreement. JICA itself calls it "the largest commitment amount through a single project loan agreement in the history of JICA, across the globe". Setting it against AIIB's annual approvals mostly measures project size and financing structure (Japanese Shinkansen technology financed on STEP-type concessional terms), not a preference by India for one lender. AIIB is a younger bank (India lending from 2017) with per-project caps and co-financing practice. Its India lending is spread across many mid-sized state projects of US$100–1,100m.
verdicts.reason: The numbers check out. The JICA primary page confirms the amount, date, tranche and borrower. AIIB's own data file shows no year of India sovereign approvals above about US$2.2bn (under ₹19,400 crore at any rate up to ₹88), against about US$2.8bn / ₹22,627 crore for the tranche. It survives as analytic: our own comparison, with an innocentReading and no implied wrongdoing. Two weaknesses stop it passing cleanly. (1) The "tied to Japanese technology" half is not in either cited source. JICA says only "using Japan's Shinkansen technology"; the tying (STEP terms: Japanese prime contractor, about 0.1% interest, 50 years, 15-year grace) is widely reported but not sourced in the record, and the claim correctly flags it as a gap. "MDB procurement is open" overstates: ADB limits procurement to member countries, while AIIB's is open internationally. (2) The stored `lab` carries a second clause that contradicts itself: "Japan's cumulative ODA (≈₹4 lakh crore) exceeds ADB's cumulative US$63.8bn (≈₹5.3 lakh crore) only if measured over its longer 1958– history". Its own figures show ₹4 lakh crore is less than ₹5.3 lakh crore, and no historical-rate calculation is given, so that clause is not supported as written.
verdicts.corrections:
1. lab: remove the clause after "any single year," (the ₹4 lakh crore vs ₹5.3 lakh crore cumulative comparison contradicts itself), or rewrite it as "Japan's cumulative ODA commitments since 1958 (JPY 6.978 tn, ≈₹4.0 lakh crore at today's rate) are smaller in today's rupees than ADB's cumulative US$63.8bn (≈₹5.3 lakh crore); a historical-rate comparison was not done (gap)."
2. d: replace "AIIB India sovereign approvals peak US$1.9bn ≈ ₹14,300 crore (2021)" with "AIIB India sovereign approvals peak US$1,896m in 2021 by the data file's date field (US$2,198m for 2020 if grouped by project-path year); either is below JPY 400bn ≈ US$2.8bn (Dec 2023)". Add that the comparison is a multi-year loan commitment against annual approvals.
3. Tying: add a source for STEP terms (JICA terms-and-conditions page https://www.jica.go.jp/english/our_work/types_of_assistance/oda_loans/standard/index.html, or a Ministry of Railways Parliament answer on MAHSR loan terms: 0.1%, 50 yr, 15 yr grace), or keep "not verified". Change "MDB procurement is open" to "ADB procurement is limited to member countries; AIIB procurement is internationally open".
4. srcs: the AIIB side of the comparison rests on all-projects-data.js, which the full record lists but the claim's srcs do not; add it there. The Embassy page supports only the cumulative JPY 6.978 tn and the annual commitments table (2023-24: JPY 893.645bn), not the tranche.
5. baseRate field: add that JICA's annual India commitments exceeded AIIB's highest India year in most years 2010–2024, so "bilateral beats AIIB" does not by itself discriminate.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the Union government (DEA, Ministry of Finance; Modi PM since 2014, Sitharaman FM since 2019) borrowed US$1.25bn from AIIB in May–June 2020. Tenure overlaps, so the date test passes. The two loans need separate dates. (1) Health loan, US$500m: the AIIB page gives "APPROVAL DATE" May 7, 2020. The only source for signing is FPJ: "the agreement was signed on May 8, 2020". That is five weeks before the 15 June Galwan clash, though after the standoff began in early May. It fits "amid the standoff" but not "while soldiers were killed". (2) CARES, US$750m: the AIIB page gives approval June 16, 2020, one day after the clash. The only source for signing is FPJ: "the loan agreement was signed on June 19 when the country was mourning the loss of its soldiers." So only one of the two loans falls after Galwan. Its timing was set by the ADB-led programme it co-finances, which ADB approved and signed on 28 Apr 2020 (ADB PDS). FPJ also says "the second loan discussion started in May 2020". Both points predate the clash.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The actor is the Government of India through the Department of Economic Affairs, which both the AIIB CARES page and the ADB PDS 54182-001 name as executing agency. The lender is AIIB, a multilateral bank headquartered in Beijing, not the PRC state. The narrative's wording "ADB lead cofinancier" is correct only for CARES. The health loan (AIIB, US$500m) was co-financed with the World Bank. The AIIB page says: "AIIB (the Bank) will co-finance this project with the World Bank (WB)".
verdicts.baseRate: Borrowing from AIIB was not unusual for India. FPJ says India "continues to be the largest borrower of AIIB... around USD 3.6 billion which is around 25 per cent of the AIIB's overall lending". India had been borrowing sovereign money from AIIB since 2017, and the COVID Crisis Recovery Facility was open to all members. Within India's own AIIB history, then, a 2020 loan is close to 100%: non-discriminating. The UPA control does not apply because AIIB began operating in 2016. The symmetric control does apply. The same "controlled by the largest shareholder" lens would call the same-month World Bank co-financed health loan and the ADB CARES loans "US-controlled" or "Japan-controlled". That would make the characterisation a statement about multilateral banks in general, not about this government.
verdicts.denialFound: Government: an anonymous Indian official quoted by Mint, cited in The Diplomat of 2021-06-14 (https://thediplomat.com/2021/06/amid-tensions-with-china-india-proceeding-with-aiib-funded-projects/): "We are not taking money from China but from the multilateral development bank. I don't see any structural change in our engagement with AIIB because of our tensions with China." The Mint original was not opened. Lender: Jin Liqun, via SCMP 2021-06-04 (https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-economy/article/3136109/china-backed-aiib-maintained-loans-india-during-border). He said AIIB "kept lending to India despite domestic pressure", and SCMP reports him "refuting claims the lender is simply a tool for China's strategic interests". No on-record ministerial answer to the Galwan-timing charge was opened. The record does not name who made the "China-controlled" charge, so nobody can be shown to have been asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: Both AIIB loans were add-ons to programmes led by other banks. The health loan co-financed a World Bank project, approved 7 May. CARES co-financed ADB's US$1.5bn CARES programme, which ADB signed on 28 Apr 2020. Their approval dates followed AIIB's COVID-facility processing cycle, which began in April–May, before the clash. The money came from a multilateral bank in which India is the second-largest shareholder (7.6% per FPJ) and India's largest source of AIIB lending. It paid for health response and PMGKY cash transfers. Signing three days after Galwan reflects a timetable already under way, not a decision taken after the clash.
verdicts.reason: The narrative survives as a two-sided "contested" record. The borrowing is on primary record: the AIIB pages show US$500m approved 2020-05-07 and US$750m approved 2020-06-16, and ADB PDS 54182-001 lists "Co-financer AIIB: US$ 750 million". The claimant's side and the counter-side are both put fairly. The source chain has one load-bearing fault. The headline figure "₹9,200 crore" appears in none of the four cited sources. FPJ, the only outlet the record credits with the rupee figures, gives only dollars: "USD 1,250 million". The ₹9,200 cr is an internal sum of c003 (₹5,521 cr) and c004 (₹3,676 cr). Both of those are mislabelled "as stated by FPJ" when they are our own conversions. The signing dates (05-08 and 06-19) rest on FPJ alone, and FPJ contradicts itself on amounts ("USD 500 million and USD 250 million" against a total of 1,250). Those dates are therefore reported, not documented. Finally, "contested" is a narrative calibration status, not a tier. Where one tier value is required, this is our own two-sided judgement, i.e. analytic, with the component loan edges documented (approvals) or reported (signings). These faults need correcting, but none of them overturns the narrative's verdict.
verdicts.corrections:
