verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: "AIIB did not slow or freeze India lending after 15 June 2020." I parsed AIIB's all-projects-data.js (481 records, fetched 2026-09-26) and summed India approvals by the record's approval-year field, excluding cancelled deals. 2019: US$820m. 2020: US$1,950m. 2021: US$1,945.7m. 2022: US$1,869m. 2023: US$1,104.8m. 2024: US$1,058.2m. 2025: US$1,639.6m. 2026 so far: US$1,250m. Every year from 2020 to 2022 is above 2 x 820 = 1,640, so the narrative's numbers are exact. The project page for the "Program for Growth, Resilience, Energy Security and Sustainability" says "APPROVAL July 16, 2026" and lists USD1000 million, which confirms the US$1bn policy loan in July 2026. One caveat: 2020 includes the US$500m COVID-19 Emergency Response loan, approved May 7, 2020, before the clash. Loans approved after the clash in 2020 total US$1.45bn: CARES US$750m on June 16, 2020, HDFC US$200m on Sept 24, 2020, and Delhi-Meerut RRTS US$500m in Oct 2020. That is about 1.77x 2019, so it still shows no freeze. CPRR: concept review was March 17, 2020 and financing approval January 18, 2023, which is 34 months as stated. The four nonsovereign cancellations are confirmed: Hero Rajasthan (2019), Ayana (approved Nov 26, 2020), AGPCGPL CGD (2021) and GreenCell (2022).
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the AIIB, the multilateral bank. The borrower is filtered on economy = "India" in AIIB's own data file. Jin Liqun was AIIB president from 2016 to January 2026, so he held the office when SCMP reported him on 2021-06-04. Narrative id narrative:1 is index 1 of the narratives array, and its text matches the claim. No identity mismatch.
verdicts.baseRate: AIIB-wide approvals more than doubled from 2019 to 2020 (US$4.08bn to US$9.30bn) because of the COVID-19 Crisis Recovery Facility. So India's "more than double 2019" does not set India apart; every major borrower rose. The better measure is India's share of all AIIB approvals: 20.1% (2019), 21.0% (2020), 21.9% (2021), 29.4% (2022). That is flat or rising through the tension window, so the conclusion holds. The share then falls to 10.3% (2023), 14.0% (2024), 16.5% (2025) and 14.5% (2026 so far), as AIIB's lending grew and spread to other members. This later fall belongs in the strongest case. The fleet's control (UPA vs NDA borrowing) does not apply, because AIIB only started lending in 2016, all under the NDA government.
verdicts.denialFound: This is not an accusation against a named party, so there is no denial to find. The parties' own on-record positions support the narrative's verdict. Jin Liqun (SCMP, 2021-06-04) said AIIB "kept loans to India when border tensions escalated last year, despite facing pressure at home" (https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-economy/article/3136109/china-backed-aiib-maintained-loans-india-during-border). An anonymous Indian official, quoted from Mint (July 2020) in The Diplomat: "I don't see any structural change in our engagement with AIIB because of our tensions with China" (https://thediplomat.com/2021/06/amid-tensions-with-china-india-proceeding-with-aiib-funded-projects/).
verdicts.innocentReading: The simple explanation for the weak-case facts: nonsovereign cancellations are routine. Sponsors refinance elsewhere or projects fail to close, and all four cancelled India deals were small private deals (US$20.5m to US$75m) while sovereign lending carried on. The CPRR delay fits ordinary state-level land acquisition and procurement delays, and the appraisal review was completed on August 27, 2020, after the clash. The 2023–24 dip fits AIIB spreading its lending across more members after COVID. None of it needs a political freeze.
verdicts.reason: The narrative survives. All three sources say what it says. AIIB's own data file reproduces the yearly figures exactly: US$820m (2019), US$1.95bn (2020), US$1.95bn (2021) and US$1.87bn (2022), plus US$1.64bn in 2025 and the US$1bn policy loan approved July 16, 2026. The Diplomat (Iwanek, 2021-06-14) says: "I did not come across evidence of any project being halted due to government intervention, let alone because of the border tensions." SCMP reports Jin saying AIIB kept its India loans. The weak-case facts also check out: four cancellations and a 34-month CPRR gap. "Unsupported" is a verdict we inferred ourselves, so the right tier is analytic, backed by documented portal data. It is not refuted. The "more than double" framing needs a caveat, because AIIB-wide approvals also more than doubled and US$500m of 2020 came before the clash.
verdicts.corrections: 1) The tier field says "unsupported", which is not a valid tier. Set tier to "analytic" and keep "unsupported" as the narrative status. The underlying approval figures can be cited as documented from the AIIB portal. 2) strongestCounter: note that the 2020 figure of US$1.95bn includes US$500m approved May 7, 2020, before the clash. Post-clash 2020 approvals were US$1.45bn: CARES US$750m on 2020-06-16, HDFC US$200m on 2020-09-24, and RRTS US$500m in Oct 2020. 3) Add a base-rate line: AIIB-wide approvals went from US$4.08bn (2019) to US$9.30bn (2020), so the better measure is India's share of the total, which was 20.1% / 21.0% / 21.9% / 29.4% for 2019–22. 4) strongestCase: add that India's share fell to 10–16% of AIIB approvals in 2023–26, and that the CPRR appraisal review was completed on 2020-08-27, after the clash. 5) Add the CPRR project page (already in the record's srcs) to the claim's srcs list, since it backs the 34-month figure.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: ADB's portfolio (2016–21) and AIIB's approvals (2017–26) did not track the party in power at the Centre. ADB CPS Final Review (April 2022), para 222 area: "Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Bihar have been the top-three states that received highest share of the ADB program in 2016-2021." Who governed those states in 2016–21: Rajasthan was BJP (Raje) until Dec 2018 and INC (Gehlot) from Dec 2018, so INC for about 3 of the 6 years. The narrative's strongestCounter says "under Congress for five of those years", which is wrong. MP was BJP until Dec 2018, INC Dec 2018–Mar 2020, then BJP again, so BJP for about 4.5 of 6 years. Bihar was ruled by the JD(U)-RJD-INC Mahagathbandhan until July 2017 and by the JD(U)-BJP NDA after that. So the three top ADB states were mostly BJP- or NDA-run during the window. The ADB list is not a clean counterexample on party. What carries it is the party-neutral income rule. That rule ("overall ADB lending to the lower income states would be 40-50% of the total ADB lending to India") comes from CPS 2013–2017, which was drawn up in the UPA period, so it came before the 2014 change of government. AIIB dates: the Andhra Pradesh approvals are all 2017–18, under TDP, so "TDP then YSRCP" is not shown by approval dates. The Tamil Nadu 2017 approval fell under AIADMK. Kerala (LDF) got approvals in 2021, 2021 and 2024. West Bengal (TMC) in 2019 and 2022. Punjab (INC) in 2021. Karnataka, Bangalore Metro, in 2017 under INC (Siddaramaiah). Chennai approvals in 2023 fell under DMK.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match. The ADB document is the India Country Partnership Strategy Final Review 2016–2021 (evaluation-document 832171), and AIIB's all-projects-data.js entries are filtered to economy "India". One caveat: ADB's measure is "share of the ADB program" (the active portfolio, which includes loans approved before 2016), not new approvals in the window. The claim's phrase "top recipients" should be read as portfolio share.
verdicts.baseRate: Both lenders deliberately spread lending across many states, so any single state receiving loans says little about party. ADB's 2016 split was 57% of the active programme to 17 lower-income states, 12% to 6 higher-income states and 31% to national agencies. AIIB's sovereign state-level approvals cover BJP/NDA states (Gujarat, Assam, MP 2018, Haryana, Maharashtra, Manipur, AP under TDP) and opposition states (Kerala LDF, West Bengal TMC, Punjab INC, Karnataka INC, TN DMK). No per-capita or income-band normalisation was done, as the narrative itself admits. So the positive hypothesis is neither shown nor disproved, and "unsupported" is the right verdict. There is a real mechanism that could make the hypothesis plausible: state external borrowing needs DEA clearance. But no lender document or party allegation found here tests it.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. No party is accused. The search found no specific allegation that DEA blocked ADB, AIIB or World Bank loans to an opposition state. Kerala's "financial blockade" complaint (Deccan Herald, https://www.deccanherald.com/amp/story/india%2Fkerala%2Fwe-are-not-asking-for-charity-kerala-cm-pinarayi-vijayan-alleges-financial-blockade-by-centre-3842098) is about borrowing limits and KIIFB, not multilateral loans.
verdicts.innocentReading: The allocation follows ADB's income-band rule set in CPS 2013–17 (drawn up under UPA): 40–50% goes to lower-income states. AIIB largely co-finances with the World Bank and ADB, and states opt in with their own proposals. State demand and project readiness, not the party at the Centre, explain where the loans go.
verdicts.reason: The narrative survives as an "unsupported" verdict. Both sources confirm its core: the ADB review names MP, Rajasthan and Bihar as the top three states for 2016–21 and gives the 40–50% lower-income-state rule, and AIIB's list includes opposition-run states at the time of approval (Kerala LDF, West Bengal TMC, Punjab INC, Karnataka INC, TN DMK). No evidence of a party effect was found. However, the ADB half of the counter is overstated. Two of the three top states were BJP- or NDA-run for most of the window, and Rajasthan was INC for about 3 years, not 5. So the ADB evidence rebuts the hypothesis through the income rule, not through party composition.
verdicts.corrections: 1. strongestCounter: replace "Rajasthan under Congress for five of those years" with "Rajasthan under Congress from Dec 2018 (about 3 of the 6 review years); MP was BJP-run except Dec 2018–Mar 2020; Bihar was NDA-run from July 2017". 2. Claim text: change "Rajasthan (INC 2018–23)" to "Rajasthan (BJP to Dec 2018, INC after)", and say the rebuttal rests on the income rule, not on the party mix. 3. Say that ADB's measure is "share of the ADB program" (active portfolio), not new approvals. 4. Say that the 40–50% lower-income-state rule comes from CPS 2013–2017, drawn up in the UPA period, which is the pre-2014 control. 5. AIIB: change "Andhra Pradesh (TDP then YSRCP)" to "Andhra Pradesh (TDP, 2017–18 approvals)", and add Karnataka (INC, 2017 Bangalore Metro) as an opposition-state example. 6. Keep "No per-capita normalisation done" and the whatWouldChangeThis falsifier. Treat the status as analytic, and name the DEA state-borrowing clearance as the mechanism a real test would have to look at.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as "ADB exited its 2014 ReNew equity (US$50m, facility 7406, approved 2014-05-16) in 2016 with 'satisfactory returns'". This fails. The cited CPSFR (April 2022) gives the ReNew exit twice, in para 65 and in Appendix 2 para 17: "ADB exited the investment in 2018 with above-average financial returns." The 2016 "satisfactory returns" sentence belongs to the next paragraph (66 / App. 2 para 18), which is about Welspun Renewables Energy: "...before it was acquired by Tata Power Renewables Energy which is also one of the leading renewable energy companies with a total capacity of about 3 GW as on 31 December 2021. ADB exited the investment in 2016 with satisfactory returns." Tata Power bought Welspun in 2016, which fits. So the correct record is ReNew exit 2018, "above-average", and Welspun exit 2016, "satisfactory". For Avaada, the CPSFR says ADB had a "successful exit ... in July 2021". Other dates check out: Avaada PDS approval 22 Feb 2019; ReNew equity 2014; Vyoman 2025.
verdicts.identityTest: Entity misattribution. The "2016, satisfactory returns" exit belongs to Welspun Renewables Energy (now in Tata Power Renewable Energy), not ReNew Power Ventures. The error is also in claim adb-aiib:c030's "d" field. The other identities hold. PDS 52126-001 names Avaada Energy Pvt Ltd (sponsor Avaada Ventures Pvt Ltd), funded by OCR equity of INR 1,753.16m and LEAP equity of US$25m. PDS 47926-014 names ReNew Private Limited, sponsors GS Wyvern Holdings Ltd and "Sumant Sinha & Cognisa Investments". Adani Green is confirmed absent from AIIB's all-projects-data.js (re-fetched over HTTP/1.1, 213 KB, zero "adani" hits). ADB site search renders results in JavaScript and returned nothing even for "renew", so ADB absence is a negative search, not a verified null.
verdicts.baseRate: ReNew is not unique. The CPSFR says ADB was the anchor equity investor in three Indian renewable platforms at once: ReNew, Welspun Renewables and Avaada. Together they held more than 14% of India's installed solar and wind capacity at end-2021, and ADB exited all three. ADB India nonsovereign lending 2016–21 was 89 transactions, 42 of them in energy, and 86% of the energy ones were renewable. AIIB has 26 India nonsovereign entries across several sponsors (Hero Future, Ayana, Avaada and others). Repeat lending to a proven sponsor is the ordinary DFI pattern. Symmetry: the same lens applied to Welspun/Tata or Avaada gives the same "favoured sponsor" picture, so it does not single out one tycoon. The record also undercounts ReNew. The CPSFR says ADB "committed to providing $540 million (including from LEAP) debt to the company across several projects that included $50 million of critical liquidity support ... during COVID-19". The file records only about US$98.6m (2016 SPVs), US$100m (Ostro) and US$331m (2025, which is after the CPSFR), so "five times" is too low for ReNew exposure.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; not asked. No ADB, AIIB or ReNew response exists because no named party making the "subsidy channel" allegation has been identified. The narrative has no proponent source, which makes it a possible strawman, and the file should say so. Web search budget was exhausted this session, so I could not look for contrary reporting.
verdicts.innocentReading: Domestic banks had hit their power-sector exposure limits and long-tenor debt for renewables was scarce (CPSFR para 16 and following). ADB's private-sector arm therefore took anchor equity in several early-stage platforms and lent to the same sponsors again as they grew. Offtake came from competitively auctioned SECI and state PPAs. ADB exited at a profit (ReNew 2018 above-average; Welspun 2016 satisfactory; Avaada 2021 successful). An equity investor earning above-average returns and exiting is the opposite of a subsidy on the equity leg. What remains unanswered is whether the debt pricing was below market, and no loan rate is in hand.
verdicts.reason: The claim's own source says something different from the claim. The CPSFR sentence "ADB exited the investment in 2016 with satisfactory returns" is about Welspun Renewables; for ReNew the report says "ADB exited the investment in 2018 with above-average financial returns." Separately, "all recorded deals at market-based OCR pricing" is not supported. Every loan claim in the file has ratePct null. Neither cited source (PDS 52126-001, the CPSFR) states pricing. Three of the deals include LEAP money, the JICA-funded Leading Asia's Private Infrastructure Fund, which is not OCR: US$25m in Avaada per the PDS, and LEAP portions in the 2016 ReNew SPVs and in Vyoman. The AIIB loan is not "OCR" at all. The overall judgment (the subsidy narrative is unsupported) probably survives, and the corrected facts, above-average returns and exits from all three anchor platforms, strengthen the counter. But the text as written contains a misattributed fact and a universal claim nobody checked, so it cannot pass. "Speculative" is not a contract tier. A narrative evaluation is our own inference, so the tier is analytic with an innocentReading.
verdicts.corrections:
1. narrative:3 strongestCounter and claim adb-aiib:c030 "d": replace "ADB exited the 2014 ReNew equity in 2016 with 'satisfactory returns'" with "ADB exited the ReNew equity in 2018 'with above-average financial returns' (CPSFR para 65; App. 2 para 17). The 2016 'satisfactory returns' exit was Welspun Renewables (para 66)." Add "ADB exited Avaada in July 2021."
2. Replace "every recorded deal is at market-based OCR pricing (not concessional)" with "Recorded ADB deals are OCR nonsovereign plus LEAP (JICA-funded, ADB-administered) tranches. AIIB lends from its own ordinary capital. Interest rates were not found in any source read (ratePct null), so below-market pricing is neither shown nor excluded." Move pricing into whatWouldChangeThis as the open test.
3. strongestCase: add the CPSFR statement that ADB "committed to providing $540 million (including from LEAP) debt" to ReNew, including US$50m COVID-19 liquidity support. Change "five times" to "at least five engagements; CPSFR puts committed ADB debt at US$540m by 2021". Add the Avaada figures: US$33m OCR plus US$33m LEAP.
4. Symmetry: note that ADB anchored three platforms (ReNew, Welspun/Tata, Avaada), not one.
5. Adani Green: write "no AIIB record (data file checked); no ADB record found in a negative search (ADB search is JS-rendered, not exhaustive)".
6. Change status/tier "speculative" to tier "analytic" with status "unsupported". Record that no named proponent of the narrative was identified and that no party was asked.
7. The compact srcs cite only 52126-001 and the CPSFR. Neither supports the pricing clause, and the Adani-absence clause needs the AIIB data file URL added.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: Japan (JICA, on behalf of the Government of Japan) lends to the Government of India, 1958 to 2025, more than ADB, AIIB and the World Bank. There is no tenure or ownership window to test, because the actor is a state lender over its whole history. The problem is the comparison window. JPY 6.978 tn is a cumulative total since 1958. ADB's US$63.8bn runs from 1986 and AIIB's from 2016. World Bank IBRD plus IDA lending was about US$104bn by end-2015 (IndiaSpend/Business Standard) and is reported at about US$142bn cumulative by 2026. The periods in the comparison do not match. The MAHSR tranche V date (2023-12-21) is correct.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass on the lender: JICA is the Government of Japan's ODA agency and the Government of India is the borrower, as the 2023-12-21 press release names them. It is looser on the instrument. The embassy sentence is "Cumulative ODA commitments exceed JPY 6.978 trillion". Those are ODA commitments, which cover loans, grants and technical cooperation, and they are commitments rather than disbursements. The claim's "Japan lends ... JPY 6.978 tn" turns that into loans only.
verdicts.baseRate: "More cheaply" does not single Japan out. Bilateral concessional ODA loans (JICA, KfW, AFD) are almost always cheaper in nominal terms than ADB OCR or AIIB sovereign loans, which are priced at SOFR plus a spread. Well over 80% of bilateral concessional lenders share this, so it is a feature of the instrument, not of Japan. "Far more" fails on scale. At about Rs 0.58/JPY, JPY 6.978 tn is about Rs 4 lakh crore. ADB alone is about Rs 5.3 lakh crore (the file's own claim c056 says this) and the World Bank is roughly twice ADB. Japan's cumulative total is smaller than ADB's alone and much smaller than all the multilateral banks together. Symmetry control (Chinese official finance vs Japanese ODA, per SPEC): the file's symmetryCheck already runs this and finds the Japan lens at least as tied. That is consistent and does not rescue the "fewer conditions" leg.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. JICA, the Embassy of Japan and MoF-DEA were not asked. The claim is a comparative narrative, not an accusation, so no denial is expected. The absence is the record.
verdicts.innocentReading: Japan is India's largest bilateral lender. That is a different category from multilateral lenders, and the embassy's sentence says exactly that. Its loans carry low nominal yen rates because concessional ODA is priced that way. MAHSR is reported at 0.1%, 50 years, 15-year grace (railwaypro, Deccan Herald, CFA). But the loans are yen-denominated, so India carries yen-appreciation risk, and the effective cost is not simply the coupon. Technology tying on MAHSR (Shinkansen) is a condition the MDBs do not impose. JICA also co-finances MDB policy-based lending, which undercuts "fewer conditions". The boring picture: MDBs and Japan are comparable in scale, and trade price against tying.
verdicts.reason: The headline "far more" is refuted by the file's own figures and by public World Bank totals. At about Rs 0.58/JPY, JPY 6.978 tn (about Rs 4 lakh crore, and ODA commitments rather than loans only) is below ADB's cumulative US$63.8bn (about Rs 5.3 lakh crore) and well below the World Bank's US$104bn+ (by 2015). So the narrative's label "scale established" is wrong: the scale leg is refuted, not established. The narrative also says "price unverified", but the MAHSR terms (0.1%, 50 years, 15-year grace) are widely reported, so price is verifiable, and it favours Japan in nominal yen terms only. "Fewer conditions" cannot stand, because the narrative itself documents technology tying on MAHSR. Sources: the embassy page confirms "Cumulative ODA commitments exceed JPY 6.978 trillion" and "largest bilateral development partner". The JICA page confirms JPY 400 bn / INR 22,627 crore, "using Japan's Shinkansen technology". Neither source says anything about Japan compared with multilateral lenders on scale, price or conditions. The comparison is the project's own inference, so it belongs in the analytic tier.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Replace the narrative text with: "Japan is India's largest bilateral lender (ODA commitments > JPY 6.978 tn since 1958, all instruments). Cumulatively it is smaller than ADB (US$63.8bn since 1986) and the World Bank (>US$104bn by 2015). Its loans carry lower nominal yen rates (MAHSR 0.1%, 50y, 15y grace, per press reports) but carry yen-currency risk, and MAHSR is technology-tied to Shinkansen."
2. Set the scale leg's status to refuted, not established. Change the narrative status from contested to "largely refuted on scale; price leg true nominally; conditions leg reversed on MAHSR".
3. In strongestCase, change "Cumulative Japanese ODA to India" to "cumulative ODA commitments (loans+grants+TC)", as the embassy's wording has it.
4. Add the World Bank cumulative total (IndiaSpend/Business Standard 2016: US$104bn; WB Finances One) to strongestCounter and srcs.
5. Replace the "price unverified" gap with the reported MAHSR terms (0.1%/50y/15y), tiered reported until the loan agreement or a Parliament answer is opened. Add the yen-denomination currency-risk caveat.
6. In claim c056, confirm the embassy figure is labelled "ODA commitments", not "loans".
7. Keep the tier at analytic, because the comparison is the project's inference. Neither cited source makes it.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: JICA committed ¥1,050,000m to NHSRCL's MAHSR between 2017-09-15 and 2023-12-21, against a 2018 ex-ante cost that planned completion in Dec 2023. The JICA yen-loan database (fetched 2026-09-26, HTTP 200) gives these approval dates: Training Institute (STEP) 2017/09/15 ¥10,453m; tranche I 2018/09/28 ¥89,547m; II 2018/10/29 ¥150,000m; III 2022/07/25 ¥100,000m; IV 2023/03/29 ¥300,000m; V 2023/12/21 ¥400,000m. The 2018 ex-ante PDF (2018_ID-P277_1_f) says: "September 2018 – December 2025 (88 months in total ...). This project will be completed when all the facilities are put into service (December 2023)." The 2018-10-01 press release says: "Completion of project: December 2023 – when the facilities are put into service". Tranche V (2023-12-21) came after the Dec-2023 target had effectively passed with construction still under way, so the chronology holds. The claim's 'from' of 2018-09-28 leaves out the 2017 training-institute loan, although the sum includes it. JICA's own tranche IV and V ex-ante sheets (2022_ID-P309, 2023_ID-P316) say "Schedule: Under discussion between the Government of India and the Government of Japan", so the lender itself did not restate a completion date.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. Every loan names the executing agency as "National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited" and the borrower as "President of India" (ex-ante section 6). The lender is JICA and the project names match the MAHSR tranche series. A database search on "Ahmedabad" for India returns only tranches I–V, with no tranche VI. A web search also found no tranche VI, and reporting says Railways will absorb the cost escalation without another JICA loan. The committed total of ¥1,050,000m is therefore complete as of the database date.
verdicts.baseRate: Schedule slippage is non-discriminating. Large Indian central-sector rail and metro projects overrun their first schedules as a matter of course (MoSPI's infrastructure monitoring regularly finds a large share of central projects delayed), and HSR megaprojects outside India do too. A 58% lender share is ordinary for Japanese ODA to Indian rail: JICA typically finances the majority of the eligible cost on metros and the DFC. Nothing here separates MAHSR from its peers in a way that implies misconduct. The finding is descriptive arithmetic.
verdicts.denialFound: none found — not asked. No accusation is made, so no denial is due. The closest thing to a response on the record is JICA's own tranche IV and V ex-ante wording: "1,806,282 million yen (F/S basis. Currently under review between the Government of India and the Government of Japan, in light of subsequent changes in the economic environment and other factors.)" (https://www2.jica.go.jp/en/evaluation/pdf/2023_ID-P316_1_s.pdf). Separately, Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw is reported as saying the whole corridor will open by 2029 (https://www.deccanherald.com/amp/story/india%2Fentire-mumbai-ahmedabad-section-of-bullet-train-project-will-open-by-2029-ashwini-vaishnaw-3745449).
verdicts.innocentReading: The ¥1,806,282m figure is a feasibility-study estimate, and JICA says it will be fixed "through detailed designs". Yen loans are committed tranche by tranche as works are contracted, so signing tranche V after the original target date is how the instrument normally works, not a red flag. The delay is mostly explained by land acquisition in Maharashtra, and later cost escalation (reported ₹1.98 lakh crore versus about ₹1.1 lakh crore) is reportedly being absorbed by Railways rather than through more JICA borrowing. The claim's stated innocent reading matches this.
verdicts.reason: The arithmetic and the quoted facts all check out against primary JICA documents: 89,547 + 150,000 + 100,000 + 300,000 + 400,000 = 1,039,547, plus 10,453 = 1,050,000, which is 58.1% of 1,806,282. The Dec-2023 completion target is quoted verbatim in both the ex-ante evaluation and the 2018 press release, and tranche V's date of 2023-12-21 is in the loan database. The claim is correctly tiered as analytic: it is our own ratio, it carries an innocent reading, and it implies no wrongdoing. The claim cannot be refuted. The only issues are small framing points. First, the training-institute loan is a separate STEP project (2017) that the construction-cost denominator probably does not cover. Without it the share is 57.6%, which still rounds to about 58%. Second, the revised cost and completion date the record calls "not obtainable" are now available as reported figures.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Set 'from' to 2017-09-15, or state that the ¥10,453m training institute is a separate 2017 STEP loan. Give both ratios: 58.1% including it, 57.6% construction tranches only. (2) Add the JICA loan-database URL to the claim's srcs in the verifier task payload; the tranche amounts come only from it, not from the two PDFs listed. (3) Add https://www2.jica.go.jp/en/evaluation/pdf/2023_ID-P316_1_s.pdf as a source, showing JICA itself says the cost is "Currently under review" and the schedule is "Under discussion" (as of Dec 2023). (4) In 'd', replace "the current cost ... and the revised completion date were not obtainable" with the reported figures, marked as reported rather than documented until a Parliament answer is found: revised cost about ₹1.98 lakh crore (https://www.deccanherald.com/india/mumbai-ahmedabad-bullet-train-cost-may-rise-to-rs-198-lakh-crore-due-to-delays-3850615) and full opening by 2029 per the Railway Minister (Deccan Herald link above). (5) Say "planned full completion (all facilities in service) December 2023" rather than implying the whole 2018–2025 implementation schedule ended in 2023, because the 2018 ex-ante's 88-month schedule runs to Dec 2025.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim: China Development Bank lent US$750m (Facility I) to Reliance Communications Ltd, with the facility agreement dated 2008-06-04. RCom existed as a listed company in 2008 (CIN L45309MH2004PLC147531) and CDB was operating, so the dates fit. The AidData GCDF 3.0 row #42654 (read from the zip at the cited URL, which returns HTTP 200) gives Commitment Date 2008-06-04, marked Estimated: No, Maturity 10, and Last Loan Repayment Date 2018-06-02. RCom's own 2015 offering circular (SGX FileID=26422, p.128) confirms the date: "On June 4, 2008, we entered into a facility agreement with China Development Bank for availing a term loan of US$750 million". Newspapers reported the loan on 15-16 May 2008, before the agreement was signed. That is announcement versus signing and does not conflict. Problem: the record's "to":"2018" is wrong. The offering circular says "As at December 31, 2014, US$518 million of the principal amount was outstanding", and RCom went into insolvency in 2019. So 2018 was only the scheduled final maturity, not the date the loan was repaid.
verdicts.identityTest: The borrower matches. The offering circular is issued by "Reliance Communications Limited (Indian Corporate Identification No. L45309MH2004PLC147531)" and lists Facility I under "INDEBTEDNESS OF OUR COMPANY". The lender is named as China Development Bank. The AidData row names "Reliance Communications Ltd." as the direct receiving agency and "China Development Bank (CDB)" as the funding agency. One identity error sits in the claim's own text, where it says c037 is a facility to RCom. The same offering circular (p.168, under "INDEBTEDNESS OF RELIANCE TELECOM") says "On March 9, 2011, RTL entered into a facility agreement with China Development Bank ... ('China Development Bank Facility IV'). Our Company has guaranteed this facility." So the borrower on Facility IV is Reliance Telecom Ltd, a subsidiary, with RCom as guarantor. The parenthetical also leaves out Facility III (c036, US$1.33bn).
verdicts.baseRate: Borrowing in dollars from export-credit agencies or ECA-style lenders to pay for network equipment was close to universal among Indian GSM operators in 2008-11, so the edge is a plain loan and does not single RCom out for anything. RCom itself borrowed from Western ECAs on the same basis at the same time, and on cheaper terms. Business Standard (2008) reports "a $500-million loan from Export Development Corporation of Canada ... for the procurement of GSM equipment ... at an interest rate of LIBOR plus one", and describes it as bringing overseas GSM loans to "$1.25 billion, including an earlier $750 million received from China Development Bank". The offering circular (p.169) records an HSBC France COFACE-supported buyer credit of US$150m to RTL on 2008-04-23 at LIBOR+1.4%. Applying the same lens to French and Canadian ECA money gives the same picture: tied equipment credit to the same borrower in the same year.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial. The party confirmed the loan when asked. The Hindu/ET report of 16 May 2008, reposted at ismb-india.blogspot.com (one of AidData's listed sources), says: "When contacted, RCom officials confirmed the development ... all regulatory approvals have been received for this. The loan is for a 10-year period." RCom also disclosed the facility itself in its 2015 offering circular. The loan's existence and terms are not contested anywhere. CDB's later insolvency petition (c039) and the lenders' claims in RCom's insolvency process concern repayment, not whether the loan exists.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is an ordinary secured commercial term loan, not concessional: AidData classes it "OOF-like", with Level of Public Liability "Private debt". The borrower was a listed telecom company raising dollar capex debt for its nationwide GSM rollout. It did so at the same time as it borrowed from the Canadian and French export-credit agencies, and on less favourable terms (LIBOR+1.8% against LIBOR+1% and +1.4%). A state policy bank backing its home equipment vendors is standard export-credit behaviour, not something peculiar to China.
verdicts.reason: The core claim survives. It is confirmed by a primary filing, RCom's own 2015 offering circular for its 6.5% notes due 2020 (links.sgx.com FileID=26422, p.128): "On June 4, 2008, we entered into a facility agreement with China Development Bank for availing a term loan of US$750 million ... the aggregate of the applicable LIBOR and a margin of 1.8%." AidData #42654 says the same thing, and several independent outlets (The Hindu/ET, Financial Express, Business Standard, Domain-B) reported the US$750m CDB loan in May 2008 with RCom confirming it. Lender, borrower, amount, date and margin all match. The 10-year tenor and the GSM-rollout purpose come from contemporary press and AidData, not from the offering circular. Since a primary filing plus two or more independent outlets are in hand, the loan edge meets "documented" once the offering circular is added to srcs. The defects are in secondary fields, not in the edge: the "to" date, the c037 borrower in the parenthetical, and the framing of the benefit as "cheap" and Chinese-equipment-tied. The ₹ conversion (₹43/US$ → ₹3,225 cr) is plausible for June 2008 but is still indicative until the RBI reference rate is fetched.
verdicts.corrections: 1) srcs: add ["Reliance Communications Ltd, Offering Circular, US$300m 6.5% Senior Secured Notes due 2020 (2015), Description of Material Indebtedness, p.128", "https://links.sgx.com/FileOpen/Reliance%20Communications%20-%20Final%20OC.ashx?App=Prospectus&FileID=26422"]. Optionally also add the Business Standard EDC piece (https://www.business-standard.com/article/technology/rcom-takes-500-mn-loan-from-edc-canada-108072801070_1.html) as independent press. Then raise the tier to documented, with upgradeIf satisfied by the offering circular in place of the FY2008-09 annual report. 2) "to": change "2018" to null, and add to d: "scheduled final repayment 2018-06-02 (AidData); US$518m principal outstanding at 2014-12-31 (OC); not shown repaid, RCom entered insolvency 2019-02". 3) text parenthetical: change to "(c035 Facility II US$300m to RCom; c036 Facility III US$1.33bn to RCom; c037 Facility IV US$300m to Reliance Telecom Ltd, guaranteed by RCom; all 2011-03-09)". Separately fix c037.t to Reliance Telecom Ltd, or re-type it as an RCom guarantee, per OC p.168. 4) benefit.how: remove "cheap". verdicts.dateTest: Claim: China Development Bank lent RCom US$1.33bn under "Facility III", signed 2011-03-09. The date matches three sources. (1) AidData GCDF 3.0 row 54349, which I read myself from the xlsx in the zip: sheet GCDF_3.0 has "Commitment Date 2011-03-09", "Commitment Date Estimated: No". (2) RCom's SGX offering circular (links.sgx.com FileID=26422, p.130): "On March 9, 2011, we entered into a facility agreement with China Development Bank for availing a term loan of US$ 1,330 million ('China Development Bank Facility III'). As at December 31, 2014, US$1,237 million of the principal amount was outstanding." (3) RCom's Annual Report 2010-11 (BSE 532712), Directors' Report: "signed facility agreement with China Development Bank (CDB) on March 9, 2011". Both parties existed and were operating on that date, so there is no tenure problem. Drawdown: ₹3,000 cr (US$665m) by 2011-03-31, and the rest in FY2011-12.
verdicts.identityTest: The lender is China Development Bank (AidData "Funding Agencies: China Development Bank (CDB)", type State-owned Policy Bank), and the offering circular names the same lender. The borrower is Reliance Communications Ltd (BSE 532712, the issuer of the SGX offering circular and the annual report). AidData lists it as "Direct Receiving Agencies: Reliance Communications Ltd." with type Recipient Private Sector. Nodes fin:china-development-bank and fin:reliance-communications are correct. The direction lender→borrower is correct. The claim does not name the promoter or the group as the actor.
verdicts.baseRate: This is the only committed loan above US$1bn in AidData's India rows marked "Recommended For Aggregates = Yes". Its size therefore does set it apart. The fact that a telco borrowed dollars from a Chinese policy bank does not. RCom took four CDB facilities in 2008–12. Aircel (CDB US$462m, 2015) and Reliance Power/Sasan (CDB, China Eximbank and Bank of China, US$1.114bn, 2010) are comparable. Most of the 113 India rows are private-sector ECBs or MoU pledges, not sovereign loans. The SPEC control is Japanese ODA to Indian public projects. JICA's HSR tranches are larger, sovereign and tied, so a large foreign official credit is not unusual in itself. What is specific here is a Chinese state bank lending to a private borrower on collateral of assigned licences. Timing is UPA-era (2011), but this is a private ECB and no minister signed it, so the UPA/NDA control does not produce a political reading.
verdicts.denialFound: none found — not asked. None is needed: RCom disclosed the loan itself, in its 2010-11 annual report and its SGX offering circular. The later dispute is about repayment and enforcement (NCLT petition 2017–18, London guarantee judgment 2020). It is covered by other claims and does not challenge whether the loan existed. My web search budget was used up, so I found no further coverage for or against.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is ordinary external commercial borrowing. After the 2010 3G auction, RCom refinanced a large, lumpy spectrum payment to the government with long-dated dollar debt from CDB at LIBOR+3.25%. It secured the loan in the usual way for telecom project finance, with charges over plant, assignment of licences and pledged subsidiary shares. In this period CDB lent routinely to buyers of Huawei/ZTE equipment around the world. The lending was commercial and the borrower disclosed it. AidData's staff comment "probably used to stave off bankruptcy" is AidData's own inference, and the edge should not import it.
verdicts.reason: The core edge holds in RCom's own primary filings. The SGX offering circular gives US$1,330m, 9 March 2011, LIBOR+3.25%, "Facility III". The 2010-11 annual report gives "₹6,000 crore (US$1.33 Billion)". So the tier should go up from reported to documented, and the record's own upgradeIf condition ("RCom offering circular (SGX) loan note matched") is now met. Two parts of the text are wrong or overstated. (a) Purpose: the annual report splits the purposes. The US$1.33bn was "for refinancing 3G spectrum fee payment", while a separate "₹2,700 crore (US$600 Million)" (Facilities II+IV) was "for equipment imports from Chinese Vendors by the Company and Reliance Telecom Limited". AidData assigns both purposes to Facility III, and the claim copies that error. (b) The superlative "largest Chinese official credit to an Indian private borrower" is our own ranking, not AidData's wording. It is true only among committed rows (Recommended For Aggregates = Yes). The raw dataset has larger private-borrower rows that are pledges or MoUs and were never committed: Reliance Power US$12bn (#43106, 2010) and IndiGo/ICBC US$2.6bn (#42647, 2014).

Per the annual report, Facility III (US$1.33bn) was for refinancing the 3G spectrum fee. Add a note: "AidData attributes both purposes to Facility III; issuer's AR splits them."

4. Superlative: change to "the largest committed Chinese official loan to an Indian private borrower among AidData GCDF 3.0 rows recommended for aggregates (larger MoU pledges: Reliance Power US$12bn #43106, IndiGo/ICBC US$2.6bn #42647 are not committed loans)".

verdicts.dateTest: Written out: CDB, China Eximbank and ICBC lent RCom a US$925.2m term loan on 2012-02-22. The dates fit. RCom was a going, listed company in 2012 (CIN L45309MH2004PLC147531, printed in its 2015 SGX offering circular). All three banks were operating lenders. RCom's own filing, the 2015 SGX offering circular (https://links.sgx.com/FileOpen/Reliance%20Communications%20-%20Final%20OC.ashx?App=Prospectus&FileID=26422, p.136), says: "On February 22, 2012, we entered into a facility agreement with China Development Bank Corporation, Export-Import Bank of China and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited for availing a term loan of US$ 925.2 million ('ICBC Facility I')." The London judgment came later (2020-05-22). The Wire, quoting Justice Teare's order, dates the underlying loan to "February 2012". Nothing in the dates is out of order.
verdicts.identityTest: The borrower is right: Reliance Communications Ltd, the same company whose offering circular describes the facility. The lender node is only partly right. The facility had three lenders: CDB, China Eximbank and ICBC. AidData #56456 is CDB's share, #98825 is Eximbank's and #98826 is ICBC's. Each share (US$308.4m) is AidData's own equal-split guess ("Amount Estimated: Yes"). Putting s=fin:icbc on the edge with the whole ₹4,535 cr credits the entire syndicate to ICBC. There is a defensible reason ICBC's name leads: the facility is called "ICBC Facility I", and ICBC Mumbai Branch sued in London "on behalf of the three Chinese banks" (The Wire). But the edge as built overstates ICBC's own exposure by about three times.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not a discriminating fact. The claim implies no wrongdoing: it records a commercial foreign-currency loan (ECB) between private parties. In 2011–12 many Indian companies had FCCBs falling due and refinanced them with foreign-currency loans. Chinese policy banks had been lending to RCom since 2008: the same file records CDB Facilities I–IV. RCom was a large buyer of Huawei and ZTE equipment. Among RCom's own long-term foreign lenders by then, Chinese state banks were the norm, not the exception. The symmetry control already in the file compares JICA, US Ex-Im and DFC. It rightly finds that tied or secured export-style lending to private borrowers is what every export-credit agency does. What sets China apart is who it lent to and how those loans ended, not the act of lending.
verdicts.denialFound: No one disputes the loan. RCom disclosed it in its own offering circular. Anil Ambani disputed only the personal guarantee. The Wire, 2020-05-23 (https://thewire.in/business/uk-court-orders-anil-ambani-to-pay-717-million-to-chinese-banks-within-21-days), quotes his spokesperson: "the matter pertains to an alleged personal guarantee for a corporate loan availed by Reliance Communications Limited (RCom) in 2012 for global refinancing ... It is emphasised that it is not a personal loan of Ambani. ICBC ... made their claim based on an alleged guarantee that was never signed by Ambani and he has consistently denied having authorised anyone to execute any guarantee on his behalf." The claim's terms.conditions field already records this dispute.
verdicts.innocentReading: RCom had US$925.30m of FCCBs to redeem on 2012-02-27. Converting them into shares was not attractive, so it borrowed the same amount from its existing Chinese lender group five days earlier. The margin (LIBOR+4.75%) and the security it gave (plant, licences, subsidiary shares) are normal for a leveraged Indian telecom company borrowing in foreign currency at the time. This was an ordinary commercial refinancing, not a political or concessional transfer.
verdicts.reason: The core claim survives, and on stronger evidence than the claim cites. RCom's own SGX offering circular (a primary issuer filing, which AidData itself cites) confirms the date, the three lenders, LIBOR+4.75%, and the security, including the "assignment of 20 unified access service licences". The Wire confirms the London litigation over the "around $925 million" February 2012 refinancing loan. The FCCB purpose is not stated in either cited source. AidData says "repay its debts" and The Wire says "global refinancing". The same offering circular, though, shows the remaining FCCBs, "aggregating USD 925.30 million", were redeemed on February 27, 2012. That is five days after signing and matches the facility almost exactly. So the FCCB purpose is a well-grounded inference from two documented facts, not a quoted statement. The errors can all be fixed: an amount typo (925.5 should be 925.2), the whole syndicate's amount booked on ICBC alone, and a killIf that confuses principal outstanding in 2020 with the original principal. None of them overturns the edge.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Amount: change US$925.5m to US$925.2m. The offering circular p.136 and AidData's own description both say 925.2 (3 × 308.4 = 925.2); 925.5 is a typo in AidData's title. Recompute the ₹ figure: about ₹4,533 cr at ≈₹49/US$, still marked approximate.
2. Sources: add the RCom offering circular [ "Reliance Communications Offering Circular (SGX, 2015), p.136 'ICBC Facility I' and FCCB note 2.29(iii)", "https://links.sgx.com/FileOpen/Reliance%20Communications%20-%20Final%20OC.ashx?App=Prospectus&FileID=26422" ]. With a primary issuer filing in hand, upgrade the tier from reported to documented for the loan terms.
3. FCCB wording: change "refinancing RCom's FCCBs" to "signed five days before RCom redeemed US$925.30m of FCCBs on 2012-02-27 (same filing); AidData: 'to help Reliance Communications repay its debts'". The purpose is inferred from matching timing and amount; it is not stated in any source.
4. Node and amount: ICBC was one of three lenders. Either split into three edges (fin:cdb, fin:china-exim, fin:icbc) at about US$308.4m each, marked estimated per AidData's equal-split guess, or keep s=fin:icbc and change lab/d to say it is the lead-named lender and the London claimant for the syndicate, with the amount being the full facility and not ICBC's share. Also set benefit.confidence to estimated at the per-lender level. The AidData ID mapping is #56456 = CDB, #98825 = Eximbank, #98826 = ICBC.
5. killIf is wrong as written. US$549.8m was the principal still outstanding in 2020, and US$796m was outstanding at 2014-12-31 (offering circular). Neither can contradict the original US$925.2m principal. Rewrite it as "court record or RCom filing shows an original facility principal other than US$925.2m".
6. Text: change "the facility later litigated in London" to "Anil Ambani's personal guarantee of this facility was enforced in London (High Court, Teare J, 2020-05-22; US$716.9m)". The case was the banks against Ambani under the guarantee, not the banks against RCom under the facility.
7. The upgradeIf is largely met already: the offering circular has the facility's terms, although the Facility Agreement itself is not public.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim is that China Development Bank withdrew its NCLT Mumbai insolvency petition against RCom on Friday 2018-01-05. ET's datePublished is 2018-01-05T14:48 IST and it was updated 2018-01-06 07:31. The article reads: "China Development Bank (CDB) on Friday withdrew its insolvency filing against Reliance Communications (RCom)". 5 January 2018 was a Friday, so the date checks out. The filing date also checks out: "CDB ... had moved the National Company Law Tribunal last November", which matches from=2017-11. There is no tenure or ownership window to test, since both parties are institutions. The dates are consistent.
verdicts.identityTest: The source names both parties: "China Development Bank (CDB)" and "Reliance Communications (RCom)", described as "the Anil Ambani-owned telecom operator". The bench was NCLT Mumbai (Justices BSV Prakash Kumar and V Nallasenapathy). The nodes fin:china-development-bank and fin:reliance-communications match. The source does not give a CIN or LEI, but there is no ambiguity. One point needs care: the "accommodating" statement came from Senior Counsel Darius Khambatta, who "represented both companies", meaning CDB and Ericsson. It is counsel's explanation made in the tribunal, not a statement from CDB's management.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not discriminating as evidence of preference. In 2017-18, creditors often withdrew or held off IBC petitions when a debtor announced a lender-approved monetisation or SDR plan. The Section 12A regime, and withdrawals before admission generally, were routine. The rest of the RCom lender consortium (SBI-led JLF, Indian banks) was also waiting for the Jio asset sale at the same time. So CDB's forbearance is typical of RCom's secured creditors, not unusual behaviour by a Chinese state lender. The symmetric control holds too: Indian PSU lenders in the same JLF did not file at all. On forbearance, CDB was, if anything, more aggressive than domestic lenders, since it was the only financial creditor that filed.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial or contrary reporting was found. Neither CDB nor RCom disputes the withdrawal. RCom's regulatory filing that day said it was working "expeditiously" to close asset monetisation in "January-March". There is nothing to deny: the event is a matter of court record, and the article is written with both parties' positions stated. A second independent outlet was not checked because the session's web-search budget had run out.
verdicts.innocentReading: A secured creditor holding 37% of secured debt drops an IBC petition before admission because the debtor has a near-term plan (the Jio sale by March 2018) to pay lenders. That recovery is worth more than going into CIRP, and CDB kept the right to refile. ET also reports possible out-of-court settlement talks, including Chinese lenders reportedly taking 70% in Dhirubhai Ambani Knowledge City. That is ordinary creditor bargaining, not favouritism. The later RCom insolvency (c040) and the Chinese banks' 2019-20 suits against Anil Ambani's personal guarantee show that the forbearance was conditional.
verdicts.reason: I opened the single cited source (ET, 5 January 2018, by Devina Sengupta) with curl. It states every material element: the Friday 2018-01-05 withdrawal, Rs 11,460 cr dues, "37% of RCom's total secured debt", "accommodating" the asset-monetisation plan running to March 2018, the right to refile, the NCLT filing made the previous November, and the sale to Jio for under Rs 24,000 cr as part of the plan. There are no errors of date, identity or amount. It is one credible outlet with named sourcing (counsel in open court, the bench, and RCom's filing), so "reported" is the right tier. It is not "documented", because the NCLT withdrawal order was not read and no second outlet was confirmed.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Summary text: change "to accommodate RCom's asset sale to Reliance Jio" to "to accommodate RCom's asset-monetisation plan (wireless and real-estate assets, incl. spectrum/tower/fibre/MCN sale to Reliance Jio for under ₹24,000 cr) running to March 2018". The source frames the Jio sale as part of a wider plan, not the sole reason. 2) Attribute the "accommodating" rationale to CDB's counsel Darius Khambatta in the tribunal, not to CDB directly. 3) benefit.confidence is "documented" but the edge tier is "reported". Set it to "reported". 4) pred "enforce" is defined as agency→subject, and CDB is a creditor, not an agency. Either keep it with the lab making clear this is a creditor IBC petition that was withdrawn, or use a creditor-action predicate if the schema has one. 5) Optionally add ET's note of reported CDB and Chinese-lender talks on a 70% stake in Dhirubhai Ambani Knowledge City as context for a possible out-of-court settlement. Mark it "reported (ET earlier report)". 6) On c040 (outside this claim's scope): in Feb 2019 RCom's board decided to pursue resolution through NCLT, and admission came on Ericsson's petition in May 2019. Check the wording "filed for bankruptcy".

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as written: "RCom (actor) enforce against CDB (t), 2019-02". Two date problems. (1) The AidData dataset is internally inconsistent. Rows #54348, #54349 and #54350 say "In February 2019, Reliance Communications filed for bankruptcy as it was unable to sell assets to repay its debts". Linked row #56456 (the ICBC/CDB/CEXIM facility) says "Reliance Communications Ltd. entered bankruptcy and liquidation procedures on November 15, 2018". (2) The legal sequence differs from "entered insolvency February 2019". Ericsson's petition was admitted by NCLT Mumbai in May 2018 and then stayed by NCLAT and the Supreme Court. On 2019-02-01 RCom's board decided to pursue resolution through NCLT. NCLAT sent RCom back into CIRP on 2019-04-30. The interim resolution professional then asked for an exclusion of 13 months (2018-04-30 to 2019-05-30), and SBI shortlisted Deloitte as IRP on 2019-05-07 (Business Standard). "February 2019" therefore dates the board's decision to seek NCLT resolution, not the start of the insolvency process. It is fine as a colloquial date but should read "board decided to seek NCLT resolution, 2019-02-01; CIRP resumed 2019-04-30". There is no conflict with a tenure or ownership window, since both entities existed throughout.
verdicts.identityTest: Reliance Communications Ltd (BSE 532712) and China Development Bank Corporation match the names in AidData row #54350 ("CDB provides $300 million loan (Facility IV) to Reliance Communications"). No identity mismatch. However, the edge's node roles are wrong under CONTRACT.md. The rule is that `enforce` runs agency→subject. c040 sets s=fin:reliance-communications and t=fin:china-development-bank, so it asserts that RCom took enforcement action against CDB. Nothing in the source says that. The claim's own `d` admits the inversion ("direction here records the debtor default toward the lender").
verdicts.baseRate: This is not discriminating as a signal about Chinese money. Almost every secured lender to RCom was left unresolved at insolvency: SBI-led Indian banks, Ericsson, and the Chinese banks together held about ₹45,000 cr of debt. Of AidData's 113 India rows, the Chinese loans to private Indian borrowers are Reliance Communications, Reliance Power/Sasan, Lanco, Adani Power Maharashtra, Essar and Aircel. Several of those borrowers (RCom, Lanco, Aircel, Essar Steel) went through the IBC, so reaching insolvency is common among Chinese-financed Indian private telecom and power borrowers. It is also common among their Indian-bank-financed peers from 2008–2012. SPEC control: the Japanese ODA comparison does not apply because JICA lends to the Union and to public-sector projects, which do not go through IBC insolvency. The honest comparison is Indian PSU-bank exposure to the same borrower, and SBI's stake in RCom was larger in absolute terms.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed on the core fact, because RCom itself announced it. RCom's 2019-02-01 board statement said it was opting for NCLT resolution because asset sales had not gone through after about 18 months. That matches AidData's wording. No CDB statement was found; CDB was not asked. AidData's line that "creditors, including the CDB, are now suing the Reliance Communications" is an unsourced staff summary. That denial belongs on the London-judgment claim, not this one.
verdicts.innocentReading: RCom was an over-leveraged telecom operator hit by the Jio price war from 2016. It borrowed from Chinese policy banks, Indian PSU banks and vendors alike. When the Jio asset sale collapsed, every creditor class was stranded. CDB's position is ordinary secured-creditor exposure in a commercial telecom failure, with nothing specific to China. CDB had earlier withdrawn its own NCLT petition (c039) to let the asset sale proceed.
verdicts.reason: The source does say what the text says. AidData #54350: "In February 2019, Reliance Communications filed for bankruptcy as it was unable to sell assets to repay its debts ... Many creditors, including the CDB, are now suing the Reliance Communications to recover unpaid debts." Reported tier is correct for AidData under CONTRACT.md. The edge as encoded still fails on three counts. (a) `enforce` is agency→subject, but s=RCom and t=CDB claims that RCom enforced against CDB. That is the opposite of the source, and the `d` field concedes it. (b) "supersedes c039" is wrong. c039 (CDB withdraws its NCLT petition, 2018-01-05, ET) is a separate, earlier event that is still true. Marking it supersededBy c040 would drop a documented forbearance event (₹11,460 cr, benefit to RCom) from the graph. The two are consecutive links in one chain, and neither replaces the other. (c) "Entered insolvency February 2019" is imprecise. February 2019 is the board's decision; CIRP resumed on 2019-04-30. AidData's own linked row #56456 gives 2018-11-15. The fact survives, but the edge in its current form does not.

Link them with a note such as "follows c039". 2) Fix the direction: either swap to s=fin:china-development-bank → t=fin:reliance-communications with pred `enforce` (CDB is a creditor with its claim in CIRP), or preferably re-predicate. The RCom insolvency is best carried as `enforce` s=NCLT Mumbai (agency) → t=fin:reliance-communications, with CDB named in `d` as a secured creditor. 3) Relabel it "RCom board opts for NCLT resolution (2019-02-01); CIRP resumed after NCLAT order 2019-04-30; CDB facilities (AidData #42654/#54348/#54349/#54350/#56456) unresolved". That would support documented tier for the event itself; the CDB claim amount stays reported until the CoC list is found. 6) killIf should be "NCLT/CoC record shows CDB claims fully settled or assigned before 2019-02", not "None".

verdicts.dateTest: The claim is that the Commercial Court (Teare J) declared Anil Ambani's personal guarantee binding and ordered him to pay US$716,917,681.51 on 22 May 2020. The article is dated 2020-05-23 05:35 IST and says the order came "on Friday", which is 22 May 2020. It also says "interest outstanding as of May 22". The underlying event was a refinancing loan of about $925m to RCom in February 2012, a period when Anil Ambani controlled and chaired RCom, so the dates line up. The earlier conditional order by Waksman J on 7 February 2020 and the March 2021 trial date that was cancelled also match the record. Small fix: the source label says "The Wire 2020-05-22", but the article was published on 2020-05-23 IST. The judgment date of 2020-05-22 is correct.
verdicts.identityTest: The source names the parties clearly. The defendant is "Reliance Group chairman Anil Ambani" and the court is "Justice Nigel Teare ... Commercial Division of the High Court of England and Wales". The claimant is "Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Ltd Mumbai Branch, on behalf of the three Chinese banks", which were ICBC Mumbai, China Development Bank and Exim Bank of China. The nodes fin:high-court-england-wales and energy:anil-ambani are the right entities. One problem: benefit.who lists only fin:icbc, but the article says the recovery goes to all three banks, with ICBC Mumbai suing on their behalf.
verdicts.baseRate: Does not apply. This edge records a single court ruling, not a pattern inferred from shared traits, so there is no set of comparable entities to test against. The symmetry controls (UPA/NDA etc.) are also irrelevant, because a court order means the same thing whoever the defendant is. The actor is a named individual, not a family, religion or ethnic group.
verdicts.denialFound: Found in the same source, and the record already holds it as c042. The Wire (PTI), https://thewire.in/business/uk-court-orders-anil-ambani-to-pay-717-million-to-chinese-banks-within-21-days: "ICBC ... made their claim based on an alleged guarantee that was never signed by Ambani and he has consistently denied having authorised anyone to execute any guarantee on his behalf"; "It is emphasised that it is not a personal loan of Ambani"; the amount will "reduce substantially" once RCom's insolvency is resolved; "the question of any enforcement in India does not arise in the near future". The spokesperson was asked for comment. I did not look for later reports of an appeal because the web-search budget was used up. The record's killIf says none was reported.
verdicts.innocentReading: The ruling holds regardless of any charitable reading. The only non-damning context is Ambani's own position: the loan was a corporate loan to RCom, he says he never signed or authorised the guarantee, and the final amount is to be "assessed subject to the outcome of the RCom Insolvency Action", so the $716.9m may come down. The claim wording should keep that point and should not describe the money as a personal loan.
verdicts.reason: I opened the source and pulled the full article text from the page's structured data (JSON-LD). It supports every figure in the claim: "the sum payable by the Defendant to the Claimant (banks) pursuant to the Guarantee is $716,917,681.51"; "It is declared that the Guarantee is binding on the Defendant"; Justice Nigel Teare; the three named banks; principal $549,804,650.16 + interest $51,923,451.49 + default interest $115,189,579.86; £750,000 costs; a 21-day deadline; and the RCom 2012 refinancing. The judge, date, currency, parties and direction of the edge are all correct, and the denial is recorded in c042. "Reported" is the right tier: this is one outlet carrying PTI wire copy that quotes the court order directly, and I did not obtain the order itself or a second independent outlet. The rupee figure is our own conversion and does not appear in the source. That makes it a precision issue, not grounds to refute.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Source label: change "The Wire 2020-05-22" to "The Wire (PTI) 2020-05-23", since the article went up 2020-05-23 05:35 IST. Keep from = 2020-05-22 as the judgment date.
2. benefit.confidence is "documented" but the edge tier is "reported". Lower it to "reported" to match.
3. benefit.who: list all three banks (ICBC Mumbai, China Development Bank, China Eximbank), or note that ICBC Mumbai sued on behalf of all three. At present only fin:icbc is named.
4. Rupee conversion: the ₹75.4/US$ rate is estimated, and the RBI reference rate in late May 2020 was about ₹75.6–76.0/US$. That would put the figure at roughly ₹5,420–5,450 cr, so write "≈₹5,400–5,450 cr (indicative)" or fetch the RBI rate for 2020-05-22. Keep "a" as indicative.
5. Add the source's caveat to d/text: the final amount is "assessed subject to the outcome of the RCom Insolvency Action".
6. The text says "summary judgment", but the source only states that the banks "sought the summary judgment" and quotes Teare J's order declaring the guarantee binding. Either write "order/judgment (on the banks' summary-judgment application)" or confirm the wording against the [2020] EWHC judgment on BAILII, which is also the upgradeIf path to "documented".

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as a sentence: Anil Ambani's spokesperson denied signing the ICBC/CDB/China Exim personal guarantee, on 2020-05-22. The source is The Wire, reproducing PTI. Its JSON-LD datePublished is 2020-05-23T05:35:40+05:30, which is Friday 22 May in London. The body says "A UK court on Friday directed…", so the statement was given on the judgment day. The claim's from=2020-05-22 is right. The facts inside the quote also agree with the source: the loan was ~US$925m, taken by RCom in February 2012 for global refinancing, and Ambani was its promoter and the guarantor at that time. Nothing is anachronistic.
verdicts.identityTest: The speaker is "A spokesperson for Anil Ambani", which is unnamed but attributed to the principal. The subject is Anil Ambani, chairman of Reliance Group and the defendant in ICBC (Mumbai Branch) & ors v Ambani, Commercial Court, Justice Nigel Teare. It is not Mukesh Ambani and not a family node. So energy:anil-ambani, a person node, is the correct denier. The target, claim:bilateral-china:c041, is the same judgment. The contra direction (denier to claim) follows the CONTRACT. The claim frames no family, religion or ethnicity.
verdicts.baseRate: Not discriminating, and it doesn't need to be: this is a contra edge that records a response, not an accusation. Almost every promoter-guarantor facing a guarantee enforcement disputes it. The denial proves nothing about the facts. It only fulfils the duty to publish the response.
verdicts.denialFound: This record is itself the denial. Quote from The Wire/PTI, 2020-05-22 (https://thewire.in/business/uk-court-orders-anil-ambani-to-pay-717-million-to-chinese-banks-within-21-days): "It is emphasised that it is not a personal loan of Ambani. verdicts.reason: I opened the source, and every element of the claim text appears nearly word for word in the article: "never signed by Ambani", the RCom 2012 corporate loan for global refinancing, and enforcement in India "does not arise in the near future". The date, actor and target all match. There is one outlet, carrying PTI copy with an attributed spokesperson, so the correct tier is reported. It is not documented, because syndicated PTI copy does not count as two independent outlets. I found no ground to refute it. One risk remains: shown without context, the edge could suggest the denial still stands. In fact it was made after the court had already ruled against it, on the same day.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: CDB extended a US$200m buyer's credit to Lanco Infratech in 2010. Lanco was an operating listed company from 2010 to 2012. It entered CIRP in 2017 and was ordered into liquidation in 2018, so the lender, the borrower and the loan window all overlap. The "2010" is weaker than the claim makes it look. The AidData row says "Commitment Date (MM/DD/YYYY)": "2010-01-01" and "Commitment Date Estimated": "Yes", so it is a placeholder year. Two sources point to a later date. Business Standard, "Chinese banks will fund Lanco plans" (URL id 111012700002, 27 Jan 2011), quotes CFO J Suresh Kumar: Lanco "is in negotiations with Chinese banks, expects to clinch the loans by September". Lanco's own release of 26 Nov 2012, which I saw only as a search snippet (MarketScreener mirror), says "China Development Bank has already sanctioned USD 200 million Buyers' Credit for Amarkantak 3 & 4, Babandh and Vidarbha". The sanction therefore probably falls between 2011 and Nov 2012, not in 2010. The date is soft but the loan is not refuted.
verdicts.identityTest: The lender is China Development Bank, a state policy bank, and it matches AidData's "Funding Agencies". The borrower matches AidData's "Direct Receiving Agencies: Lanco Infratech Ltd." (Recipient Private Sector). One caveat: buyer's credits for these plants would normally be booked at the project companies (Lanco Amarkantak Power Ltd, Lanco Babandh Power Ltd, Lanco Vidarbha Thermal Power Ltd). AidData codes the loan to the parent, so the edge is at group level. The node has no CIN; all identity fields are null. The node uses a fin: prefix for an Indian borrower company, but I found no existing co:/inventory id for Lanco in the repo, so no id collision.
verdicts.baseRate: This kind of loan was common, not distinctive. In the 2009–13 boom, Chinese equipment-tied export and buyer's credit was normal for Indian private coal developers that bought Chinese BTG (boiler, turbine, generator) sets: Reliance Power Sasan (CDB/ICBC/BOC), Adani Power Maharashtra, Lanco, Essar, KSK and others. That is well above the 80% line for developers using Chinese boilers. By the file's own AUDIT, Lanco ranks about 6th by size among AidData's private Indian borrowers. The claim alleges no wrongdoing, so a common property does no harm as long as the edge is not used to imply one.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; I did not ask anyone. No denial is needed: the borrower announced the sanction itself in its 26 Nov 2012 release. Lanco Infratech is in liquidation, so there is no live company to answer.
verdicts.innocentReading: Lanco had ordered six 660 MW supercritical units from Dongfang Electric (BS, Jan 2011). Chinese ECA and policy-bank buyer's credit is the usual financing that comes with Chinese equipment, and it is often cheaper than Indian rupee project debt. The plants' delays are put down to land acquisition and financing problems (CEA Broad Status Aug 2020, quoted in the AidData row), not to the lender. The same lens applied to the SPEC control (JICA loans to Indian public projects, or US Ex-Im and DFC tied loans) gives the same neutral reading: tied export credit to a buyer of home-country equipment.
verdicts.reason: The AidData GCDF 3.0 zip is reachable: HTTP 200, 28.6 MB. Row #53777 says what the claim says: "In 2010, China Development Bank and Lanco Infratech Limited ... signed a $200 million buyer's credit agreement to the support the construction of Units 3 & 4 (1320 MW) of Lanco Amarkantak ..., the Babandh Power Station (1320 MW), and the Vidarbha Power Station (1320 MW)", and "all have encountered major delays". AidData marks 2010 as estimated, and contemporaneous reporting (Jan 2011: still negotiating) plus Lanco's Nov 2012 wording put the sanction around 2011–12. That also makes the ₹900 cr figure, which uses the ₹45/US$ rate, likely too low. At 2011–12 rates (about ₹47–55/US$) it would be roughly ₹950–1,100 cr. Fix the date and rupee fields; do not kill the claim.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: Adani Power owned Adani Power Maharashtra Ltd (APML) as an SPV/subsidiary at the time of the 2013-04-22 Tiroda syndicated loan. The source supports this for 2013. The edge has from=null and to=null, so as written it says the ownership is still open, and that is wrong. APML was one of six wholly owned subsidiaries (APML, Adani Power Rajasthan, Adani Power (Mundra), Udupi Power Corp, Raipur Energen, Raigarh Energy Generation) amalgamated into Adani Power Ltd. The board approved the scheme in March 2022. The appointed date was 2021-10-01. The scheme was declared effective in Feb/Mar 2023. IndiaInfoline, quoting the exchange filing, says "the Scheme is now effective from the Appointed Date, i.e. October 1, 2021" (https://www.indiainfoline.com/news/mergers-acquisitions/adani-power-and-6-subsidiaries-merge). APML has not existed as a separate entity since then. The edge must be closed.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity matches. AidData GCDF 3.0 rows #53783 and #54345 name "Adani Power Maharashtra Ltd (APML)" as the Direct Receiving Agency, typed "Recipient Joint Venture/Special Purpose Vehicle". The Description says: "On April 22, 2013, Adani Power Maharashtra Ltd (APML) — a special purpose vehicle and subsidiary of Adani Power — signed a $480 million syndicated loan agreement with China Development Bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), and the Standard Chartered Bank for the 3300 MW Tiroda Thermal Power Project." Neither entity record carries a CIN (both identity blocks are null), so the match rests on name plus project, and that is unambiguous here.
verdicts.baseRate: Nearly all Indian private thermal IPPs (close to 100%) are built through a project SPV owned by the sponsor, e.g. Reliance Power/Sasan Power, Lanco/Lanco Babandh, CLP India/Jhajjar. This fact does not single Adani out. The edge is a structural ownership link, not an insinuation, so a high base rate does not defeat it. It does mean the edge carries no inferential weight beyond linking the loan to the listed parent.
verdicts.denialFound: none found — not asked. Nothing is in dispute: Adani Power's own filings describe APML as a wholly owned subsidiary until the merger.
verdicts.innocentReading: Using a ring-fenced SPV to hold a project and raise limited-recourse debt is standard in Indian power project finance. The subsidiary relationship implies nothing beyond the corporate structure, and the SPV was later folded into its parent in a routine internal consolidation.
verdicts.reason: The AidData row says what the claim says: APML is "a special purpose vehicle and subsidiary of Adani Power". Nothing refutes the ownership fact. The edge is not refuted, but it is badly time-bounded. It has no from/to dates, even though APML was amalgamated into Adani Power (appointed date 2021-10-01; effective 2023), and it says "percentage not stated" when Adani Power's filings describe APML as wholly owned. Reported is the right tier for an AidData-only source. It becomes documented once the Adani Power exchange filing or annual report subsidiary schedule is attached.

Add "a": 100 if the tier is raised on the filing. verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: Essar, with CDB and PetroChina International, signed a US$1bn funding-for-fuel financing agreement on 2013-05-21. The date checks out. AidData #42618 gives "Commitment Date 2013-05-21, Estimated: No". Reuters, via Business Standard ("Last Updated: May 21 2013 | 6:45 PM IST"), says "Essar Energy Plc on Tuesday signed…", and 21 May 2013 was a Tuesday. ET (dated 22 May 2013) also says "on Tuesday signed". The signing happened in Mumbai during Li Keqiang's visit. The signatories held these posts at the time: Ravi Ruia (Essar Group vice-chairman), Hu Huaibang (CDB chairman 2013–2018) and Lihua Wang (CEO, PetroChina International). from=2013-05-21 and to=null are right for a pledge that has no recorded drawdown. Rupee conversion: the rate in May 2013 was about ₹54.5–55.5 per US$, so ≈₹5,500 cr is fine as an indicative figure, and the record already flags it.
verdicts.identityTest: This passes at node level but the signing entity in the text is wrong. AidData says "India's Essar Oil signed a three-way MoU". The two contemporaneous outlets both name the London-listed parent. ET: "Essar Energy, the London-listed parent of Essar Oil — on Tuesday signed a three-way unique debt financing deal with China Development Bank (CDB)… and PetroChina to raise $1 billion of external commercial borrowings". Reuters/BS: "Essar Energy Plc on Tuesday signed a $1 billion financial cooperation agreement with the China Development Bank and PetroChina International Co. Ltd." Essar Oil comes into it only as the refinery and product supplier ("debt would be backed by a supply of refined fuels by Essar Oil, a subsidiary of Essar Energy"). The target node energy:essar is the Essar Group node, so the edge still points at the right group. The lender is also a partial fit. AidData's structured field says "Funding Agencies: Unspecified Chinese Government Institution", with PetroChina as the implementing agency. CDB is named only in the AidData title and description, but ET and Reuters both name CDB, so s=fin:china-development-bank is supported.
verdicts.baseRate: 23 of the 113 AidData India rows (20%) have status "Pipeline: Pledge", so being a pledge does not make this row unusual. 54 of 113 rows go to "Recipient Private Sector" borrowers. Only two India rows are dated 2013-05-21, both from the Li Keqiang Mumbai visit (#42618 Essar and #42620 SDP Services), and both are pledges. What does set this row apart is the resource-backed structure: ET calls it "the first oil-for-loans agreement between an Indian corporate and CDB". Among the India rows this is effectively 1 of 113, so it discriminates in structure only. It says nothing about wrongdoing, and the claim does not suggest any.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. Essar was not asked. None is needed, because the claim makes no accusation; it records a signing that the company publicly staged during a Premier's visit. What remains open is whether the ECB was ever drawn. I found no follow-up in the Reuters/BS or ET reporting, and the OIES 2016 paper on Chinese loans-for-oil does not mention Essar or India.
verdicts.innocentReading: This was a headline agreement signed for a state visit, with only a pledge behind it. Details "were not immediately known" (Reuters). Pricing and the mechanics of crediting shipments against the loan "still needed to be worked out", and ET's officials saw it as a "preamble to a larger strategic deal" involving PetroChina equity in Vadinar. That is ordinary export-prepayment or offtake-backed ECB financing for a refiner exporting Euro-5 gasoline. It is the same thing Western trading houses and ECAs do, and the claim's own framing, "resource-backed pledge, not a commitment", already reads it this way.
verdicts.reason: The core facts hold up in the AidData row I extracted and in two independent contemporaneous outlets (ET 2013-05-22, Reuters via Business Standard 2013-05-21): the date, the US$1bn, the three parties, the Mumbai signatories, the 7–10-year Vadinar product exports and the 2–3× coverage. The claim itself calls this a pledge, and AidData agrees ("Status: Pipeline: Pledge; Recommended For Aggregates: No"). So nothing refutes it, and 'reported' is the right tier for a pledge with no drawdown evidence. Four field-level errors remain. (1) The signatory is Essar Energy plc, not Essar Oil. (2) "Non-binding MoU" is not in any source: AidData says "MoU", while ET and Reuters say "financing deal" and "financial cooperation agreement". The only property it carries, a borrower that later became insolvent, is shared by 3 of the 4 largest private borrowers from Chinese banks in India (RCom, Aircel and Lanco; Sasan is the exception). The finance SPEC's Japanese-ODA control does not apply directly because this is private telecom debt.
