verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: "PN3 (DPIIT, 17 Apr 2020, announced by PIB 18 Apr 2020) screens FDI from land-border countries. It did not cover CDB and China Eximbank debt, which had stopped before 2016." In the local AidData GCDF 3.0 India extract (113 rows), CDB's last commitment is #54342, Aircel, US$462m, 2015-03-27. China Eximbank's last is #96694, Essar, 2013. So "receded by 2016" holds for the policy banks, and it predates PN3 by four years. The date test fails on the causal clause in `d`: "largely stopped by 2016 as RCom, Aircel and Lanco defaulted". Those insolvencies came after lending stopped (Lanco NCLT 2017, Aircel 2018, RCom 2019; CDB's NCLT petition against RCom was Nov 2017). Lending cannot have stopped because of later defaults, although distress may have been visible earlier. Chinese state commercial banks (BOC, ICBC) kept lending: 2016 is US$653m across 8 rows (Air India, GAIL, HPCL, SBI HK, RIL, IL&FS), which is more than 2015's US$527m aggregate-eligible. Rows for 2017–2020 are small (US$80m, 0, US$101m, US$91m). The record gives `to: null`, but PN3 was amended by Press Note 2 (2026 Series), issued 15 Mar 2026 after the 10 Mar Cabinet decision. It allows stakes up to 10% non-controlling via the automatic route (Business Standard, 16 Mar 2026).
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. `fin:press-note-3-2020` is DPIIT Press Note No. 3 (2020 Series), amending para 3.1.1 of the Consolidated FDI Policy 2017. PIB PRID 1615711 matches, dated 18 Apr 2020. `fin:china-development-bank` matches the "China Development Bank (CDB)" Funding Agency in the AidData rows. No person, family or ethnic group is framed as the actor.
verdicts.baseRate: In the AidData India extract, 0 of 113 rows are equity or FDI. By flow type: 82 loans, 14 grants, 5 technical assistance, 4 scholarships, 8 "Vague TBD". So "PN3 does not touch these flows" is true of 100% of the file's records, which makes it a scope statement rather than a discriminating finding. Symmetry control (Japanese ODA): the same lens gives the same result. PN3 does not govern JICA sovereign loans either, and Japan is not a land-border country. The lens treats both lenders alike. Screening peers from 2020: Australia's FIRB threshold cut to $0, EU guidance of March 2020, and Germany, Italy and Spain tightening screening. These show pandemic-era screening was common. But India's rule is keyed to country (land border), unlike Australia's general threshold.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable in the usual sense: no party is accused, and the claim clears one. The government's own stated reason is in the PIB release: "for curbing opportunistic takeovers/acquisitions of Indian companies due to the current COVID-19 pandemic" (https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1615711). I found no statement from DPIIT, RBI or CDB saying whether PN3 applies to debt; none was asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: PN3 was written to stop distressed-price takeovers of Indian firms. It reached equity and beneficial ownership, the channel for takeovers. It was later notified under the FEMA (Non-debt Instruments) Rules. Plain loans fall under the separate RBI ECB framework. Chinese policy-bank lending to India had already stopped by 2015. That fits the lenders' exposure to a weak group of borrowers, but it also fits bilateral politics after 2014 (the 2014 CDB/Eximbank pledges for SBI, ICICI and a Gujarat park were never carried out). Neither source says why the lending stopped.
verdicts.reason: The core inference survives. The PIB text quoted verbatim amends FDI policy para 3.1.1: "an entity of a country, which shares land border with India or where the beneficial owner of an investment into India is situated in ... can invest only under the Government route". Its para 3.1.1(b) covers "transfer of ownership of any existing or future FDI". Nothing in it reaches non-convertible loans. The AidData sheet confirms CDB/Eximbank commitments ended in 2015/2013 and that no India row is equity. Three parts fail as written, and each needs fixing: (1) `d` says "every" AidData record is debt, but only 82 of 113 are loans; (2) "on commercial grounds" / "as RCom, Aircel and Lanco defaulted" is found in neither source and fails the date test, since the insolvencies (2017–19) came after the last commitments (2013–15); (3) calling PN3 a "general" rule is inaccurate, because it applies only to land-border countries, and it stayed in force until the March 2026 amendment. With these fixed it holds as analytic; it cannot be documented because the "does not govern debt" point is our own reading of scope.
verdicts.corrections: Change text: replace "which had largely receded by 2016 on commercial grounds" with "whose last commitments in AidData are 2015 (CDB, Aircel) and 2013 (China Eximbank); the reason is not stated in either source". Change "a general pandemic-era screening rule" to "a country-keyed (land-border) screening rule adopted during the 2020 market crash, stated aim to curb opportunistic takeovers". Change d: replace "Every Chinese official-finance record ... is debt" with "82 of 113 AidData India rows are loans, the rest grants/TA/scholarships/vague; none is equity or FDI". Replace "largely stopped by 2016 as RCom, Aircel and Lanco defaulted" with "stopped after 2015; the borrowers' insolvencies (Lanco 2017, Aircel 2018, RCom 2019) came later, so defaults did not cause the stop, though earlier distress may have contributed". Add that Chinese state commercial banks (BOC/ICBC) continued syndicated lending to Indian PSUs and RIL in 2016–2020 (e.g. #98207 Air India US$309m in 2016; #98602 ONGC Videsh 2020), and say whether PN3 covers them (it does not). Say "FDI (equity and compulsorily convertible instruments)" instead of "equity", and note that PN3 would apply if a Chinese lender converted debt to equity or took equity under an IBC resolution plan. Record the amendment: Press Note 2 (2026 Series), issued 2026-03-15, allows ≤10% non-controlling stakes via the automatic route; cite Business Standard 2026-03-16 (https://www.business-standard.com/economy/news/dpiit-amends-press-note-3-to-ease-fdi-norms-for-border-countries-126031600356_1.html). Add a source for the debt/non-debt line, the FEMA (Non-debt Instruments) Amendment Rules 2020 notification. Change killIf to: "any Chinese policy-bank loan to an Indian borrower after 2015, or any DPIIT/RBI instruction applying PN3 to ECB lenders".

It returns: 2023 World 33,478,898,362; Japan 24,222,457,725 (72.35%); Russia 4,109,957,000; Germany 3,750,162,876; France 1,227,754,450; US 26,202,000; China null. 2014: World 21.04bn, Japan 13.70bn (65%), China null. 2010: World 25.99bn, Japan 17.23bn (66%), China 0. verdicts.identityTest: Partial fail on two points. (1) The edge source is fin:jica, but the IDS figure is 'Japan', the whole creditor country. That can include JBIC and other Japanese official lenders, not only JICA. (2) The claim says China 'appears only as a commercial lender to private firms'. The AidData GCDF 3.0 file the record cites contradicts this. I downloaded the zip and extracted the 113 India rows. By direct-receiving-agency type, 54 loans went to the private sector, but 10 went to state-owned companies, 7 to state-owned banks and 1 to another state-owned company. Examples: #98207, ICBC's share of the US$970m Air India Dreamliner sale-and-leaseback (Aug 2016). AidData codes it Guarantee Provided = Yes, Guarantor = Government of India, and quotes 'The Government of India issued a guarantee for this deal'. #42657, a CDB US$200m loan agreement with India Exim Bank (17 Sep 2014; not recommended for aggregates). #98602, BOC's part of the ONGC Videsh syndicate (2020). Also BOC/CCB/ICBC loans to SBI, PNB, Bank of India, REC, IRFC, GAIL and HPCL (2004–2017). The record's own 'd' field already says 'private/SOE borrowers', so the headline text contradicts its own detail. The sovereign guarantee on the Air India deal also means 'China records no sovereign claim' holds only for the IDS *bilateral* series. It does not hold for Indian public-sector or publicly guaranteed borrowing in general.
verdicts.baseRate: The property is discriminating. Among India's South Asian neighbours, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal and the Maldives all carry China as a material PPG bilateral creditor in IDS. India's zero is unusual. Japan being the top bilateral creditor is common across Asian ODA recipients (Bangladesh, Vietnam, Philippines, Indonesia), so the Japan half on its own is not distinctive. The UPA/NDA control makes no difference: Japan's share was 66% in 2010 (UPA), 65% in 2014 and 72% in 2023 (NDA), and China's bilateral line was nil throughout.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The claim accuses no one and implies no wrongdoing, so no party was asked and there is no response to record. The primary confirmation named in upgradeIf (the DEA Status Report on India's External Debt) is still unretrieved.
verdicts.innocentReading: The record's own innocent reading holds: India does not take sovereign Chinese loans and never joined the BRI, and Chinese banks lent where Indian buyers took Chinese equipment. There is also a classification point. IDS files the Chinese state banks that did lend to Indian public entities (ICBC, BOC, CCB) as commercial creditors, so they never show up in the bilateral line. Part of China's 'absence' is therefore an artefact of how creditors are classified, not a complete absence of public-sector exposure.
verdicts.reason: The numbers survive: IDS confirms Japan US$24.22bn of US$33.48bn (72%) in 2023, and China null or zero in 2010, 2014 and 2023. The conjunction does not survive. 'Appears only as a commercial lender to private firms' is contradicted by the AidData dataset the record itself cites. Chinese state banks lent to Indian SOEs and state banks (ONGC Videsh, GAIL, HPCL, REC, IRFC, SBI, PNB, Exim Bank of India), and one ICBC exposure (Air India, 2016) carried a Government of India guarantee. The absolute 'only … private firms' and the unqualified 'no sovereign claim' are wrong as written. Keep the claim as analytic only after the text is corrected.
verdicts.corrections: text: replace 'China records no sovereign claim in 2010/2014/2023 and appears only as a commercial lender to private firms' with 'China records no PPG bilateral (official-creditor) claim in IDS for 2010/2014/2023; in AidData GCDF 3.0 its lending to India is state-bank commercial credit, mostly to private firms (54 of 82 loans) but also to SOEs and state banks (ONGC Videsh, GAIL, HPCL, REC, IRFC, SBI, Exim Bank of India), including ICBC's share of a GoI-guaranteed Air India lease (2016, #98207).' lab: change 'China absent from sovereign books, present only as commercial lender to private firms' to 'China absent from India's PPG bilateral creditor line; present as a state-bank commercial lender, mainly to private firms'. s: change fin:jica to a Government of Japan node, or add a note that the IDS 'Japan' figure is all Japanese official bilateral debt and not JICA alone. Add the 2010 and 2014 Japan shares (66%, 65%) to 'd' as the UPA/NDA control. Add to innocentReading that IDS classifies ICBC, BOC and CCB as commercial creditors, which by construction keeps them out of the bilateral series. Tier stays analytic; upgradeIf (the DEA Status Report) is unchanged.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: "RCom (IBC 2019), Aircel (IBC 2018) and Lanco (CIRP 2017) entered insolvency after borrowing from CDB/China Eximbank in 2008–2015; Sasan kept servicing." The loans come before each insolvency (RCom 2008/2011/2012 → 2019; Aircel 2015-03-27 → 2018; Lanco 2010 → 2017), so the dates pass. Two problems remain. First, the only evidence that Sasan kept servicing is the US Ex-Im OIG report, which records the first US$28.4m payment to US Ex-Im in March 2015. That is a different lender from the Chinese syndicate, and nothing in the record covers Sasan's servicing from 2015 to 2020, even though the edge runs to 2020. Second, the label says Sasan was "refinanced" while the text says it "continued servicing". These contradict each other and neither is sourced for the Chinese tranche.
verdicts.identityTest: Borrowers match the AidData "Direct Receiving Agencies" field: Reliance Communications Ltd. (#42654, 54348–50, 56456, 98825–6), Reliance Power Ltd. (#54362, 92020, 92021 = Sasan), Aircel Ltd. (#54342) and Lanco Infratech Ltd. (#53777). Identities are fine. The claim fails on how the set was chosen. It is not "the four largest". AidData India extract, recommended-for-aggregates rows only. (1) Counting only policy banks (CDB + China Eximbank): RCom ≈US$3,296m, Reliance Power/Sasan US$667m, Aircel US$462m, Essar Energy US$300m (#96694, China Eximbank 2013), Sistema Shyam US$255m (#67448), then Lanco US$200m in sixth place. (2) Counting all Chinese banks: RCom US$3,605m, Sasan US$1,000m, Aircel US$462m, APML US$333m (#53783/54345), SSTL US$325m, Essar US$300m, RIL US$220m, Vedanta US$210m, then Lanco US$200m in ninth. Lanco only reaches the top four by adding the US$600m Anpara/Himavat MoU (#53778), which AidData codes "Pipeline: Pledge" and marks not for aggregates. If pledges count, IndiGo (US$2.6bn), SRM Energy (US$1.19bn), IDBI (US$1.2bn) and Essar (US$1bn) all rank above Lanco. The claim text also says "policy banks", but the RCom figure of US$3.6bn and Sasan's "≈US$1bn Chinese share" both include ICBC or BOC, which are commercial banks. The definition changes partway through the sentence.
verdicts.baseRate: With a set chosen consistently, the "3 of 4" figure does not hold. Top four by policy-bank lending (RCom, Sasan, Aircel, Essar Energy): 2 in IBC (RCom, Aircel), Sasan unverified after 2015, and Essar Energy plc itself never went through Indian IBC. Top four by all Chinese banks (RCom, Sasan, Aircel, APML): 2 of 4. APML (Adani Power Maharashtra, Tiroda) never entered IBC. Every recommended private borrower of US$100m or more (10 entities: RCom, Sasan, Aircel, APML, SSTL, Essar, RIL, Vedanta, Lanco, CLP): 3 in formal insolvency (RCom, Aircel, Lanco), or 4 if you count SSTL, which RCom absorbed in 2016–17 and which went into RCom's 2019 IBC. That is roughly 30–40%, a moderate rate that is worth publishing, not 75%. For context, other lenders to the same borrowers lost money too: SBI-led Indian consortia (RCom, Aircel, Lanco) and SEK/Nordic Investment Bank (co-lenders on Aircel). The losses do not single out Chinese lenders.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial exists, and none is needed. The claim is our own analysis of lender outcomes and accuses nobody. No party was asked. The one linked response in the record, the Ambani spokesperson's statement in The Wire on 2020-05-22 that the RCom guarantee was never signed (c042), concerns the guarantee, not this ratio.
verdicts.innocentReading: The record's own innocent reading holds and is stronger than the claim itself. Chinese policy banks lent equipment-tied credit to the most leveraged 2G-era telecom groups and merchant coal-power groups of 2008–2015. Those two sectors collapsed for everyone after the 2012 2G-licence cancellation (Supreme Court, February 2012), the Jio tariff war (2016–17) and the coal-block cancellations and shortages (2014). Indian public-sector banks lost more to the same borrowers. Where Chinese banks lent to regulated or diversified borrowers (Adani Power Maharashtra with a PPA, CLP Jhajjar, RIL, Vedanta, and the SOEs Air India, GAIL, ONGC and SBI), they did not end up in insolvency. So the result reflects which sectors they lent to, not anything about the banks as lenders.
verdicts.reason:
The main error is the denominator. "The four largest Indian private borrowers from Chinese policy banks" is false as stated. In AidData GCDF 3.0 (the claim's own source), Lanco's US$200m ranks sixth among policy-bank borrowers and ninth among borrowers from all Chinese banks. It only enters the top four by counting a non-binding US$600m pledge, and applied consistently that rule would bring in larger pledges such as IndiGo, SRM, IDBI and Essar. With the correct top four (Essar Energy or APML in place of Lanco), 2 of 4 entered insolvency, not 3. A mixed selection rule produced the headline ratio. Other problems:
- None of the four cited sources supports Lanco's 2017 or Aircel's 2018 insolvency. AidData #53777 says only that Lanco's projects were "delayed … financial problems", and #54342 says nothing about Aircel's insolvency.
- The evidence that Sasan kept servicing is a 2015 payment to US Ex-Im, not to the Chinese lenders.
- The label ("refinanced") contradicts the text ("continued servicing").
The underlying facts (RCom, Aircel and Lanco insolvencies) are true public record, so the claim should be restated as an analytic with the correct denominator, not killed.

Insolvency: RCom 2019, Aircel 2018, Lanco 2017, plus SSTL through its merger into RCom; the others did not enter IBC or are unverified. Or (b) all ten private borrowers of US$100m or more, giving 3 (or 4) of 10. 2. Do not count Lanco's #53778 pledge unless all pledges are counted. 3. Use "policy banks" or "Chinese banks" consistently. RCom's US$3.6bn includes ICBC's US$308m, and Sasan's US$1bn includes BOC's US$333m. 4. Fix the label: change "one refinanced (Sasan)" to "Sasan: no insolvency; servicing of the Chinese syndicate after 2015 unverified". verdicts.dateTest: Restated: "China (state/state banks) holds India's sovereign in a debt trap, 2010–2023." The IDS API returns all three years (lastupdated 2025-12-03). 2010: counterpart China = 0. 2014 and 2023: no China value (null). The AidData Chinese loan rows run 2004–2020 and peak in 2008–2016, so the IDS years cover that window. The windows line up, and the date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: The WB API is India (IND), series DT.DOD.BLAT.CD, "PPG, bilateral (DOD, current US$)", so the actor and instrument are correct. A caveat: that series only covers bilateral official creditors. PPG debt owed to Chinese state commercial banks (ICBC, BoC) would be recorded under the commercial-bank or private-creditor series, not DT.DOD.BLAT.CD. So "no recorded sovereign bilateral debt" is true but narrow. It does not show zero PPG exposure to Chinese state banks. On AidData identity, of the 66 India loan rows that AidData recommends for aggregates: 49 are "Private debt", 15 are "Other public sector debt" (SBI HK, GAIL, HPCL, ONGC Videsh, REC, IRFC, India Exim, PNB, Bank of India, Union Bank), and 1 is "Central government-guaranteed debt". That last row is AidData 98207: ICBC's estimated US$309.43m share of the US$970.29m sale-and-leaseback for nine Air India 787s, Aug 2016. AidData's description says: "The Government of India issued a guarantee for this deal." The claim's phrase "commercial loans to private firms" is therefore wrong for 16 of 66 rows (24%).
verdicts.baseRate: For almost every large economy, bilateral official debt is mainly owed to Japan, Germany and France, and India fits that pattern. It is the opposite of the BRI-debtor profile: in AidData's debt-distress cases, China is typically the largest bilateral creditor. Figures checked in the IDS API for 2023: Japan US$24.22bn of US$33.48bn = 72.3% (confirmed); Russia 4.11; Germany 3.75; France 1.23. For 2014 and 2010 Japan's share was also about 65%, with China 0 or absent. So the "debt trap" property does not hold for India in any year tested. Chinese-bank participation in PSU syndications is small (US$5–90m each, about US$0.5bn in total) and routine for Indian PSUs borrowing offshore.
verdicts.denialFound: This is a debunk, so there is no accused party to answer. The relevant official position is India's own: it declined the 2017 Belt and Road Forum and has not endorsed BRI in SCO declarations (e.g. the 2023 New Delhi Declaration). Sources: MEA Rajya Sabha answer on OBOR (https://www.mea.gov.in/rajya-sabha.htm?dtl%2F39055%2Fquestion+no1043+one+belt+one+road+initiative=) and WION/Tribune reporting on SCO statements. verdicts.innocentReading: The debunk is itself the boring reading. Chinese state banks lent to Indian private and PSU borrowers as ordinary commercial or ECA-style syndicate lenders, at LIBOR-plus. When private borrowers failed (RCom, Aircel, Lanco), the loss sat with the Chinese banks and with promoters' guarantees, not with the Indian sovereign. The strongest version of the anti-debunk case is not covered in this narrative: India is the largest borrower of the Beijing-headquartered AIIB, though India is also its second-largest shareholder (documented in adb-aiib.json). That is multilateral lending, not bilateral Chinese debt, and does not show a debt trap. It should still be named in strongestCase so the debunk is tested against its best counter.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated claim: JICA and the Government of India (borrower: President of India; executing agency NHSRCL) signed tied ODA loans for MAHSR on 0.1%, 50-year, 15-year-grace terms, 2017-09-15 to 2023-12-21. The JICA loan database, fetched 2026-09-26, gives these rows: Training Institute ¥10,453m (2017-09-15, STEP, Tied); MAHSR (I) ¥89,547m (2018-09-28, Tied); (II) ¥150,000m (2018-10-29, Tied); (III) ¥100,000m (2022-07-25, Tied); (IV) ¥300,000m (2023-03-29, Tied); (V) ¥400,000m (2023-12-21, Tied). The ex-ante evaluation for tranche I is dated to the L/A of 2018-09-28. All signings fall within the windows of the actors involved: the 2015 Joint Statement, the E/N of September 2017, and Jaitley and then Sitharaman as Finance Minister. Every tranche carries 'Tied', so the string is not limited to tranche I. The dates pass.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match. The ex-ante evaluation names 'Project for Construction of Mumbai – Ahmedabad High Speed Rail (I)', 'Borrower: President of India', 'Executing Agency: National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited'. The 2017-09-15 release names 'Project for the Construction of Training Institute for Mumbai-Ahmedabad High Speed Rail … 10,453 … 0.1 … 50 … 15 … Tied', with the other three loans in the same package 'General untied'. The amount needs a fix. '¥1.05tn' equals the five construction tranches (¥1,039,547m) plus the training institute (¥10,453m), which is exactly ¥1,050,000m. Neither cited source states that total; it is a sum taken from the JICA database. The record's own entity label says '¥1,039,547m across five tranches', so the file is internally inconsistent unless the narrative says the training institute is included.
verdicts.baseRate: JICA loan database, India, all sectors: 346 rows fetched 2026-09-26. Counting by number of loans, about 17 are Tied, Japan tied or STEP (about 5%). The rest are General, Partially or plain untied, apart from 8 rows from March 2021 whose tying status did not parse. So 'most India loans are untied' holds by count. Counting by value after May 2014, tied loans make up about ¥1.55tn of about ¥4.7tn (about one-third), and MAHSR is most of that. MAHSR is not the only tied programme, however. Dedicated Freight Corridor Phase 1 and 2 have several tied tranches: 2009-10-27, 2010-03-31 (STEP), 2010-07-26 (STEP), 2013-03-28 (STEP), 2016-03-31, 2020-03-27 and 2022-03-31, about ¥0.62tn in total. Chennai Metro Phase 2 (I) and (II), 2018-12-21 and 2022-03-31, about ¥149bn, are also Tied. Within flagship Japanese rail loans to India, tying is the norm rather than something unique to MAHSR. SPEC control (UPA against NDA): the UPA-era DFC loans of 2009–13 were already STEP-tied. The same lens gives the same reading for both governments, a disclosed commercial tie, so the claim holds under the symmetry check.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial exists, and none is needed. The party imposing the condition, JICA, states it in its own evaluation and releases. Railways Ministry reporting (Deccan Herald / India Infra Hub, 'No loan renegotiation with Japanese on bullet train project', https://indiainfrahub.com/news/no-loan-renegotiation-with-japanese-on-bullet-train-project-says-railways/) confirms the loan terms stand. Press reporting also says Japan agreed to relax STEP conditions so Indian firms could bid for some packages. Neither JICA nor NHSRCL was asked by this platform (not asked).
verdicts.innocentReading: A tied loan at 0.1% over 50 years is the standard Japanese STEP bargain. Japan finances a first-of-its-kind technology transfer (Shinkansen) on near-grant terms in exchange for Japanese prime contractors or content. The 2015 Joint Statement committed both governments to using Japanese HSR technology, and the tie is openly disclosed in every JICA release. The same arrangement already applied to UPA-era DFC loans and to Chennai Metro Phase 2. It is a routine commercial feature of Japanese ODA and says nothing about political leverage over either government.
verdicts.reason:
The claim's central sentence is confirmed verbatim in the primary source. JICA ex-ante evaluation, §3(9): 'the government of Japan and the government of India have agreed that the tied loan will be made for the fund procurement condition in order to utilize the technology and knowledge of Japan for the development.' The JICA database and releases show 'Tied' on all six MAHSR loans and 'General untied' on the other loans in the same signing packages. The 0.1%/50-year/15-year-grace terms are in both releases. Nothing in the chronology, identity or source chain breaks the claim, and the symmetry control holds. Four smaller defects need correcting, but none of them refutes the claim:
(a) The narrative implies MAHSR (plus the training institute) is the exception. In fact the DFC Phase 1 and 2 tranches (about ¥0.62tn, largely signed under UPA) and Chennai Metro Phase 2 are also Tied.
(b) ¥1.05tn includes the ¥10.45bn training institute and is a database sum, not a figure from either cited source.
(c) 'Reserving core Shinkansen packages for Japanese suppliers' in strongestCounter is not in the evaluation. It paraphrases STEP rules, which were reportedly relaxed so Indian firms could bid for some civil packages.
(d) 'Near-grant' overstates for general-untied loans at 1.2–1.5% over 30 years and for the DFC locomotive loan at Yen LIBOR+10bp. 'Not a political one' is our own inference and should be labelled analytic.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: JICA lent to the Government of India (borrower "President of India", executing agency NHSRCL) the MAHSR tranches I–V plus the training institute, 2017-09-15 to 2023-12-21, at 0.1%, 50 years, 15 years' grace, tied. The JICA search page confirms all six rows: 2017/09/15 ¥10,453m; 2018/09/28 ¥89,547m; 2018/10/29 ¥150,000m; 2022/07/25 ¥100,000m; 2023/03/29 ¥300,000m; 2023/12/21 ¥400,000m. Each row reads "0.1 50 15 Tied". One exception: the training institute's consulting portion has a 10-year grace, not 15. The ex-ante evaluation says "This project will be completed when all the facilities are put into service (December 2023)" and schedules the ex-post evaluation for "After the start of the high-speed rail operation (from 2023 onwards)". So "delay" is documented. The Railways Minister now puts first service (Surat–Bilimora) at August 2027 and the full corridor at 2029, which means no ex-post evaluation can exist yet. The "no ex-post evaluation yet" part passes the date test.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The JICA rows name "National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited" as executing agency on every tranche, and the ex-ante names "Borrower: President of India". This matches fin:nhsrcl and min:ministry-of-finance in the file. No family, religion or ethnicity is framed as the actor.
verdicts.baseRate: Tied procurement is discriminating within JICA's India book. MAHSR tranches and the STEP training institute are "Tied", while most other India loans in the same releases are "General untied" (c007). The ex-ante evaluation gives the reason: "the government of Japan and the government of India have agreed that the tied loan will be made ... to utilize the technology and knowledge of Japan". Cost overrun and delay are not discriminating. Large Indian rail and metro projects and foreign HSR exports routinely slip. The SPEC control (Chinese official finance) produces the same "vanity loan" reading for China's HSR export: Jakarta–Bandung ran on China Development Bank dollar loans at about 2%, had an overrun and needed a top-up loan. On cost and delay the lens is symmetric, and harsher on the Chinese terms. My own grant-element arithmetic for 0.1%/50y/15y grace (semi-annual, equal principal): 85% at the DAC 7% LMIC discount rate, 76% at 5%, 44–58% at 2–3%, 25% at 1%. So "near-grant" holds against rupee or DAC benchmarks but not against yen-market rates. That is exactly the yen-risk caveat.
verdicts.denialFound:
No direct response to the "vanity" label from NHSRCL or JICA; NHSRCL.in resets the connection (curl exit 35, verified 2026-09-26), so it was not asked. The government's position:
(1) PM Modi, 2017-09-14: Japan is "gifting this to her, almost for free" (ANI and Business Standard, https://www.business-standard.com/article/current-affairs/modi-lauds-japan-as-india-s-friend-for-bullet-train-loan-at-0-1-interest-117091400601_1.html). Contested on yen-depreciation grounds by Business Standard, "Do the maths: India's first bullet train isn't 'free of cost'" (https://www.business-standard.com/article/economy-policy/do-the-math-india-s-first-bullet-train-isn-t-free-of-cost-as-modi-claims-117091800116_1.html).
(2) Railways Minister's Lok Sabha written reply, Feb 2026: "Expenditure amounting to ₹86,939 crore has been incurred on the project till 31.12.2025" and "The final cost of the project can be reasonably ascertained only after the completion of all associated works" (via https://deshgujarat.com/2026/02/12/%E2%82%B986939-crore-spent-on-mumbai-ahmedabad-bullet-train-project-till-dec-2025-govt/). The opposition's "not economically viable" line (Congress, 2017) is also on record.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a concessional sovereign loan. The tied condition is the stated price of Japanese Shinkansen technology transfer. The rate is below any market rate India could get. The overrun and delay fit the ordinary pattern of first-of-kind Indian mega-projects: land acquisition, a change of government in Maharashtra, and a 21 km tunnel. They do not need a lender-driven story. The narrative already holds both sides and only asserts what the JICA record supports.
verdicts.reason:
Not refuted. The two cited JICA sources confirm, word for word, the load-bearing documented elements: 0.1%, 50 years, 15 years' grace, "Tied", the NHSRCL executing agency, the ¥1,806,282m ex-ante cost, the planned in-service date of December 2023, and an ex-post evaluation due only after operations start. Operations have not started (first section 2027), so "no ex-post evaluation yet" is true. NHSRCL really is unreachable.

The claim is a contested narrative that weighs both sides, so its tier must be analytic. Two parts are not in the cited sources:
- "Near-grant" is our inference, and it depends on the discount rate: about 85% grant element at 7%, but only 25–58% at yen-market rates of 1–3%.
- "Cost is real": the cited JICA pages show no cost escalation. The escalation figure (₹1.08 → ₹1.98 lakh crore) is reported, not documented. It comes from ET/Swarajya (March 2026) and Deccan Herald, citing unnamed officials, and the government told Parliament the final cost cannot yet be ascertained.

The framing survives. Its sourcing and wording need the fixes listed in corrections.

verdicts.baseRate: Among the 55 bidder-listed notices: none were single-bid, the mean was 5.6 bidders, and 12 of 55 had three or fewer. L&T is India's largest E&C contractor, and only about 3–6 firms (L&T, Tata Projects, KEC, GIL/Tata, Alstom, Siemens) can pre-qualify for design-build rail or system packages above ₹700 cr. verdicts.innocentReading: L&T is the largest Indian EPC firm. It won the three EDFC-3 (P150158) works contracts as L1 in open RFB competitions where the notices list the rivals and their prices. On CP-303, L&T bid ₹2,870.99 cr against KEC-Longjian at ₹2,991 cr (4.2% higher), IL&FS JV at ₹2,996.5 cr, and GR Infra-Kyivmetrobud at ₹3,040 cr, among others. verdicts.reason: The core numbers reproduce from the WB procnotices API. L&T's lead-firm INR award total is exactly ₹6,076.46 cr. There are 370 award notices when PMGSY P124639 is read at rows=200, and 11 projects carry INR prices. But the claim text says EDFC-3 was won "all three packages, rivals unpublished", and the cited P150158 source contradicts this. Each of the three L&T award notices publishes its rivals. CP-303 (IN-DFCCIL-1848-CW-RFB) lists seven evaluated bidders with prices, e.g. "GR INFRAPROJECT LIMITED ... PJSC KYIVMETROBUD ... Bid Price at Opening INR 30,400,000,000.00". IN-DFCCIL-1846 and IN-DFCCIL-1847 list KEC-Ansaldo/Hitachi as evaluated at ₹997.7 cr and ₹1,012.6 cr, plus rejected Tata, Alstom, Kalindee and Texmaco bids. Two lesser problems. First, the denominator is a truncation artifact: PMGSY was read at rows=200 of 430 notices. The full INR total is ₹31,234 cr (L&T 19.5%), and my re-parse of the same 370 notices gives ₹30,537 cr (19.9%) rather than ₹29,919 cr. Second, the "1–5%" loss margins are actually 1.3% and 5.8%. Of the 55 ICB award notices, only 7 are DFCCIL's: P114338 has 3 and P131765 has 4. 47 are POWERGRID's (P115566 PSDP-V has 40, P101653 PSDP-IV has 7), and 1 is NHAI/MoRTH's (P121185, Monte Carlo). verdicts.baseRate: For the WB side I rebuilt the counts from the five API pulls, taking each notice's Awarded plus Evaluated bidder blocks. The distribution matches the claim exactly: 2x4, 3x8, 4x17, 5x7, 6x6, 7x2, 8x1, 10x4, 11x3, 13x1, 14x1, 17x1. The mean is 5.636 and there is no award with a single bidder. After removing the 4 duplicate notices, the figures are 298/51 = 5.84 mean over 51 unique awards. Several notices also list Rejected bidders, so bids actually received are higher than "evaluated". "20 foreign-led" depends on how you define it. By the country field alone I count about 16 (Alstom UK/Oy, NCC-SA x3, Isolux x3, Sichuan x3, TBEA, Xian XD, Baoding, Hyundai, Beijing NRR). You only reach about 20 if you also count Indian subsidiaries or JVs of foreign parents (ABB Ltd, Alstom T&D JVs, Siemens JV, Alstom Consortium). Note that NCC-SA is led by an Indian group. For the domestic control I confirmed 16 of 88 with bidder counts, mean 4.25, and no sole-bidder flag. But those 16 are 6 airport PPP concessions from one 2019 round, 7 spectrum-auction winners, 2 ISTS transmission tariff auctions and 1 TOT bundle. None of them is a works or supply procurement. The spectrum count is the number of participants in the whole auction, repeated for each winner: the 2022 auction's "4" appears 4 times and the 2024 auction's "3" appears 3 times. There are really about 11 independent events, and their mean is about 4.5.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The claim accuses no party of wrongdoing. No response was sought from DFCCIL, POWERGRID or the World Bank, and none was needed for an analytic comparison. None found; not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The claim's own innocent reading (the gap is partly disclosure) is correct, but it leaves out other boring explanations. First, the two samples are different kinds of things. On one side are ICB supply and EPC packages, mostly POWERGRID conductor, insulator, tower and transformer lots, a market with many Indian and Chinese makers. On the other side are concession, spectrum and tariff auctions, which have few eligible bidders by design. Second, they come from different periods: 2011–16 against 2019–25, and the later period includes the July 2020 land-border (GFR) order that removed Chinese bidders. Third, the domestic figures are inflated by repeated counts. Any of these alone could produce a gap of about 1.4 bidders, before competition is considered at all.
verdicts.reason: The numbers check out against the World Bank API: the bidder distribution, mean 5.64 and zero single-bid awards are exact, and the domestic register gives 16/88 with mean 4.25. What fails is the claim as a graph edge. It is an IBRD→DFCCIL edge, but 47 of the 55 awards are POWERGRID's and only 7 are DFCCIL's. The one WB source it cites (P115566) contains no DFCCIL award. And 4 of the 55 are the same contract listed under two projects. The domestic comparison is also not like for like (auctions and PPPs, not works procurement) and counts the same auction more than once. The finding is analytic and does not imply wrongdoing. It survives as a base rate or narrative, not as a DFCCIL edge.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: the World Bank financed Indian ICB contracts that Chinese firms won between 2011 and 2016. The signature dates in the notices run from 16-Mar-2011 (Hyundai C-34204) to 03-Oct-2016 (Package 203). The Chinese wins are Baoding Tianwei (17-Mar-2011, INR 1,698,979,587), Xian XD (21-Feb-2012, INR 867,740,916), TBEA Shenyang (28-Aug-2012, INR 368,971,480), Sichuan Yibin x3 (18-Jul-2012 twice under P115566, 23-Mar-2012 under P101653, totalling ₹40.53 cr) and Beijing NRRDI (signed 03-Oct-2016, INR 4,710,000,000 = ₹471 cr). Every date and amount in the record's `d` field matches the API. STEC: technical bids were opened 2020-03-16, before the 23-Jul-2020 Order, and the LOA was issued 2020-12-09. Nothing in the chronology is inconsistent.
verdicts.identityTest: The P131765 notice names the awardee as "M/s. Beijing National Railway Research & Design Institute of Signal & Communication Group Co. Ltd.", Country: China. The notice does not name CRSC. CRSC's own site (crsc.cn/g4307.aspx) and the Wikipedia CRSC page link it as a wholly owned subsidiary of China Railway Signal & Communication Co. (CRSC Research & Design Institute Group, CRSCD). The alias is correct, but the CRSC link comes from outside the cited source. IBRD as financier of EDFC-2 is confirmed by the 2014 prequalification notice ("has applied loan for financing from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) towards the cost of EDFC 2 Project"). The awarder was DFCCIL; IBRD is not a party to the contract. That is acceptable only because the edge is `analytic`, not `award`.
verdicts.baseRate: I re-parsed the five projects the file's baseRates entry cites (P115566, P101653, P131765, P114338, P121185). Counting ICB award notices that list at least one other bidder gives exactly 55 notices, 7 with a Chinese winner and 18 with at least one Chinese bidder, so the file's arithmetic reproduces. However, 4 of the 55 are the same contracts posted under both P115566 and P101653 (CD-1714, CD-1715, INS-1428, INS-1716), and the P115566 copy of INS-1428 is marked "This notice has been cancelled". After removing duplicates there are 51 distinct contracts: 7 Chinese wins (13.7%) and 16 with a Chinese bidder (15 of 50 if the cancelled notice is also dropped). 47 of the 55 notices come from POWERGRID (P115566/P101653), so the sample is a transmission-equipment base rate, not "WB ICB awards in India". Chinese wins are clearly not universal (well under 80%), so the rate does discriminate, and it is the claim's own content. SPEC control (Japanese ODA): JICA-tied WDFC procurement is excluded from the file. Under STEP terms the same lens would show Japanese prime contractors near 100% by design, so the claim makes no symmetric comparison and should not suggest one.
verdicts.denialFound: This claim alleges no wrongdoing, so no denial is needed for IBRD or CRSC, and none was sought. On the STEC half, NCRTC's statement via PTI: "Approvals have to be taken at various levels for bids that are funded by multilateral agencies. This bid was also awarded following the set procedure and guidelines" (https://www.theweek.in/wire-updates/national/2021/01/03/del41-ncrtc-rrts-project.html; https://www.nationalheraldindia.com/india/chinese-firm-given-contract-worth-rs-1126-crore-for-delhi-meerut-rail-tunnel-even-as-lac-standoff-continues).
verdicts.innocentReading: Under World Bank and ADB member-eligibility rules the lowest evaluated responsive bidder must be awarded. In 2011–16 Chinese transformer, insulator and signalling makers routinely bid on POWERGRID and DFCCIL ICB packages and sometimes came in lowest (L1). The 23-Jul-2020 GFR Order itself preserves this for STEC. Its para 3(b) would ordinarily scrap a tender past the qualification stage, but Annex II para D says: "In projects which receive international funding with the approval of the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), Ministry of Finance, the procurement guidelines applicable to the project shall normally be followed, notwithstanding anything contained in this Order". So an ADB-funded L1 award to STEC was procedurally permitted even after the Order.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives. Every amount, date and awardee matches the World Bank procnotices API. Raw counts reproduce exactly (7/55 Chinese winners, 18/55 with a Chinese bidder), and the innocent reading for STEC is backed by the Order's own Annex II-D carve-out for internationally funded projects. Two corrections are needed, and neither changes the direction of the finding. (1) The denominator double-counts 4 contracts cross-posted under P101653, so the true figures are 7 of 51 distinct contracts and 16 of 51 with a Chinese bidder. (2) "WB ICB awards in India" overstates a five-project sample that is 85% POWERGRID. The STEC conclusion also compares across lenders (World Bank baseline, ADB award), which is inference, so the tier stays analytic. The CRSC identity rests on CRSC's corporate site, not on the cited notice.

The baseRates entry "Chinese-firm winners..." should read numerator 7 / denominator 51, and the label should note the duplicates. srcs: the claim-level srcs passed to review list only P115566 and P131765, but P101653 is required for the third Sichuan Yibin win (INS-1281, 23-Mar-2012), and P114338 and P121185 are required for the denominator. Add CRSC's corporate page (http://www.crsc.cn/g4307.aspx) as the source for the "CRSC's Beijing institute" alias, since the WB notice names only "Beijing National Railway Research & Design Institute of Signal & Communication Group Co. Ltd.". `d`: add that ₹471 cr was L1 against three Indian-registered JVs (Kalindee–Kyosan ₹494.8 cr, Siemens ₹564.47 cr, L&T–Ansaldo ₹625 cr), so the notice lists 4 bidders in total. innocentReading: cite GFR Order 23-Jul-2020 Annex II para D (lender guidelines prevail for DEA-approved internationally funded projects) as the specific rule that made the Dec-2020 STEC LOA procedurally permissible. verdicts.dateTest: Claim: NCRTC opened Package 4 financial bids on 2020-06-12 and issued the LOA to STEC on 2020-12-09. The dates hold. NH/PTI: bids were invited on 2019-11-09. UTN: "the Technical bids for this contract package were opened on 16 March 2020". UTN is dated 2020-06-12 and says "NCRTC has today opened financial bids". ADB Procurement Plan Rev 7.0, Pkg-4: "153,570,000.00 09-Dec-2020 Awarded to M/s Shanghai Tunnel Engineering Co. Ltd. LOA Date: 09-Dec-2020". Galwan was 2020-06-15. PIB Order was 2020-07-23. So "bids pre-dated the clash and the Order" is true of Galwan. It is not true of the LAC standoff as a whole, which began in early May 2020, before the financial-bid opening. The award came after both. PIB confirms the transition rule that matters here: "If this stage has been crossed, ordinarily the tenders will be cancelled and the process started de novo." Package 4 had crossed that stage, so cancellation was the default the Order prescribed. The claim's counterfactual premise is therefore sourced, but only if the Order reached a tender financed by ADB under an existing loan agreement. That point is unverified: the Order's annexures (pibcms.nic.in) could not be retrieved, DNS failed, and the record itself lists this as a gap.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match. ADB PP names "M/s Shanghai Tunnel Engineering Co. Ltd." for Pkg-4, which is the TBM tunnels from New Ashok Nagar to Sahibabad plus one underground station. UTN names "Shanghai Tunnel Engineering Co. Ltd. (STEC)" with the same scope, including Anand Vihar. NCRTC is the awarder in all three press sources. The claim says Afcons was L5. ADB PP confirms Afcons won Pkg-8, the Meerut TBM tunnels, at est. US$208.38m, LOA 2020-11-26. CONFLICT: Tribune (Dikshit) says "The Chinese company's quote was a few crores less than that of the Turkish company Gulermak", which makes Gülermak the runner-up. UTN has L&T as L2 at ₹1,170 cr and Gülermak as L3 at ₹1,326 cr. NH/PTI does not name L&T or give its price. The "L&T lost by ₹44 cr" leg therefore rests on UTN alone, and a cited source contradicts it. It is not "reported ×2" as the STEC node claims.
verdicts.baseRate: It is not discriminating that the L1 bidder won. Under ADB open competitive bidding with international advertisement, the award goes to the lowest-evaluated responsive bidder essentially 100% of the time. A Chinese firm winning a lender-financed Indian contract is not new either: the record's own WB notices list Baoding Tianwei (2011), Xian XD and Sichuan Yibin (2012), TBEA Shenyang (2012) under UPA, and Beijing NRRDI/CRSC (2016) under NDA. So the property appears under both governments. Of the 19 awarded RRTS packages (ADB PP), STEC won 1, worth US$153.57m or 12.5% of value. L&T won 3 (35.1%) and Afcons 2 (28.9%). The L1 margin of about 3.8–3.9% over L2 is ordinary in competitive tunnelling tenders. Symmetry check against the SPEC control of Chinese finance vs Japanese ODA: JICA-tied WDFC procurement restricts the field to Japanese firms by design. Under the same "who gained" lens that would show a larger, structural benefit to the lender's nationals, so the STEC case is the milder one.
verdicts.denialFound: NCRTC spokesperson via PTI, National Herald, 2021-01-04: "Approvals have to be taken at various levels for bids that are funded by multilateral agencies. This bid was also awarded following the set procedure and guidelines." PTI/NH also: "According to the ADB's procurement guidelines, vendors from all member countries of the bank are eligible to participate in the bidding process without any discrimination." (https://www.nationalheraldindia.com/india/chinese-firm-given-contract-worth-rs-1126-crore-for-delhi-meerut-rail-tunnel-even-as-lac-standoff-continues). Neither the claim nor the record contains a response from STEC, ADB, or DoE/MoF on whether a waiver or exemption from the Order was used. It is not known whether they were asked. No wrongdoing is alleged, so nothing needs denying beyond NCRTC's procedural statement.
verdicts.innocentReading: This was an ADB-financed international competitive bid, and the lender's rules made all member-country firms eligible, China included. Technical bids were opened in March 2020, and the financial bids on 2020-06-12, before Galwan and before the 23 July Order. STEC was L1 by a few percent, and NCRTC waited about six months for multilevel approvals, including ADB's, before issuing the LOA. The loan agreement arguably took precedence over a domestic GFR order issued later. Cancelling would have risked a breach of the lender's procurement rules and delayed an 82-km corridor on which every other civil package had already been awarded. This is a routine procedural outcome, not a favour.
verdicts.reason: The claim's core facts survive. STEC was L1 at ₹1,126 cr (UTN, NH/PTI), and the LOA was issued on 2020-12-09 at est. US$153.57m (ADB PP, primary). PIB's text confirms the "ordinarily cancelled and started de novo" rule. NCRTC's response is on the record. But the claim as written fails on four specific points. (1) The ₹1,126.89 cr figure does not appear in any cited source. UTN and NH both say "Rs 1,126 crore", and ADB gives only a US$ estimate. The .89 figure is also inconsistent with the "₹44 cr" gap: 1,170 − 1,126.89 = 43.11. (2) "≥₹44 cr" is not a floor. A de-novo rebid could have come in lower, and nothing shows L&T would have held ₹1,170 cr. At best it is "≈₹43–44 cr if bids were unchanged". (3) "6–12 months" has no source anywhere in the record. (4) The idea that cancellation was available "under the July 2020 Order" assumes the Order reached a tender financed by ADB under an existing loan agreement. The record's own gap entry admits the annexures that would settle this were not read. One more problem: a cited source (Tribune) names Gülermak, not L&T, as the narrow runner-up, and the claim does not disclose this conflict. The ledger row stays analytic, but only once these numbers are corrected.

Change "cancelling … would have cost ≥₹44 cr plus 6–12 months" to "on the bids as opened, the next-lowest price was ₹1,170 cr (≈₹44 cr, 3.9% higher); a de-novo rebid's price and delay are unknown". Delete "6–12 months" unless sourced. Qualify "under the July 2020 Order" with "if the Order applied to ADB-financed tenders under existing loan agreements — unverified (DoE Order annexures not read)". Add to d: "Tribune (2021-01-04) reports STEC's quote was 'a few crores less than' Gülermak's, which conflicts with UTN's ranking (L&T L2 ₹1,170 cr; Gülermak L3 ₹1,326 cr); L&T's L2 price rests on UTN alone". The source is the ADB Procurement Plan, "Date of this Procurement Plan: 23 August 2021 (Rev 7.0)". Every award falls inside that plan's window, so the chronology is consistent. The record has from and to set to null. They should be 2020-03-19 and 2021-04-15, with asOf 2021-08-23 (Rev 7.0). Later revisions or contract variations could change the shares.

Ltd." (P4), "Ircon International Limited" (P19) and "VNC-KEC (JV)" (P5A). L&T and Afcons are Indian private EPC firms; Afcons is a Shapoorji Pallonji group company. verdicts.baseRate: L&T and Afcons are routinely L1 or finalists on large Indian metro and RRTS viaduct and tunnel civil packages, under both UPA and NDA (DMRC Phase 2/3, MAHSR, Mumbai and other metros). Two firms holding about 60–65% of the civil value is typical for this sector, so the property does not single these awards out. On P4 the incumbents lost to a lower foreign bid. Urban Transport News lists five financial bids: STEC ₹1,126 cr (L1), L&T ₹1,170 cr, Gulermak ₹1,326 cr, Tata Projects-SKEC ₹1,346 cr, Afcons ₹1,400 cr. That points to price competition rather than capture. No symmetry test against a UPA-era corridor has been done. The arithmetic implies no political alignment, so the SPEC controls (UPA vs NDA, BJP-run vs opposition-run states) are not directly engaged.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; not asked. The claim alleges no wrongdoing, so no response is required. Neither NCRTC, ADB, L&T nor Afcons has commented on concentration.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is ADB open competitive bidding with international advertisement on very large packages. Only a few firms (L&T, Afcons, Tata Projects, a few foreign tunnelers) can qualify and bid, and they split packages by lowest price. On P4 five bidders competed, and the two dominant firms placed L2 and L5. The shares are ADB estimated package values, not signed contract prices.
verdicts.reason: The quantitative core holds against the cited primary source. I re-summed the PDF's "List of Awarded Completed Contracts": 19 packages, US$1,223.82m. L&T (P3 243.10 + P7 98.57 + P17 88.37) = 430.04 (35.1%). Afcons (P6 144.69 + P8 208.38) = 353.07 (28.9%). STEC P4 153.57 (12.5%). Ircon P19 98.50 (8.0%). L&T plus Afcons = 63.99%. It is correctly labelled "estimated value" and correctly tiered analytic, being our own arithmetic on a documented plan with no wrongdoing implied. The source check is only partial for two reasons. First, "Package 4 drew five bidders" is not in the cited ADB PDF. It is confirmed by Urban Transport News (2020-06-12), which the file lists but the claim's srcs does not. Second, "₹1,000 cr+ viaduct/tunnel packages" overstates the case: at ₹73.5/US$, P7 (≈₹725 cr), P17 (≈₹650 cr) and P19 (≈₹724 cr) are under ₹1,000 cr, and P17 and P19 are trackwork and traction, not viaduct or tunnel. Neither defect breaks the claim, so it survives as analytic with corrections.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out: "World Bank sanctions list (as served 2026-09-26) contains 54 India-registered rows of 1,520; 52 of them dated 2010-2026". I re-fetched the API on 2026-09-26. Without a key it returns 401. With the public apikey header used by worldbank.org/debarred-firms it returned 1,520 rows (LAST_REFRESH_DATE 2026-09-26). India has 54 rows, and 52 of them have DEBAR_FROM_DATE of 2010 or later (the other two are GAP International and Surendra Singh, both 2001). The dates check out. One caveat: this is a snapshot of who is ineligible right now. Debarments that have run out are removed, so the list is not a count of every sanction since 2010. For example, the fixed-term debarments that followed the 2008 health-sector review in India have expired and are no longer on it. The narrative's "52 debarments 2010-2026 ... in 16 years" treats the snapshot as a full history, which it is not.
verdicts.identityTest: The claim names the four cases wrongly and miscounts. The rows labelled "Controlled Affiliate of a Sanctioned Entity" break down as follows. Fedders Lloyd: 7 (PSL Engineering x2, Airserco, Fedders Electric, Lloyd Electrical, Regal IT, Lloyd Infotech). A2Z: 11 (9 on 2021-03-17 and 2 on 2021-05-28). Madhucon: 5 (Nama Hotels, Madhucon Mega Mall, Madurai-Tuticorin Expressways, Madhucon Heights, Madhucon Infra). Chasha Lands and Joyluck Venture: 2. That makes 25 affiliate rows for the four cases. There is also a 26th Indian affiliate row, Lotte Data Communication R&D Center India LLP, which belongs to a Korean-parent case. The claim's figure of 30 only works if you add the 5 principal rows: Fedders Lloyd (listed twice), Madhucon Projects, A2Z Infra Engineering and Techfab International. So "30 are affiliate extensions" is wrong. It should say 30 rows belong to four cases: 5 principal rows and 25 affiliate rows. The fourth case is Techfab International, debarred 2019-05-07. Chasha and Joyluck are only its affiliates (both carry the same case marker, *477), so "Chasha/Joyluck" as the case name is wrong. Also, "54 Indian firms" really means 54 rows. That includes 4 rows for individuals (Surendra Singh, Laxminarayan Mallick, Laxmi Narayan Construction, Arputharaj Devaraj) and duplicate entries for the same entity (Fedders Lloyd x2, PSL Engineering x2, the Laxminarayan alias set x3).
verdicts.baseRate: 54/1,520 = 3.6% is arithmetically correct, but the denominator makes India look smaller than it is. 633 of the 1,520 rows (42%) are cross-debarments that the World Bank copies from other banks: ADB 329, EBRD 125, IDB 111, AfDB 39. None of them are Indian, while 260 are Chinese. Counting only the World Bank's own 887 sanctions, India has 54, or 6.1%. That ranks India 3rd of all countries, after China (127) and Viet Nam (57). Counting only post-2010 own sanctions and leaving out affiliate rows, India has 26 of 521 (5.0%), ranked 5th after China, Nigeria, Viet Nam and Bolivia. Across the whole list, affiliate rows make up 286 of 1,520 (19%), so extending debarments to affiliates is not unusual to India. The claim that India is not disproportionately targeted depends on comparing against India's share of IBRD/IDA lending, and the record admits that share is "not computed here". India's cumulative share of World Bank commitments is probably around 6-10%, which suggests India is not an outlier. But nobody has done that calculation, and the record's own killIf test (a comparison weighted by the loan portfolio) has not been run.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is our own inference about how a sanctions system behaves, not an accusation against anyone. There is no accused party whose response is needed, and I found no allegation of targeting to answer. Nobody was asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The number of debarments reflects which cases the World Bank's investigators (INT) happen to pursue, plus automatic extensions to affiliates and cross-debarments copied from other banks. It does not reflect a policy about any country. India's count is driven by three or four large infrastructure groups whose subsidiaries were debarred along with them. India's share on the list is roughly the same as, or below, its likely share of lending. The Chinese-vs-Japanese control in the fleet SPEC applies the same way: China's large count (387) is mostly cross-debarments (260). The UPA-vs-NDA control does not tell the two apart, because the Indian affiliate clusters fall in 2016-2022 and the ongoing debarments date from 2011 onward.
verdicts.reason: The 3.6% share and the 52 post-2010 rows check out against the live API. The claim's specific structural statement is wrong: only 25 of the 52 rows (26 counting the Lotte affiliate) are affiliate extensions, not 30. The figure 30 counts the principal firms too. The fourth case is Techfab International, not "Chasha/Joyluck". The headline 3.6% is also halved by cross-debarments copied from other banks; on the World Bank's own sanctions India is 6.1% and ranked 3rd, which weakens "no sign of disproportionate targeting" as it is framed. The conclusion probably still holds, but it rests on a lending-share comparison that nobody has computed. Keep the claim at analytic only after the text is corrected.
verdicts.corrections: text/lab: replace with "Indian-registered entities are 54 of 1,520 rows (3.6%) on the WB ineligibility list as of 2026-09-26. Excluding 633 cross-debarments from other MDBs (none Indian), India is 54 of 887 WB-originated rows (6.1%, 3rd after China and Viet Nam). Of 52 post-2010 Indian rows, 30 belong to four cases (Fedders Lloyd, Madhucon, A2Z, Techfab International): 5 principal rows and 25 controlled-affiliate rows. Share vs India's share of IBRD/IDA commitments not yet computed." d: change "30 of these are 'controlled affiliate' rows" to "25 are controlled-affiliate rows of four cases (26 including Lotte Data Communication India LLP); with the 5 principal rows the four cases account for 30". Replace "Chasha/Joyluck" with "Techfab International (affiliates Chasha Lands, Joyluck Venture India)". Add that the list is a current snapshot and expired debarments drop off, so it is not a 2010-2026 history. Add that "54 firms" is 54 rows, including 4 individual rows and duplicate entries. Remove "no sign of disproportionate targeting" from the text until the lending-weighted comparison in killIf is computed, or rephrase it as "not an outlier by count; lending-weighted test pending". srcs: note that the API needs the public apikey header used by worldbank.org/debarred-firms (it returns 401 without it). Raw data re-fetched to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-india-corporate-intelligence/f532d734-1afb-5ca9-b34e-a813ae9f9a94/scratchpad/wb.json.

verdicts.dateTest: Stated as an actor-action-time claim: World Bank-financed borrowers (NMCG, BRLPS, MoRTH) directly selected 8 providers, with contracts signed 2017-02-17 to 2021-12-07 (notices dated 2018-08-24 to 2022-09-16). There is no tenure claim, so there is nothing to overlap. One caveat: consultant CDS and DIR "small assignment" award notices only appear in the STEP-era feed (2016 onward). The pre-2016 part of the sample is almost entirely ICB/QCBS large awards, so 0 direct selections before 2016 reflects what was published, not what happened. verdicts.identityTest: The awarding entities match the notices. verdicts.dateTest: Written as a sentence, the claim is: World Bank ICB and ADB lender rules produced more bidders than Union domestic awards, lender side 2011–2016 (plus one ADB package in 2020), domestic side 2019–2026. The two windows do not overlap. Every one of the 55 bidder-listed WB notices is dated 2011–2016 (my recount by year: 2011:2, 2012:10, 2013:25, 2014:5, 2015:6, 2016:4, 3 undated). The domestic register runs 2019–2026, which is after the 2017 Public Procurement (Make in India) preference order and the July 2020 GFR land-border restriction. So the comparison mixes lender versus domestic with pre-2017 versus post-2019 policy regimes and with UPA/early-NDA versus late-NDA. There is no lender-funded bid-count data after 2016: 315 of 370 notices (85%) are in the STEP awardee-only format. The claim text's "85% of sample opaque" is correct. The narrative's own wording, "85% of recent lender-funded awards", is wrong: 85% is the share of the whole 370-notice sample.
verdicts.identityTest: The lender side is not "lender-funded procurement" in general. It is 55 WB ICB award notices (15% of the sample), most of them from POWERGRID PSDP IV–V and EDFC projects. ICB is the method reserved for the largest packages. WB-funded NCB and shopping contracts, and all post-2016 RFB notices, are outside the bid-count sample. The domestic side is not "domestic government procurement" either. Of its 88 records, 59 are auctions (34 coal-block revenue-share auctions, 7 spectrum lots). The 16 records with a bidder count come from about 6 processes: one 2018–19 airport PPP tender counted six times (bidders 7/7/6/6/3/3); the 2022 and 2024 spectrum auctions counted 4 and 3 times, where the bidder number is capped by the telecom oligopoly (4 and 3 licensees); two transmission TBCB auctions; and one road. The domestic mean of 4.25 therefore counts lots of the same auction repeatedly, and it compares concessions and auctions with works and goods contracts. The entity labels also overreach. JICA is India's largest bilateral lender and its STEP loans are tied to Japanese prime contractors (the file itself excludes JICA WDFC awards as "Japanese tied procurement"). That is lender-funded procurement that is less open to foreign firms, which contradicts the general subject "lender-funded procurement".
verdicts.baseRate: From the WB API (P115566, P101653, P131765, P114338, P121185), my recount found 83 contract-award notices. 55 list evaluated bidders, all of them ICB. Mean is about 5.96 by name count (the file says 5.64); the minimum is 2; single-bid awards are 0/55; awards with ≤3 bidders are 8 by my count (the file says 12). For an outside domestic comparator: the LEAP/XKDR study of 1,000 randomly sampled state CPPP road and water tenders (2018–19, five states) found competition "lower than the normative thumb-rules from the literature" and "several awarded tenders that attracted only single bids". That supports the direction for small state-level works, but those are not the same size class as WB ICB packages, and the study found no correlation between bidder numbers and contract value. Having zero single-bid awards does not set the lender side apart: the file's own symmetry check says "neither register contains a documented single-bidder award". The top-winner shares are similar and depend on the lens (L&T 20% of WB value, 35% of ADB RRTS; PSU-GoI 30.5% and Reliance 26% of the domestic register).
verdicts.denialFound: none found — not asked. No accused party; this is a comparative claim. No DoE, MoF or World Bank statement comparing bidder counts was found. The file's own symmetryCheck concedes that "the difference is partly one of disclosure".
verdicts.innocentReading: Lender rules require international advertisement and publication of evaluated bidders for ICB, which is used only for the largest packages. So the "more open" result is largely true by definition: the lender's rulebook selects the biggest, most-advertised contracts and discloses their losers. The domestic register mostly holds auctions and concessions, where bidder numbers are capped by market structure (3–4 telecom licensees) or where foreign firms cannot enter by design (coal blocks for Indian companies, spectrum for licensees). It also mostly does not publish bidders. The observed gap therefore measures differences in method, disclosure format and contract type, not in how competitive the procurement actually is. Tied bilateral lending (JICA STEP) runs the other way.
verdicts.reason: The sources confirm only the narrow parts of the claim. From the WB API: 55 ICB notices list evaluated bidders, none is a single-bid award, and the mean is about 5.6–6. From UTN: "A total of five national and multinational bidders participated", with STEC L1 at Rs 1,126 cr and L&T L2 at Rs 1,170 cr. They do not support the comparative claim, and the evidence cannot carry a "well-supported" status. (1) The domestic comparator is the platform's own register, not a primary source. Its 16 bidder counts come from about 6 auctions or PPP processes counted per lot, so it is not comparable with works/goods ICB. (2) The time windows do not overlap (2011–16 vs 2019–26) and straddle domestic foreign-bidder restrictions. (3) The lender sample is 15% of notices, chosen by a disclosure format that ended in 2016 and limited to the most competitive method. (4) Under the fleet's Chinese vs Japanese control, the same lens applied to JICA tied STEP loans gives the opposite reading, so "lender-funded procurement" as a class is not more open. (5) The file's own symmetry check says the difference "is partly one of disclosure" and that neither register has a single-bidder award. What survives is an analytic observation about WB ICB 2011–2016, not a well-supported comparison.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Downgrade status from "well-supported" to "contested" and tier the narrative as analytic, with innocentReading = disclosure, method (ICB applies only to the largest packages) and contract-type effects.
2. Narrow the claim to: "World Bank ICB contract awards in India, 2011–2016, that published evaluated bidders (55 of 370 sampled notices) averaged about 5.6 bidders with no single-bid award; no like-for-like domestic comparator exists in the platform's data."
3. In strongestCase, replace "The domestic control register records bidder counts for only 16 of 88 awards (mean 4.25)" with a note that these 16 come from about 6 auctions or PPP processes counted per lot (airport PPP ×6, spectrum 2022 ×4, spectrum 2024 ×3, 2 TBCB, 1 road) and are not procurement of works.
4. In strongestCounter, change "85% of recent lender-funded awards" to "315 of 370 sampled award notices (85%), i.e. every post-2016 STEP-format notice".
5. Add as a counter: JICA STEP tied loans (WDFC, MAHSR) restrict prime contractors to Japanese firms. Lender-funded procurement is not uniformly more open, and excluding JICA from scope makes the generalisation wrong.
6. Add the time-window confound (WB 2011–16 vs domestic 2019–26; 2017 PPP-MII order and the 2020 GFR land-border rule apply only to the domestic window).
7. Add the external domestic comparator (LEAP/XKDR, 1,000 state CPPP tenders 2018–19, single-bid awards present) as partial support, labelled as state-level and small-contract.
8. Re-verify the "≤3 bidders in 12 of 55" figure: my recount gets 8.
9. The RRTS "three countries" counts lead firms only; SKEC in the Tata JV is Korean.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim is: Chinese firms won lender-funded Indian equipment packages in 2011–2016, and were then shut out after July 2020. The World Bank API confirms the equipment wins and their dates. Baoding Tianwei won C-34209-S016-1: 'Contract Signature Date: 17-Mar-2011 ... Contract Price: INR 1,698,979,587.00'. Xian XD won C-34210-S017-1 (INR 867,740,916, Feb 2012). TBEA Shenyang won the Seoni reactor package (INR 368,971,480, notice 28-Sep-2012). Sichuan Yibin won the Dehradun IS01 insulator package (P101653, evaluated Mar-2012, INR 52,494,923) and P260-IS03/IS04 (Jul-2012, INR 108.3m and 244.5m). Beijing National Railway Research & Design Institute won EDFC Package 203 (P131765, Oct-2016, 'Contract Price: INR 4,710,000,000.00'). One date is wrong: every Chinese insulator win is from 2012. The 2013 insulator packages (P290-IS01 and IS02, Apr-2013) were won by BHEL, with Zhejiang Jinlihua and Sichuan Yibin losing. The '2020 cut-off' does not survive the file's own record. (a) The 2016 EDFC signalling contract was terminated by DFCCIL on 18 June 2020, officially for slow progress (about 20% done in four years), which was before the July GFR Order. (b) STEC received its RRTS Package 4 LOA on 2020-12-09, after the Order. So the break was neither clean nor dated to the Order.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities in the World Bank notices match the claim: Baoding Tianwei Baobian, Xian XD, TBEA Shenyang, Sichuan Yibin Global and Beijing NRRDI of Signal & Communication (the CRSC subsidiary), all listed as 'Country: China'. The identity failure is in the counter. It names STEC as 'the first large Chinese civil-works award in the NCR', and that is false. Delhi High Court, DMRC v. J. Kumar-CRTG JV (O.M.P.(COMM) 603/2020, judgment 25.04.2022, https://indiankanoon.org/doc/24486984/): 'On 22.05.2012, M/s J. Kumar-CRTG JV ... submitted a bid of ₹ 909.1917 crores plus USD 1,09,09,423.3. On 16.07.2012, DMRC issued a Letter of Acceptance'. That contract was DMRC Phase III CC-24: TBM tunnels plus the Lajpat Nagar, Vinoba Puri, Ashram and Hazrat Nizamuddin stations. It was built by a JV with China Railway Tunnel Group (CRTG), on a JICA-funded project in Delhi, eight years before STEC. Search results also report an L&T–Shanghai Urban Construction Group JV on the Phase III Mandi House–Jama Masjid section (2012). That one is not verified here.
verdicts.baseRate: From the file's own count, Chinese firms won 7 of 55 bidder-listed World Bank ICB awards in India in 2011–2016 (12.7%), and 18 of 55 awards (33%) had at least one Chinese bidder. That supports 'regular participants who sometimes won' in equipment packages. It does not support 'routine winners'. Five of the seven wins are in 2011–2012 on POWERGRID alone, so the sample is concentrated in one borrower and one product class. Symmetry control (UPA vs NDA): Chinese wins fall under both, 2011–12 under UPA and 2016 under NDA. The pattern is not party-specific, so the control gives no partisan reading.
verdicts.denialFound: Not a denial case, since no wrongdoing is alleged. The parties' stated positions: NCRTC told PTI that vendors from all ADB member countries were eligible 'without any discrimination'. In June 2020 the government said the RRTS tender had 'not been finalised' (India TV). DFCCIL said it ended the Beijing NRRDI contract for poor progress, not for nationality (ANI, 18 June 2020: https://www.aninews.in/news/national/general-news/dfccil-terminates-rs-471-crore-contract-with-chinese-company-citing-slow-progress20200618165931/). Nobody from the Chinese firms was asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: Under ICB rules for World Bank, ADB and JICA loans, Chinese firms from member countries could not be excluded, and they won when they were L1. That happened mostly in commodity equipment (transformers, reactors, insulators), where Chinese prices were lowest. Some of the change after 2020 is contract performance (the DFCCIL termination was officially for slow progress) plus a registration-and-clearance rule. It is not a ban: PIB says bidders 'will be eligible to bid ... only if the bidder is registered with the Competent Authority', with MEA/MHA clearance. The Order also does not name China.
verdicts.reason: The narrative is marked 'established', which is not a valid tier. Its stated counter is factually false. The J. Kumar–CRTG JV, with China Railway Tunnel Group as partner, received a DMRC Phase III tunnel-and-station LoA on 16.07.2012 for ₹909 cr + USD 10.9m in Delhi (Delhi HC judgment, 25.04.2022). So STEC was not the first large Chinese civil-works award in the NCR, and the 'unusual in kind' explanation for the objections to STEC falls away. 'Shut out only after 2020' also overstates the PIB text, which describes a registration and clearance requirement, not a ban. The file itself contradicts it twice: the 2016 Chinese signalling contract was terminated in June 2020, before the Order, and STEC was awarded after the Order in December 2020. The equipment-package facts are documented from World Bank notices. The synthesis ('routine', 'shut out', the cut-off date) is our own inference and belongs at analytic.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the Government of India ended K.V. Subramanian's IMF Executive Director term about six months early, in "May 2025". His tenure began November 2022 for three years and was due to end around 31 October 2025. The dates fit and the ~6-month figure is correct. The date needs a fix, though. BS 2025-05-05 says: "The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC), in an order dated April 30, had decided to end Subramanian's three-year term at the IMF that was to conclude this October, with immediate effect." BS 2025-05-03 says the IMF site listed the post as vacant "as of May 3". BS 2025-05-05 says the IMF listed him as ED "till May 2". So the decision date is 2025-04-30. It became public on 2025-05-03, not "May 2025" generally.
verdicts.identityTest: The person is correct: Krishnamurthy V. Subramanian, former CEA (2018-21), India's ED at the IMF from November 2022, representing India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Bhutan. The acting body is wrong. The edge uses s=min:ministry-of-finance, but the source names the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC order dated April 30). The Ministry of Finance (DEA) handles IMF nominations but did not take the decision according to the source. The IMF spokesperson says only "a decision by the government of India."
verdicts.baseRate: The trait is rare, so it does discriminate. Former Finance Secretary Subhash Garg, quoted in BS 2025-05-05: "This is the first time that the term of an India ED at the Fund has been terminated. Governments can usually recall a person, post them elsewhere or announce a successor early." Earlier India EDs appointed under the UPA (e.g. Arvind Virmani, Rakesh Mohan) and under the NDA (Surjit Bhalla) served their terms without a formal termination. Symmetry: there is no UPA-era case to compare. The termination was ordered by the NDA government against its own former CEA appointee, so the claim does not frame a political opponent.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and it is unknown whether he was asked. Neither Business Standard article carries any comment from Subramanian. His Wikipedia entry records no statement, denial or reply from him. The Government of India gave no official reason (BS 2025-05-03: "no official explanation has been issued for his early departure"). The only on-record response from the institution is the IMF spokesperson's (BS 2025-05-05): "The appointment and termination of any member of the executive board is a decision for member countries to make. The termination of ED Subramanian is a decision by the government of India... We wish him well." Related named-party material, not yet in the record: Congress alleged "financial impropriety" (The Hindu, 2025-05-06). Union Bank of India admitted "lapses" in buying about 2 lakh copies of India@100 for about Rs 7.25 crore (BS, Indian Express, CNBC-TV18, 2025-05-06/07). An ISB panel reviewed his role (Mint/Moneycontrol, 2025-05-15). None of these confirms the government's actual reason.
verdicts.innocentReading: The government may simply have wanted a different ED in place before the IMF board voted on Pakistan's financing (about 9 May 2025), or have been reshuffling the post for policy reasons. That would be a personnel decision within its discretion that implies nothing about Subramanian's conduct. The Union Bank book purchase could be a procurement failure at the bank itself (the bank flagged its own lapses and suspended a GM) and not wrongdoing by the author. His criticism of IMF datasets is ordinary behaviour for a member-country ED. The government's reason has never been officially stated, and the impropriety reading rests entirely on unnamed sources.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives, but only because it is hedged correctly. Both Business Standard sources, fetched via curl after WebFetch returned 403, say what the claim says. On who decided, BS 2025-05-05: "The premature exit ... was a call taken by the Government of India, the Fund's spokesperson told Business Standard." On the ~6-month cut: "three-year term ... was to conclude this October." On the reasons: "Sources linked Subramanian's termination to allegations of impropriety in the promotion of his recent book titled India@100, and his criticism of IMF data sets." BS 2025-05-03 also has "sources cited in the report [Indian Express] suggest Subramanian had raised concerns about certain IMF datasets" and the Pakistan-vote timing. The claim attributes the reasons to unnamed sources and says no official reason was given. That is accurate, so it is not a false conjunction. It is a conjunction of different evidence grades, though. The termination and who decided it are documented: an ACC order, an on-record IMF spokesperson, and wide independent coverage (Indian Express, HT, Mint, TOI). The reasons rest only on unnamed sources, and a named party (Congress) asserts impropriety. Keeping "alleged" for the combined text is correct and conservative. The two fixes that matter are the wrong body (MoF instead of ACC) and the vague date.
verdicts.corrections: 1) s: change min:ministry-of-finance to the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (e.g. gov:acc / "Union Cabinet — ACC"). Cite BS 2025-05-05: "The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC), in an order dated April 30". 2) Date: set from/date to 2025-04-30 (ACC order, immediate effect), publicly reported 2025-05-03. Fix debt:c019 "to" to 2025-04-30. 3) Split the record. Make a documented enforce edge ACC→per:krishnamurthy-subramanian that says only "term terminated with immediate effect, ~6 months early; IMF spokesperson on record that it was GoI's decision". Move the reasons (IMF-dataset friction, India@100 promotion) into a separate alleged claim or narrative, attributed to unnamed sources in BS and Indian Express, keeping contra debt:c021. 4) Correct the attribution in d: the book-impropriety line in BS 2025-05-05 is BS's own "sources", not only a relay of Indian Express. 5) Add the named-party and documentary context to the reasons claim: Congress allegation (The Hindu, 2025-05-06), Union Bank of India's admission of procurement lapses over about 2 lakh copies worth about Rs 7.25 cr (BS/IE, 2025-05-06/07), and the ISB review (2025-05-15). State that none of these is an official government reason. 6) debt:c021: record "none found — not known whether asked; GoI gave no official reason; IMF spokesperson statement is the only on-record response". 7) Add a successor note: Urjit Patel was appointed India ED in August 2025 (TOI/IE, 2025-08-29), and the post was held in the interim reportedly by Parameswaran Iyer.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated, the claim is: Subramanian (actor) gave no recorded response (did) to the reported reasons for his recall (thing), around 3–5 May 2025 (when). The timing is consistent. Business Standard (2025-05-05) says the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet order of 30 April 2025 ended his term "with immediate effect". The IMF site listed him as ED until 2 May. He served from 1 Nov 2022 and was due to leave in Oct/Nov 2025. The press attempts to reach him happened during the 3–5 May 2025 news cycle, so they fall inside the right window. No later statement from him on the reasons turned up. His 2026 media appearances (NDTV 2 Sep 2026, India Today 16 Sep 2026, BusinessLine 20 Jul 2026) are about the economy, not the recall.
verdicts.identityTest: Passes. Krishnamurthy V. Subramanian: former Chief Economic Adviser (2018–21), and IMF Executive Director for the India/Bangladesh/Sri Lanka/Bhutan constituency from Nov 2022 to Apr/May 2025. This is the same person named in Business Standard and ThePrint. He is not Arvind Subramanian, the earlier CEA who also left early. The node per:krishnamurthy-subramanian is correct.
verdicts.baseRate: Recalled or removed officials often decline to comment while the story is live. Serving and recently serving Indian government nominees and ex-officials usually stay silent on reasons the government has not officially given.
