So silence tells us little and should not be read as an admission. The same test applies on the other side: the Ministry of Finance also "did not respond to a query" (Business Standard, 2025-05-05). Non-response is recorded for the government side too and carries no more weight there.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial found. He was asked and did not answer. ThePrint, Moushumi Das Gupta, 2025-05-05 (https://theprint.in/india/krishnamurthy-subramanian-had-6-months-still-left-in-his-tenure-at-imf-why-did-modi-govt-recall-him/2615392/): "Subramanian was not available for comment despite repeated attempts to contact him on his mobile phone." The same article: "Government sources said, following the curtailment of his service, Subramanian resigned from his post citing personal reasons." That is second-hand, from government sources, not his own statement. Neither Business Standard source (2025-05-03, 2025-05-05) mentions asking him. The 2025-05-05 piece records only that the IMF spokesperson answered by email and that "The Ministry of Finance did not respond to a query on the matter." The PTI piece on the Union Bank book purchase (ThePrint, 2025-05-06) carries no comment from Subramanian.
verdicts.innocentReading: He stayed quiet on unofficial, source-based allegations while an ACC decision was fresh and while the Union Bank procurement review and an ISB review (Mint/Moneycontrol, 15 May 2025) were under way. Silence at that point is routine and consistent with innocence. It is not evidence for or against the book-promotion or IMF-dataset explanations.
verdicts.reason: The decisive problem is the claim's wording, "asked/not asked unknown". That is false: ThePrint (5 May 2025) says reporters tried repeatedly to reach him by mobile phone and he was not available for comment. So the record says "asked, no response", with one named credible outlet as the source. The claim also has an empty srcs array, and neither cited Business Standard article says anything about approaching him. The edge as written is therefore unsourced and factually wrong about whether he was asked. The underlying finding, that no response from him is on record, survives, but at the tier of one credible outlet: reported. "Alleged" is the tier for the accusation in c020. It is the wrong tier for a documented non-response.
verdicts.corrections: 1) d/text: replace "No response recorded — asked/not asked unknown." with: "Asked, no response on record: ThePrint (2025-05-05) reports Subramanian 'was not available for comment despite repeated attempts to contact him on his mobile phone.' Government sources told ThePrint he 'resigned from his post citing personal reasons' after the curtailment; this is not a first-hand statement from him. No public rebuttal of the book-promotion or IMF-dataset explanations found as of 2026-09-26." 2) srcs: add ["ThePrint — 2025-05-05", "https://theprint.in/india/krishnamurthy-subramanian-had-6-months-still-left-in-his-tenure-at-imf-why-did-modi-govt-recall-him/2615392/"]. 3) tier: change alleged to reported. 4) Add a note to c020 that the Ministry of Finance also did not respond to Business Standard's query (2025-05-05), so non-response is shown on both sides. Also note the Union Bank of India regulatory filing (reported by PTI via ThePrint, 2025-05-06: "there were certain lapses in the procurement, which are being examined by the bank"). That filing is a primary record bearing on the book-purchase part of c020 and should be sourced there, not here. 5) Keep pred "contra" and direction per:krishnamurthy-subramanian to claim:debt:c020, but label it lab "Subramanian's response (none; asked by ThePrint)" so the contra does not read as a denial.

verdicts.dateTest: As written: IMF lent about US$7bn to the Ministry of Finance, secured against 67t of gold (47t Bank of England, 20t UBS), in May 1991. The actor window overlaps: the Chandra Shekhar caretaker government ran until 21 Jun 1991 and the Rao/Manmohan Singh government from 21 Jun 1991. The dates inside the claim are wrong, though. Indian Express (Shaji Vikraman, 5 Apr 2017, which Wikipedia itself cites) says: "Between July 4 and 18, 1991, the RBI pledged 46.91 tonnes of gold with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan to raise $400 million." That means the 47t tranche was July 1991, not May. Only the roughly 20t SBI-held confiscated gold, handled as a sale-and-repurchase with UBS for about $200m, belongs to May 1991. The IMF drawings were also not in May 1991. From memory, and not verified here because imf.org returns 403: a first-credit-tranche stand-by plus a CCFF drawing were made in January 1991, and the main 20-month stand-by arrangement was approved in October 1991, under the new government.
verdicts.identityTest: The counterparty is wrong. The source for the gold facts says it was pledged to "the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan", central banks that "insisted on physical delivery of gold". It was not pledged to the IMF. The UBS tranche was a sale with a repurchase option, which is not a pledge. Also, the 20t was confiscated gold given to SBI, not RBI reserves. So the gold secured bilateral central-bank and bank financing, not the IMF stand-by or CCFF. The borrower node min:ministry-of-finance is acceptable for IMF drawings (Government of India). The gold transactions were RBI and SBI transactions, not MoF's. Even the Wikipedia page contradicts its own "$7bn from the IMF" line in the same sentence: the gold was airlifted "to raise $600 million".
verdicts.baseRate: Borrowing from the IMF with conditionality during a balance-of-payments crisis was near-universal for 1980s–90s developing-country crisis borrowers, so it does not discriminate. Gold pledged as collateral to central banks is rarer, but it is not an IMF feature: the IMF lends to members against quota and does not take gold collateral. Symmetry: the same crisis borrowing ran across a Janata Dal (S)/Congress-supported caretaker government (January and May 1991) and a Congress government (July and October 1991). No partisan asymmetry is available.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; nobody was asked. Not a wrongdoing claim. Contrary factual reporting exists: the Indian Express (5 Apr 2017, https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/in-fact-how-govts-pledged-gold-to-pull-economy-back-from-the-brink/) places the 46.91t pledge in July 1991 and names BoE and BoJ as the lenders against it. It also says the gold was repurchased before December 1991.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is the ordinary sequence of a balance-of-payments emergency. India drew IMF resources (January 1991 CCFF plus first-tranche stand-by, October 1991 stand-by), which carried standard conditionality. Separately, it raised short-term bridge money by pledging or selling gold to BoE, BoJ and UBS, because commercial markets were closed after the rating downgrades. The two strands happened at the same time but were separate transactions. Merging them ("IMF loan secured by gold") is a popular myth. It inflates the "IMF dictated reforms" story by implying the IMF held India's gold.
verdicts.reason: Fatal: the claim's load-bearing link, that the IMF loan was "secured against ~67 tonnes of pledged gold", is false according to the reporting Wikipedia itself cites. The gold secured about $400m from the Bank of England and Bank of Japan (July 4–18, 1991) and about $200m through an SBI–UBS sale-and-repurchase (May 1991). It was not IMF collateral. The dates are wrong (47t was July, not May), and one counterparty is missing (Bank of Japan). The US$7bn figure is sourced by Wikipedia to a popular book (Meredith 2007). It is not an IMF figure, and it probably conflates total multilateral and bilateral support. From memory, not verified: IMF drawings were closer to about US$4bn across January–October 1991. The source is a tertiary Wikipedia sentence, and it is internally contradictory ("$7 billion from the IMF by pledging 67 tons" versus "to raise $600 million"). Because the claim conjoins separate transactions into a causal and collateral relationship that none of the primary accounts states, it fails the conjunction test as written.
verdicts.corrections:
Kill debt:c025 as written and replace it with separate edges:
(1) fin:imf -> min:ministry-of-finance, pred loan. Text: "IMF CCFF drawing + first-credit-tranche stand-by (Jan 1991) and 20-month stand-by arrangement (approved Oct 1991)". Leave the amount null, or use "~US$1.8bn (Jan) + ~US$2.3bn (Oct)" flagged as unverified. Tier reported until an RBI Annual Report 1991-92 or IMF Annual Report 1992 figure is sourced. Remove "US$7bn" and a=14000 (the Rs-crore arithmetic rests on the wrong base).
(2) Bank of England + Bank of Japan -> RBI, pred loan: about US$400m secured by a pledge of 46.91t of gold, 4–18 July 1991, repurchased before December 1991. Tier reported (Indian Express 2017), documented if the RBI History Vol. 4 is cited.
(3) UBS <- SBI: sale-and-repurchase of about 20t of confiscated gold for about US$200m, May 1991 (airlift 21–31 May). Tier reported.
Drop the phrase "empirical anchor of the 'IMF dictated the 1991 reforms' narrative", or move it to a narrative with an innocentReading noting that the gold was not IMF collateral. Replace the Wikipedia-only sourcing with the Indian Express URL, plus the RBI or IMF primary source when reachable.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: "India's total external debt stock (all borrowers) grew about 14.0%/yr from end-2004 to end-2014 and about 4.6%/yr from end-2014 to end-2024." The windows are calendar-year snapshots. UPA held office from May 2004 to May 2014 and NDA from May 2014 onward. So the 2014 value includes about 7 months of NDA, and 2004 includes about 7 months of UPA. The misalignment is small and cuts both ways. The alternative cut (2004-13 = 14.8%, 2014-23 = 3.9%) does not change the result. The date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: The series is right. World Bank IDS DT.DOD.DECT.CD, "External debt stocks, total (DOD, current US$)", India. Fetched 2026-09-26, lastupdated 2026-07-13. Values: 2004 = 123,644,485,822; 2014 = 457,507,409,077; 2024 = 716,456,023,890. These reproduce 13.98% and 4.59% exactly. The target node is wrong. The edge points to min:ministry-of-finance, but DT.DOD.DECT is TOTAL external debt: private non-guaranteed borrowing, commercial borrowings, NRI deposits and short-term trade credit, as well as sovereign debt. Public and publicly guaranteed debt (DT.DOD.DPPG.CD) was only $64.9bn of $123.6bn in 2004, $152.5bn of $457.5bn in 2014, and $238.9bn of $716.5bn in 2024. So roughly two-thirds of the 2014 and 2024 stock is not a Ministry of Finance borrowing decision at all.
verdicts.baseRate:
The UPA-to-NDA slowdown is not specific to India. I computed the same World Bank series for seven peer emerging markets, 2004-14 CAGR vs 2014-24 CAGR:
- Brazil: 9.7% vs 0.8%
- Indonesia: 7.8% vs 3.7%
- Mexico: 10.0% vs 0.8%
- Turkey: 9.6% vs 2.2%
- South Africa: 13.0% vs 1.7%
- Thailand: 9.7% vs 2.7%
- Philippines: 2.6% vs 5.7%

Six of seven (about 86%) show the same sharp deceleration. That is above the 80% threshold, so the pattern does not discriminate: it reflects the global cycle (the 2004-14 emerging-market credit boom and post-2008 quantitative easing, then a strong dollar after 2014). The symmetry test also runs the opposite way to the naive spin once scaled to GDP. India's US$ GDP grew 11.1%/yr in 2004-14 and 6.3%/yr in 2014-24. External debt as a share of GDP went 17.4% (2004), then 22.4% (2014), then 19.1% (2024). Sovereign-only (PPG) CAGR was about 8.9% in 2004-14 and about 4.6% in 2014-24.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed and none was found; nobody was asked. The claim is analytic and alleges no wrongdoing against any party, so no response was sought.
verdicts.innocentReading:
The boring explanation that fits the data: the gap is mainly the global cycle, shared by about 86% of peer emerging markets, together with slower US$ nominal GDP growth after 2014. Two further effects reduce the post-2014 dollar figure: the dollar strengthened, and the rupee depreciation shrank the US$ value of rupee-denominated external liabilities (FPI holdings of government securities, rupee NRI deposits). Growth and retrenchment in private corporate ECB/NRI borrowing, which is not sovereign policy, also moves the total. Scaled to GDP, the ratio rose under UPA and fell modestly under NDA. The difference is small, and the cyclical factors above can explain it.

The innocent reading as filed contains two errors:
1. "A lower 2014 base mechanically compounds faster" (in the claim text) and "compounding off a ~3.7x-larger base mechanically produces a lower percentage growth rate even under identical policy" (in innocentReading and symmetryCheck) are false. CAGR does not depend on scale. Identical policy, meaning identical growth rates, gives an identical CAGR whatever the base. A base effect only exists if absolute increments are held fixed. Even then NDA added less in absolute terms: +$259bn against +$334bn under UPA.
2. The 2013 taper tantrum points the wrong way. Rupee depreciation lowers the US$ value of rupee-denominated debt, so it depressed the UPA-window figure rather than inflating it.
verdicts.reason: The numbers and the source are confirmed exactly, and "analytic" is the right tier for a comparison of our own making. But an analytic claim rests on its innocentReading, and the one given here is arithmetically false. It says a larger or smaller base "mechanically" changes CAGR, and the claim text even inverts which base is lower. It also gets the direction of the taper-tantrum valuation effect backwards. The edge is also pinned to the Ministry of Finance, although about two-thirds of the stock is non-sovereign. As written, the claim does not survive. It should be kept as analytic only after the rationale is replaced with the peer base rate (about 86%) and the debt/GDP scaling.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Claim text: delete "since a lower 2014 base mechanically compounds faster". Replace with: "6 of 7 peer EMs (BRA, IDN, MEX, TUR, ZAF, THA; not PHL) show the same 2004-14 to 2014-24 deceleration in World Bank DT.DOD.DECT.CD, so the gap is not partisan-discriminating. Ext. debt/GDP was 17.4% (2004), 22.4% (2014) and 19.1% (2024)."
2. innocentReading: remove the base-effect sentence and the claim that the taper tantrum raises the UPA figure. Replace with the global cycle, slower US$ GDP growth (11.1% vs 6.3%), the post-2014 dollar/rupee valuation shrinking rupee-denominated liabilities, and the private ECB/NRI share.
3. Target node: change "t" from min:ministry-of-finance to a total-external-debt / India-economy node. Otherwise restrict the claim to PPG (DT.DOD.DPPG.CD: $64.9bn, $152.5bn, $238.9bn; about 8.9% vs 4.6% CAGR).
4. symmetryCheck narrative: apply the same fix. Remove the "3.7x-larger base mechanically produces a lower percentage growth rate" wording.
5. Note in "d" that the calendar-year cut places 2014 partly in NDA tenure; the alternative 2004-13 / 2014-23 cut gives 14.8% / 3.9%.
6. killIf values: PPG was $205.3bn in 2021 and $214.9bn in 2023, which is consistent as stated.

verdicts.dateTest:
Claim as a sentence: IMF (actor) dictated India's reform programme in 1991. Two dated steps:
(1) CCFF plus first-credit-tranche drawing, January 1991, under the Chandra Shekhar government (FM Yashwant Sinha). Indian Express, 2017: "India had managed to get a bit of a breather with the first tranche of $755 million from the IMF". This came before the Rao government (sworn in June 1991), so it cannot have conditioned the Rao reforms.
(2) Stand-by arrangement (SBA): negotiated July–August 1991, Board approval October 1991. The devaluation (early July 1991) and the Industrial Policy Statement (24 July 1991) came before Board approval. That is consistent with prior actions, but equally consistent with a home-grown design. The record never states the SBA date or amount.
Gold pledge chronology is wrong in the record:
- 20 t of confiscated gold went to UBS on a sale-and-repurchase basis, 21–31 May 1991, for $200m. Chandra Shekhar government; Sinha signed the file.
- 46.91 t were pledged to the Bank of England and Bank of Japan, 4–18 July 1991, for $400m. Repurchased before December 1991.
Both were bridge borrowing from other central banks and a Swiss bank. Neither was collateral for the IMF loan.
The counter's phrase "after the 1991-93 facility was repaid" is loose. The SBA ran roughly 1991–93, but repurchases continued later in the decade (not verified this session).
verdicts.identityTest:
Actor attribution is only partly right. The structural conditions the strongestCase lists (de-licensing, trade liberalisation, opening sectors to foreign participation) are written into the World Bank Structural Adjustment Loan/Credit (report P-5678-IN, sanctioned 12 Nov 1991, $250m IBRD plus SDR 183.8m IDA). Wikipedia, Economic_liberalisation_in_India: "This specified deregulation, increased foreign direct investment, liberalisation of the trade regime...".
The IMF CCFF was compensatory financing for the oil shock with little conditionality. The SBA's core conditions were macro-stabilisation.
So "IMF" should read "IMF and World Bank (Bretton Woods conditionality)". The strongestCase's "the government pledged national gold reserves as collateral to secure the loan" names the wrong counterparty. Indian Express, 2017: "the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan were willing to lend but not without a collateral. It was pointed out to them that India was a depository of the IMF ... but that didn't help."
verdicts.baseRate:
Close to every upper-credit-tranche IMF stand-by and World Bank structural adjustment loan of 1980–95 carried policy conditionality, and many ran alongside devaluation and trade liberalisation (general knowledge, not quantified this session). "Borrowed under conditionality and then liberalised" therefore does not separate India in 1991 from other borrowers of the period. It cannot by itself show dictation as opposed to agreement.
Symmetry control:
- India's 1981 Extended Fund Facility under Indira Gandhi's Congress government carried conditionality too; India reportedly drew only part of it and ended it early (general knowledge, not verified this session).
- The 1991 reforms were continued by non-Congress governments: United Front 1996–98, NDA 1998–2004. The World Bank's own 1995 assessment, quoted by Indian Express 2010: "the reforms initiated in 1991 will not be reversed, as demonstrated by the reform plans and actions in states with non-Congress Party governments."
Applied to other governments, the same lens produces the same picture, so it is not a party-specific finding.
verdicts.denialFound:
No direct denial by the government that the IMF dictated the reforms was verified this session. WebSearch budget was exhausted and imf.org and dea.gov.in are blocked. The government's recorded response on the gold pledge: Manmohan Singh told Parliament it was a "painful necessity" (Indian Express 2017, https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/in-fact-how-govts-pledged-gold-to-pull-economy-back-from-the-brink/).
The accusing side is on record: opposition leaders called the 1991 Budget and New Industrial Policy a "command budget from the IMF" (Free Press Journal, cited in Wikipedia Economic_liberalisation_in_India).
The lenders' own record, World Bank declassified Country Economic Memoranda reported by Indian Express 2010 (https://indianexpress.com/article/news-archive/web/how-wb-imf-got-india-to-adopt-reforms-in-1991/), says they "chivvied and cajoled India into economic liberalisation". Its wording to the Rao government: "the only real options for India are whether the adjustment is made in the context of an orderly, growth-oriented adjustment program with external financial support, or through a disorderly and painful process".
That is pressure and leverage, not a written dictation.
verdicts.innocentReading: India was days from sovereign default: reserves under three weeks of imports, a downgrade below investment grade, and IMF and World Bank lending halted until a budget passed. Any government had to borrow from the Bretton Woods institutions, and their standard conditionality overlapped heavily with a liberalisation agenda already argued inside the Indian establishment since the Rajiv Gandhi-era partial reforms of the mid-1980s. The Rao–Singh team chose the sequence and in places went beyond the conditions, for example the scale of industrial de-licensing. Later governments of other parties continued the reforms after the leverage ended. Crisis plus lender leverage explains the timing and speed. Home ownership explains the content and durability. "Dictated" overstates the first and ignores the second.
verdicts.reason:
"Contested" is the right calibration and it survives. The documented record (World Bank declassified memoranda via Indian Express 2010; SAL P-5678-IN) shows strong IMF/World Bank leverage and explicit structural conditionality. It does not show that the IMF alone wrote the programme, and the reforms outlived the leverage.
The record carries a load-bearing factual error: it calls the gold pledge collateral for the IMF loan. The gold went to UBS (May 1991, $200m, Chandra Shekhar government) and to the Bank of England and Bank of Japan (July 1991, $400m) as bridge finance, not to the IMF.
The strongestCase also puts on the IMF stand-by/CCFF the structural conditions that sit in the World Bank SAL.
The only source is Wikipedia, a tertiary and internally inconsistent source: it says both "emergency loan of $7 billion from the IMF by pledging 67 tons" and that the gold went to the BoE and UBS.
The status holds, but the text must be corrected before publication.
verdicts.corrections:
1. strongestCase: replace "the government pledged national gold reserves as collateral to secure the loan" with: "the government sold-and-repurchased 20 t of gold via UBS (May 1991, $200m, Chandra Shekhar govt) and pledged 46.91 t with the Bank of England and Bank of Japan (4–18 July 1991, $400m) as bridge finance before the IMF stand-by, a measure of how constrained the position was." Source: Indian Express 2017.
2. strongestCase: change "the stand-by arrangement and CCFF drawdown ... conditioned on ... de-licensing, opening protected sectors" to "IMF stand-by (macro-stabilisation conditions) and World Bank Structural Adjustment Loan P-5678-IN of 12 Nov 1991 ($250m IBRD plus SDR 183.8m IDA; deregulation, FDI, trade, interest rates, capital markets, PSU reform)".
3. strongestCase: note that the January 1991 CCFF and first-tranche drawing ($755m per Indian Express) came before the Rao government, so they cannot have conditioned its reforms.
4. claim wording: consider "The 1991 reforms were dictated by the IMF and World Bank", since the conditionality claim rests mostly on the World Bank SAL.
5. strongestCounter: soften "after the 1991-93 facility was repaid" to "after the 1991–93 stand-by ended", since repayment dates are not verified.
6. srcs: add Indian Express 2010 (World Bank declassified CEMs), https://indianexpress.com/article/news-archive/web/how-wb-imf-got-india-to-adopt-reforms-in-1991/ ; Indian Express 2017 (gold pledge), https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/in-fact-how-govts-pledged-gold-to-pull-economy-back-from-the-brink/ ; World Bank report P-5678-IN, http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/999451468260069468/pdf/multi0page.pdf . Mark Wikipedia as tertiary; its "$7 billion IMF loan by pledging 67 tons" is wrong.
7. Add the opposition charge "command budget from the IMF" as the alleged-side record. Add the government response (gold pledge a "painful necessity") as the response, and record that no denial of IMF dictation was located this session.
8. Symmetry: add that the 1981 EFF under Congress had conditionality and that UF and NDA governments continued the reforms after 1996.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: "India's external-debt position (2023–24) does not support the claim that a crisis is coming." The data window is 2000–2024 (World Bank IDS), and the three cited API series match exactly. DT.DOD.DECT.CD gives 101.13bn (2000), 647.56bn (2023) and 716.46bn (2024). DT.DOD.DECT.GN.ZS gives 18.04% for 2023. DT.TDS.DECT.EX.ZS gives 10.16% for 2023. DT.DOD.DSTC.ZS (short-term share, not cited in the file) is 19.63% for 2023 and 19.48% for 2024, which fits "roughly one-fifth". The 1991 comparison also holds: World Bank debt service was 32.96% of exports in 1990 and 32.03% in 1991, consistent with "30–35%". The record is stale, though. The RBI released data for end-March 2026 on 29–30 June 2026 and the file ignores it: stock US$762.8bn, debt/GDP 20.8% (up from 19.8%), debt service 5.8% of current receipts (down from 6.6%), short-term share 19.6%, short-term debt to reserves 21.6%, and residual-maturity short-term debt 47.3% of reserves (IANS/IBTimes, 30 Jun 2026). None of this changes the verdict, but the asOf should move to the latest figures.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is right: country code IND is the Republic of India's total external debt stock, and each indicator code is the one named in the srcs. One problem: no proponent of the "heading for a crisis" narrative is named or cited, so the claim being rebutted has no source. That makes it a potential strawman. The record should cite who actually makes the claim (outlet, commentator or party) or say that none was found.
verdicts.baseRate: For comparable economies, 18–21% of GNI/GDP and 6–10% debt service to exports/receipts sit in the low-risk band for lower-middle and middle-income borrowers. Both are far below India's own 1990–91 figures (about 33% debt service, reserves 6.8–9% of debt). The ratio of reserves to total debt is where the file goes wrong. By FI.RES.TOTL.DT.ZS, reserves exceeded the full debt stock only in 2004–2010 (106–135%). They were 69.8–89.3% in 2011–2018 and 82.6–104.5% in 2019–2024, with 90% in 2024. So "reserves have historically comfortably covered the stock" is false as written: reserves cover short-term debt about five times over, but not the total stock. The "sovereign share has been shrinking" point is only half right. PPG/total fell from about 80% (2000) to about 35% (2010), then stayed flat at 33–35% from 2010 to 2024 (34.2% in 2019, 33.2% in 2023, 33.4% in 2024). Symmetry: the same lens applied under the UPA (2004–14) and NDA (2014–24) shows no partisan discontinuity in debt/GNI or debt service. The file's symmetryCheck already records this for the Union control.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable in the accused-party sense, because there is no accused party. The relevant official position is the RBI's own end-March 2026 statement, as carried by IANS/IBTimes on 30 Jun 2026 (https://www.ibtimes.co.in/indias-external-debt-increases-762-8-billion-non-government-borrowings-rise-rbi-903415). It reports that "Debt service ... declined to 5.8 per cent of current receipts at end-March 2026 from 6.6 per cent", that government debt fell while non-government debt rose, and that there was a US$24.6bn valuation effect. The file names no proponent of the crisis claim, so their side was not recorded either.
verdicts.innocentReading: The nominal US$ stock grows sevenfold simply because GDP grew, private corporate ECB and NRI-deposit liabilities rose, and dollar valuation moved. Measured against the economy (debt/GNI flat at 18–21%), against earnings (debt service 6–10% of receipts) and against reserves (short-term debt about 20% of reserves), there is no crisis trajectory. In addition, 29.4% of the debt is rupee-denominated, which removes currency-mismatch risk on that slice.
verdicts.reason: The finding that the claim is unsupported holds. The cited World Bank series confirm every number in the narrative, and the newer RBI end-March 2026 release points the same way: debt service is falling and the short-term debt/reserves ratio is moderate. So the verdict is not refuted. Two supporting statements in strongestCounter are inaccurate or overstated and must be fixed. First, reserves have NOT historically covered the total stock; they were below 100% in most years since 2011 and at 90% in 2024. Second, the PPG share stopped shrinking around 2010. Beyond that, the stock data is stale (it ends in 2023–24), and the claim being rebutted has no named proponent. This is our own inference built on documented data, so the tier is analytic.
verdicts.corrections: 1) strongestCounter: replace "foreign-exchange reserves ... have historically comfortably covered the stock" with "reserves covered short-term debt about five times over (short-term debt/reserves 21.6% at end-March 2026, RBI) and 90% of the total stock in 2024 (World Bank FI.RES.TOTL.DT.ZS); reserves exceeded the full stock only in 2004–2010." Add srcs FI.RES.TOTL.DT.ZS: https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/FI.RES.TOTL.DT.ZS?format=json&date=1990:2024&per_page=100. 2) strongestCounter: replace "sovereign (PPG) share ... has been shrinking" with "the PPG share fell from about 80% (2000) to about 35% (2010) and has been flat at 33–35% since; RBI reports government external debt declined in FY26 while non-government debt rose." 3) Add the RBI end-March 2026 data to both sides. For strongestCase: stock US$762.8bn, debt/GDP up to 20.8% from 19.8%, short-term share up to 19.6%, residual-maturity short-term debt 47.3% of reserves. For strongestCounter: debt service 5.8% of current receipts, 29.4% rupee-denominated. Source: RBI press release (fetch rbi.org.in), or as interim https://www.ibtimes.co.in/indias-external-debt-increases-762-8-billion-non-government-borrowings-rise-rbi-903415. 4) Cite the short-term share: add DT.DOD.DSTC.ZS to srcs. 5) The "20–25% debt-service distress range" in whatWouldChangeThis is uncited; mark it analytic or cite a threshold source (e.g. IMF/WB LIC-DSF). 6) Name at least one real proponent of the "heading for crisis" claim, or add "no named proponent found this session", to avoid a strawman. 7) Keep status "unsupported" and the tier analytic, and update asOf to reflect the end-March 2026 data.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: IMF/World Bank control Indian policy, now (2023–26). IMF window: India's last use of Fund resources was the 1991–93 SBA/CCFF, fully repaid on 31 May 2000 (Wikipedia 'India and the International Monetary Fund'; BusinessToday 2025-05-10, 'India hasn't taken an IMF loan since 1993'). So no IMF conditionality has been in force at any point in the 2014–26 or 2004–14 windows. World Bank window: lending is continuous across UPA and NDA. The debt figures are dated 2023, which fits a present-tense assessment. The date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: The actors are institutions and there is no person or family actor, so there is no ethnic or religious framing. One label is wrong. The strongestCounter calls the US$39.3bn 'multilateral (IBRD+IDA) debt', but World Bank indicator DT.DOD.MWBG.CD is 'IBRD loans and IDA credits (DOD, current US$)'. That is World Bank debt only. Total multilateral debt would also include ADB, AIIB, NDB and IFAD, so the label understates the multilateral slice. The IMF clause names the right facility (1991–93).
verdicts.baseRate: Having a World Bank lending programme with conditions is nearly universal among IBRD/IDA-eligible middle-income borrowers (≈100%), so it does not discriminate. Having a live IMF programme with binding macro conditionality does discriminate (Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Egypt, Argentina, among others), and India is outside that set: 0 drawings since 1993. Receiving Article IV advice applies to 100% of IMF members, the US and China included, so it does not show control either. The symmetry control (UPA 2004–14 vs NDA 2014–26) gives the same reading. Both borrowed from the World Bank, including DPLs (UPA's 2009 US$2bn Banking Sector Support DPL; NDA's COVID-era DPLs and 2023 Low-Carbon DPL), and neither held an IMF programme.
verdicts.denialFound: There is an institutional response of the relevant kind, although not a denial of 'control' as such. In December 2023 the Government of India publicly rejected the IMF's 2023 Article IV debt warning. The Finance Ministry called the >100%-of-GDP projection 'a worst-case scenario and is not fait accompli' and said any contrary interpretation was 'misconstrued'. India's Executive Director K.V. Subramanian dissented formally. Sources: https://www.business-standard.com/economy/news/imf-cautions-india-on-govt-debt-vulnerabilities-centre-disagrees-123121901166_1.html ; https://www.deccanherald.com/business/economy/imfs-projection-of-govt-debt-exceeding-100-of-gdp-by-fy28-is-misconstrued-finance-ministry-2822830. This supports the strongestCounter's statement that India 'often does' ignore Article IV advice, and it should be added as a source.
verdicts.innocentReading: India is a long-standing World Bank borrower. It chooses which projects and DPLs to seek, and conditions attach only to those operations. It receives the same Article IV surveillance every IMF member receives and publicly disputes it. Where Indian policy and IFI advice line up, that reflects a shared technocratic consensus and Indian officials' own policy choices. It does not show external control.
verdicts.reason: The narrative record survives because the evidence supports its 'unsupported' verdict. I checked both cited World Bank API figures directly. IBRD+IDA debt was 39,283,871,000 in 2023 and total external debt stock was 647,556,415,555.5 in 2023, about 6.07%. Both match the record. The IMF-leverage counter is also correct: no IMF drawing since 1993, repaid by May 2000, confirmed by secondary sources since imf.org is blocked. Because this is our own assessment, it belongs in the analytic tier, not documented. The record has three weaknesses, listed under corrections, but none of them overturns the status: (1) the 'multilateral' label is wrong; (2) the IMF-no-drawing statement has no source in srcs; (3) the strongestCase omits the strongest real channel, World Bank Development Policy Loans. DPLs carry policy prior actions and tranche triggers, including Kerala DPO1 triggers that named state legislation, after which DPO2 (P170521) was dropped. AUDIT.json in the same directory already documents this. That evidence still fits 'influence through voluntary, borrower-chosen operations' and not 'control'. A dropped DPO actually shows the borrower can walk away.
verdicts.corrections: 1. strongestCounter: change 'multilateral (IBRD+IDA) debt was only US$39.3bn' to 'World Bank (IBRD+IDA) debt was US$39.3bn'. Also add the total multilateral figure (indicator DT.DOD.MLAT.CD), or say it was not retrieved. 2. srcs: add a source for the IMF claim ('no IMF financing since 1993; repaid 31 May 2000'), e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_and_the_International_Monetary_Fund or https://www.businesstoday.in/india/story/india-hasnt-taken-an-imf-loan-since-1993-gul-panag-gives-pak-journalist-a-reality-check-congratulates-on-loan-475745-2025-05-10, and flag the IMF lending-history page (https://www.imf.org/external/np/fin/tad/extarr2.aspx?memberKey1=430) as blocked in the voids. 3. strongestCase: add World Bank DPLs/DPOs with policy prior actions and triggers as the strongest channel, citing the 2023 Low-Carbon DPL P181032 and the Kerala DPO1 P169907 legislative triggers, and add to strongestCounter that DPO2 P170521 was dropped when the triggers were not met. Also run the symmetry control explicitly (UPA 2009 US$2bn Banking Sector DPL vs NDA DPLs). 4. strongestCounter: add the December 2023 Finance Ministry and Executive Director rejection of the IMF Article IV debt projection, with the Business Standard and Deccan Herald URLs, as evidence that the advice is non-binding and contested. 5. The status 'unsupported' stands. The record should state that the narrative is analytic (our own assessment).

verdicts.dateTest: The claim is: Government of India (ACC) terminated K.V. Subramanian as IMF Executive Director, effective 30 Apr 2025. His tenure ran from Nov 2022 and was due to end around Oct/Nov 2025, so the termination falls inside it. Tribune/PTI: "The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet has terminated Subramanian's services effective April 30". BS 3 May 2025: the recall "takes place less than a week before the IMF board to decide on a proposal for financial help to Pakistan". The dates line up. The Pakistan-vote timing is a coincidence of dates and does not show a motive.
verdicts.identityTest: The person is Krishnamurthy V. Subramanian, former CEA (2018-21), IMF ED for the India/Bangladesh/Sri Lanka/Bhutan constituency from Nov 2022. Both BS articles name him with that office and those dates, so the identity matches. The book is India@100 (Rupa Publications).
verdicts.baseRate: Curtailing an IMF ED's term early is rare. EDs normally serve out their terms or leave for another post, so the early exit itself is unusual. That supports only the fact of removal, not either stated motive. I did not find a comparable early recall from another constituency to use as a symmetry test. The UPA/NDA and state controls in the SPEC do not apply to one personnel decision.
verdicts.denialFound: Subramanian was asked and did not respond. ThePrint/PTI: "Subramanian was not available for comment despite repeated attempts to contact him on his mobile phone" (https://theprint.in/india/krishnamurthy-subramanian-had-6-months-still-left-in-his-tenure-at-imf-why-did-modi-govt-recall-him/2615392/). I found no later public statement from him. The IMF said on the record: "The termination of ED Subramanian is a decision by the government of India" (BS 5 May 2025). Government of India: no official reason given. Tribune/PTI: "The reasons for Subramanian's exit have not been officially announced." Government sources also say he "resigned from his post citing personal reasons" after his service was curtailed.
verdicts.innocentReading: The government can recall a nominated ED at any time and does not have to give a reason. The early recall could reflect a routine wish to put its own nominee in place before a sensitive board vote (Pakistan EFF review), or a reshuffle. On this reading, Subramanian's formal "resignation citing personal reasons" is the whole story. The book-promotion and IMF-data reasons come only from unnamed government sources. Those sources have their own motive to frame the exit.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the narrative as written. It is correctly held as contested. Both cited Business Standard URLs open and say what the narrative attributes to them. BS 5 May: "Sources linked Subramanian's termination to allegations of impropriety in the promotion of his recent book titled India@100, and his criticism of IMF data sets that were not received well by the institution". It also carries the IMF's on-record statement that the termination was India's decision. The fact of removal is documented: the IMF confirmed it on the record and the ACC order is reported by several outlets. Both causal limbs, "for criticising the Fund" and "for misconduct", rest only on unnamed government sources. BS, PTI/ThePrint and Tribune may all carry the same sources, so they are not independent. The government gave no official reason and Subramanian did not respond. Under CONTRACT, anonymous sourcing does not meet "reported" (which needs named sourcing or documents). The motive claim therefore belongs at "alleged" with a contra, inside a contested narrative. It must not be promoted to an edge.
verdicts.corrections: 1) strongestCounter: replace "nor has Subramanian himself been found on the record responding" with "Subramanian was asked (PTI/ThePrint: 'not available for comment despite repeated attempts'). No response is on record." 2) strongestCounter overstates the IMF statement. It rules out the IMF removing him, but not India removing him because his criticism of IMF data strained relations. Change "directly contradicting any reading in which the IMF pushed him out for criticising it" to "rules out the IMF as the decision-maker; it does not address India's motive". 3) Add the ACC order effective 30 Apr 2025 (Tribune/PTI https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/nation/govt-fires-imf-director-6-months-ahead-of-tenure/amp) and ThePrint as sources. 4) Split the claim into limbs: (a) removal by GoI, documented; (b) misconduct (book promotion; govt sources say he "pressurised and intimidated" organisations to buy it), alleged by unnamed sources; (c) IMF-data criticism, alleged by unnamed sources; (d) Pakistan-vote timing, analytic coincidence. 5) Add to innocentReading the government-sources account that he "resigned citing personal reasons". 6) upgradeIf: the reported Union Bank of India bulk order (~2 lakh copies, ~Rs 7.25 crore; see nationalheraldindia.com) confirmed by a bank board record, RTI or Parliament answer. Congress's demand for a probe (Deccan Herald) is a named-party allegation that can be cited as such.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a sentence, the claim is "IMF lent India (Ministry of Finance) US$7bn / ≈₹18,060 cr with liberalisation conditions in 1991". The IMF money came in two separate pieces under two governments. (1) January 1991, Chandra Shekhar government, FM Yashwant Sinha: a CCFF drawing of Rs 1,884 cr (US$1.025bn) and a first-credit-tranche drawing of Rs 1,450 cr (US$789m), total Rs 3,334 cr (US$1.814bn). (2) The FM's request letter of 1991-08-27 and the IMF's approval of 1991-10-31, Rao government, FM Manmohan Singh: an 18-month stand-by arrangement of SDR 1,656m (≈US$2.2bn), paid out in instalments. The first instalment was SDR 85m in November 1991. The single "1991" date with to=null hides this two-stage, two-government timeline. The conditions in terms.conditions (51% foreign equity, 20% PSU disinvestment) are dated to the 1991-07-24 Budget speech, which is not an IMF document. The rupee conversion also fails the date test. It applies the post-July rate of ₹25.8/US$ to all of it, but the January drawings went through at about ₹18.4/US$ (Rs 3,334 cr / US$1.814bn).
verdicts.identityTest: The lender identity fails for the amount. The Wikipedia sentence reads: "The Government of India's immediate response was to secure an emergency loan of $7 billion from the International Monetary Fund by pledging 67 tons of India's gold reserves as collateral security." This merges two different creditors. The gold (47t to the Bank of England, 20t to UBS) backed commercial borrowing, and the same article says that raised about $600m. IMF purchases are not secured by gold. The Economic Survey 1991-92 passage quoted by V. Srinivas lists the crisis financing as separate items: "gold backed external borrowing, purchases from the Fund and the provision for quick disbursing aid from the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and several bilateral donors." So US$7bn is at most a multi-creditor total and cannot sit on an IMF→MoF edge. The borrower is also loose. IMF purchases are made by the member (Government of India, with RBI as fiscal agent), so min:ministry-of-finance can stand as shorthand, but the edge should say so.
verdicts.baseRate: Close to 100% of upper-credit-tranche IMF stand-by arrangements carry conditionality (performance criteria and structural benchmarks). So "with liberalisation conditions" tells you nothing that separates India 1991 from any other SBA. India's own record shows the same: the 1981 EFF also had conditions. On the control named in the finance SPEC (UPA 2004–14 against NDA 2014–26 Union borrowing), the lens gives the same null for both: India has had no IMF arrangement since the 1991–93 SBA ended. The 1991 edge is also outside the fleet's 2000–2026 window, so it can only work as literature or narrative calibration, not as symmetry evidence.
verdicts.denialFound: A response is on record, though it is not a denial of the loan. FM Manmohan Singh in the 1991-92 Budget speech (24 July 1991), quoted in V. Srinivas, "India at 70: IMF Relations" (https://taxboard.rajasthan.gov.in/images/India_at_70.pdf): "It has been alleged by some people that the reform program has been dictated by the IMF and the World Bank... the conditions we have accepted reflect no more than the implementation of the reform program as outlined in my letters of intent sent to the IMF and the World Bank, and are wholly consistent with our national interests. The bulk of the reform program is based on the election manifesto of our Party." The IMF's own history (quoted in the same document) says the devaluation "was not made at the insistence of the Fund". The record should carry this as the contra on the conditionality framing.
verdicts.innocentReading: This was a standard balance-of-payments rescue. India drew on its quota under the CCFF (oil-price shock from the Gulf War) and the first credit tranche in January 1991, then took an ordinary SBA in October 1991, with structural benchmarks the government says it wrote into its own letter of intent. Other creditors (World Bank SAL, ADB, Japan and other bilateral donors, plus gold-backed commercial borrowing) supplied the rest of the roughly US$7bn often quoted for the whole package. The IMF was one lender among several, not the source of US$7bn.
verdicts.reason: The amount at the centre of the edge (a=18,060 cr, i.e. US$7bn from IMF to MoF) is wrong on the evidence I could open. Wikipedia does say "$7 billion... from the IMF", but that sentence ties it to a gold pledge that went to the Bank of England and UBS, not the IMF. The Economic Survey 1991-92, as quoted, puts IMF money at US$1.814bn (Rs 3,334 cr) in January 1991 plus an SDR 1,656m (≈US$2.2bn) SBA approved 1991-10-31 and drawn in instalments. That is about US$4bn committed, roughly Rs 8,000–9,000 cr, not Rs 18,060 cr. The claim is also a conjunction problem. The terms.conditions list (51% foreign equity, 20% PSU disinvestment) comes from a Wikipedia paragraph describing Singh's Budget-speech reform programme, not IMF loan conditions, so the edge implies something its source does not say. The d-field honestly flags "unverified", but a flag does not rescue a numeric amount that is known to be wrong. imf.org returned 403 and the RBI History ch.12 PDF sits behind a CAPTCHA, so the upgrade path is still open. After correction the edge can stand at reported, or be split into two edges.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Replace a/amountCr 18060. Either split into two edges or use a sum with components in d. Edge 1: IMF→India (MoF), 1991-01, CCFF US$1.025bn (Rs 1,884 cr) + first credit tranche US$789m (Rs 1,450 cr) = Rs 3,334 cr, source Economic Survey 1991-92 pp 4-17 as quoted at https://taxboard.rajasthan.gov.in/images/India_at_70.pdf. Edge 2: IMF→India, SBA SDR 1,656m (≈US$2.2bn), requested 1991-08-27, approved 1991-10-31, 18 months (later extended), first instalment SDR 85m in Nov 1991; the rupee amount must be the amount actually drawn, converted at the drawing-date rate, not ₹25.8 applied to the whole. 2. Remove the US$7bn figure from the IMF edge. If kept, move it to a narrative or multi-creditor 'package' note (IMF + World Bank SAL + ADB + bilateral + gold-backed BoE/UBS borrowing), and note that Wikipedia wrongly ties the gold pledge to the IMF. 3. terms.conditions: drop "foreign-equity liberalisation up to 51%" and "PSU disinvestment up to 20%" as IMF conditions; Wikipedia attributes them to the 1991-07-24 Budget speech. Replace with the structural-benchmark areas in the programme (industrial policy, trade liberalisation, domestic pricing, public-enterprise reform, financial sector, tax reform, expenditure control) and the targets (reserves above 1.5 months of imports by end-1992/93, inflation ≤6%, CAD about 2.5% of GDP). 4. terms.instrument: "CCFF + first credit tranche (Jan 1991); upper-credit-tranche SBA (Oct 1991)". 5. from: "1991-01" / "1991-10-31"; add the office-holders (FM Yashwant Sinha for January, FM Manmohan Singh for the SBA). 6. Add a contra carrying Manmohan Singh's 1991-07-24 Budget speech statement that the conditions reflect India's own letter of intent. 7. srcs: add the Srinivas/Economic Survey source. Keep upgradeIf (IMF LOI/EBS/91/… staff report, RBI History vol. 4 ch. 12, Economic Survey 1991-92 from indiabudget.gov.in). killIf is already met for the US$7bn amount.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out, is "RBI borrowed from the Bank of England against 47 t of gold, 1991-05-21 to 05-31, raising US$600m." Wikipedia does say this: "The Reserve Bank of India had to airlift 47 tons of gold to the Bank of England and 20 tons of gold to the Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) to raise $600 million ... The gold was transported to London via a chartered plane from May 21 to May 31, 1991" (citing a 2009 Telegraph piece). The primary record gives different dates. RBI History Vol. 4, excerpted in Business Standard on 4 Sep 2013: "the Reserve Bank in July 1991 pledged 46.91 tonnes of gold with the Bank of Japan (BoJ) and the Bank of England (BoE) and raised a loan of US$ 405.0 million. This loan was redeemed by the Reserve Bank by repayment between September and November 1991." Rangarajan's memoir, excerpted in ThePrint, says: "46.91 tonnes of gold were dispatched in four consignments by air beginning 4 July." The May 1991 shipments were a different deal: SBI's 20 t to UBS ("gold was dispatched in four consignments in May 1991"). So the claim's 1991-05-21 to 05-31 window belongs to the UBS deal. The BoE/BoJ pledge actually runs from 4 July to November 1991 (disbursed in July, repaid Sep–Nov). That also moves it after the 21 June 1991 change of government. The claim's own killIf ("Primary record gives different tonnage or dates") is met.
verdicts.identityTest: Counterparty is incomplete. The official history names the Bank of Japan and the Bank of England together as lenders on the 46.91 t pledge, not the BoE alone. The US$600m total also joins two transactions with different actors. (1) RBI pledged its own reserve gold to BoJ/BoE for US$405m. (2) State Bank of India sold 20 t of government-owned confiscated gold to UBS with a repurchase option, for about US$200m ("Twenty metric tonnes (MT) of gold from the government account was made available to the SBI for sale with a repurchase option to yield a little more than US$ 200.0 million"). The UBS leg was not an RBI loan, and its gold was not RBI's. That also affects c009, whose borrower should be SBI (on Government of India gold), not wel:rbi. So the claim is a conjunction: it takes a secondary source's merged account and assigns the combined amount and the wrong dates to one counterparty pair.
verdicts.baseRate: Gold-collateralised borrowing from other central banks is a standard emergency tool; for example, Italy borrowed from the Bundesbank against gold in 1974 and Portugal pledged gold in the 1970s–80s. Nothing about it is discriminating, and no wrongdoing is implied. The SPEC control (UPA 2004–14 vs NDA 2014–26 borrowing) has no equivalent gold pledge on either side. The closest later event is the RBI's 2009 purchase of 200 t from the IMF, which went the other way. The symmetry check therefore neither helps nor hurts the claim, which fails on facts, not framing.
verdicts.denialFound: None needed and none found (not asked). This is not an accusation. The official account is the RBI's own history, Vol. 4, together with the RBI Annual Report 1991-92 and a Rajya Sabha answer by MoS Finance Pankaj Chaudhary, both cited by The Quint. It contradicts the Wikipedia dates and amount.
verdicts.innocentReading: Wikipedia's 2009 newspaper source merged the May SBI–UBS sale-and-repurchase with the July RBI–BoE/BoJ pledge into one "RBI airlift, US$600m, May 21–31" story. The record then took that merged account at face value.
verdicts.reason: The only source is Wikipedia. It does say what the claim says, but the RBI's official history contradicts it on date, counterparty and amount. The 46.91 t pledge was made in July 1991 (shipped from 4 July) to both the Bank of Japan and the Bank of England, for US$405m, and was repaid Sep–Nov 1991. The May 1991 shipments and roughly US$200m belong to a separate SBI sale-and-repurchase of government gold to UBS. The edge as written (BoE→RBI, 21–31 May, US$600m) is wrong on each of these points, and its own killIf is triggered. It should be superseded by a corrected edge, which can be tiered documented because the RBI official history, the RBI Annual Report 1991-92 and a Rajya Sabha answer all agree.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Kill c008 as written and set supersededBy to the new id.
2. New edge fin:bank-of-england + fin:bank-of-japan → wel:rbi, pred loan, tier documented.
   - lab: "1991 gold pledge — 46.91 t with BoJ and BoE"
   - a: US$405m, about ₹1,045 crore at the post-devaluation ≈₹25.8/US$ (flag the rate as ours, not the source's)
   - from: 1991-07-04, to: 1991-11 (repaid Sep–Nov 1991)
   - srcs: RBI History Vol. 4 excerpt (https://www.business-standard.com/article/opinion/when-gold-saved-the-day-for-india-113090401144_1.html); Rangarajan, Forks in the Road, excerpt (https://theprint.in/pageturner/excerpt/how-chandra-shekhar-govt-and-rbi-hatched-a-plan-to-lease-out-indias-gold-in-1991/1236610/); RBI Annual Report 1991-92 and the Rajya Sabha answer as cited at https://www.thequint.com/news/webqoof/india-brings-100-tonnes-gold-from-uk-viral-post-pledged-gold-july-1991-fact-check
   - Split per lender is not stated, so either split `a` or record both lenders as jointly responsible for the total.
3. Fix c009:
   - borrower: SBI (fin:sbi), not wel:rbi; the gold was Government of India confiscated gold
   - instrument: sale with repurchase option, effectively gold-collateralised
   - amount: about US$200m, split into a spot sale plus an additional UBS loan
   - dates: shipped in four consignments in May 1991; repurchased Nov/Dec 1991
   - source: the same RBI History excerpt
4. Delete the "US$600m total" and the Wikipedia-only sourcing. Keep Wikipedia only as a pointer.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the State of Kerala argued in Original Suit No. 1 of 2024 that the Union (Ministry of Finance) went beyond its Article 293 power when it imposed a Net Borrowing Ceiling (NBC) for FY2023-24. The ceiling was set by Letter No. 40(1)/PF-S/2023-24 dated 27.03.2023, and the suit was decided by an SC order dated 01.04.2024. The dates line up. The order says 'Letter No. 40(1)/PF-S/2023-24 (dated 27.03.2023): Through this letter, the Defendant has imposed a 'Net Borrowing Ceiling'' and ends 'DATED: 01.04.2024'. The edge's from='2023' matches the letter. The under-utilisation Kerala claims covers FY2020-21 to FY2022-23. The over-borrowing the Union relies on covers FY2017-18 to FY2019-20. Both periods fall inside the same Union government's term, so there is no tenure gap. Status after the order: SC Observer still lists the case as pending, with no Constitution Bench hearing recorded. On 19 Dec 2025 the MoF cut Kerala's Jan-Mar 2026 limit by about ₹5,944 crore (The Federal). The claim is therefore still live and not superseded.
verdicts.identityTest: The parties match: 'State of Kerala …Plaintiff(s) versus Union of India …Defendant(s)', 2024 INSC 253, bench of Surya Kant J and K.V. Viswanathan J. The order names the actor as 'the Defendant – Union of India', not the Ministry of Finance by name. The letter reference PF-S (Public Finance–States division, Department of Expenditure, MoF) supports attributing it to min:ministry-of-finance. That is a reasonable inference, but the source does not state it.
verdicts.baseRate: The ceiling itself does not single out Kerala. The NBC is 3% of GSDP for every state. In March 2022 the Department of Expenditure told all states that borrowing by state PSUs/SPVs serviced from the state budget counts toward the ceiling. Reporting names Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Punjab as affected, and cash-flow stress hit both AP (then YSRCP) and Kerala. The same approach reads the same way for the SPEC control (BJP-run vs opposition-run states), because the rule applies to all states. What does set Kerala apart is that it is the only state that sued under Article 131. It is also the size of its own adjustments: FY2021-22 ₹9,197.15 cr, FY2022-23 ₹13,067.78 cr, FY2023-24 ₹4,354.72 cr. These come from its own admitted over-borrowing in FY2017-20 and off-budget KIIFB/pension-company borrowing. Any claim of discrimination would be analytic. This claim only records the plea, so no discrimination is asserted.
verdicts.denialFound: The Union's response is in the same order and is already carried as literature:c018. Para 20: over-utilised by '₹2,941.82 crores till F.Y. 2022-23'. Para 28: 'Central Government has an inherent power as a lender to impose conditions'; off-budget borrowings are includable 'if they are used to by-pass the conditions imposed under Article 293'. Para 33: the hardship 'is actually a consequence of its own actions'. Para 36: the Union gave consent for ₹13,608 crore, via circulars dated 08.03.2024 and 19.03.2024. Minister Sitharaman also said there was 'no proposal to relax borrowing limits for Kerala, other states' (Business Standard, 4 Dec 2023). Source: https://indiankanoon.org/doc/191833676/
verdicts.innocentReading: This is an ordinary fiscal-federalism dispute. Since 2022 the Union has applied a uniform 3%-of-GSDP ceiling that counts off-budget and public-account borrowing for every state. It also deducted Kerala's admitted past over-borrowing. Kerala disputes whether Article 293(3) allows this. The SC found no interim case for Kerala and sent the constitutional questions to five judges. No one is accused of wrongdoing, only of reading Article 293 differently.
verdicts.reason: The source says everything the claim says. Quotes from the order: 'quantified as three percent of the projected Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) for the F.Y. 2023-24, which came to INR 32,442 crores'. 'the ceiling has also been applied to certain borrowings by such enterprises'. 'whether INR 24,434 crores as claimed in the written note or INR 10,722 crores as alternatively claimed'. 'we find prima facie merit in the submission of the Union of India that after inclusion of off budget borrowing …the State has no unutilized fiscal space' (para 27). 'we have referred the matter to a larger bench of five judges' (para 29). The claim records a party's pleading and carries a contra (c018), so 'alleged' is correct under CONTRACT. The fact that the plea was made is documented; the substance of the plea is not yet decided. I could not refute it. The remaining problems are framing and schema issues, not errors of fact.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Text: scope the 'prima facie merit' phrase. Write: 'at the interim-injunction stage, on the fiscal-space/under-utilisation question (para 27); the Court declined to decide the Article 293 reading (para 29), and its observations have "no bearing on the final outcome" (para 39)'. As written, it can be read as a merits ruling for the Union.
2. Text: 'referred Article 293 to a Constitution Bench' is accurate. Better: 'referred five questions (paras 9–10), including the scope of Art 293(3), the FC-recommendation consultation question and the RBI debt-manager role, to a five-judge bench; still pending as of Sept 2026'.
3. Field `a`: 24434 on an MoF→Kerala edge wrongly suggests the Union acted on ₹24,434 crore. That figure is Kerala's claimed under-utilised space. Set a=32442 (the ceiling actually imposed) or null, and keep 24,434/10,722 in benefit.amountCr.
4. Field d: 24,434 was 'claimed in the written note'/'in negotiations with the Union'. 10,722 was 'orally prayed during the hearing'. Add the stated need of ₹26,226 crore (para 5(iii)).
5. Field pred: CONTRACT defines 'enforce' as cancellation, suspension, freeze, investigation, sanction or debarment. A borrowing ceiling is a loan condition, so 'law' (s = the NBC letter 40(1)/PF-S/2023-24 or MoF/Department of Expenditure → Kerala) fits better. Alternatively, keep the edge and note that the actor is 'Union of India (DoE PF-S letter)' as named in the order.
6. Add a note: the Union gave consent for ₹13,608 crore during the proceedings (para 36). Add a later lead: the 19 Dec 2025 cut of about ₹5,944 crore (thefederal.com).

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: the World Bank published India's DB ranks of 142 (DB2015, Oct 2014, data to Jun 2014), 130 (DB2016), 130 (DB2017), 100 (DB2018), 77 (DB2019) and 63 (DB2020, Oct 2019). The record's from 2014 / to 2019 matches the publication dates. The GIA review covered DB2016–DB2020, and irregularities were found only in DB2018 and DB2020 (China DB18–20; Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia and UAE DB20). So "across the editions later found manipulated" overstates things. DB2015–DB2017 and DB2019 were not found manipulated, and most of India's climb (130→100→77) came in DB2018 and DB2019. DB2015 was never reviewed. The window overlaps, but the wording needs narrowing. Date test passes with a wording fix.
verdicts.identityTest: Partial fail. The edge subject is min:ministry-of-finance. The DB rank is a World Bank output about the economy "India". The nodal body for India's Ease of Doing Business reforms and for promoting the rank was DIPP/DPIIT (Ministry of Commerce & Industry), which already exists in the inventory as fin:dpiit (worldbank-projects.json). The "benefit.who = MoF" is also unsourced: the reputational use was by the Union government and PM, not specifically MoF. The object fin:doing-business-report is correct. The rank values are correct per the Wikipedia table, whose India row reads "63 || 77 || 100 || 130 || 130 || 142" for 2020→2015. But the record's `lab`, and entity note line 712, say "130 (DB2017/18)". That is wrong because DB2018 = 100.
verdicts.baseRate: 4 of 190 economies (about 2%) had corrected irregularities in the GIA verification of 2020-12-08, so the property "not found irregular" is shared by about 98% and does not discriminate. India's 79-place as-published climb is among the largest in the index, which does discriminate. But CGD (Sandefur & Wadhwa, 2018-02-05) found it is "mostly an artefact of methodological changes": under a consistent methodology India "rose only 5 places" in DB2018, and the DB2017 rank would have been 123, not 130. The 142→63 series also crosses methodology breaks. DB2016 back-revised India's DB2015 rank to 134. Symmetry check: under the UPA control, as-published ranks were 116–134 (DB2006–DB2014) with no comparable climb. Applying the same "rose during a manipulated edition" lens to Saudi Arabia (92→62) gives a real irregularity finding, so the lens can detect one, and for India it did not.
verdicts.denialFound: This is not an allegation, so no contra is strictly required. On the record: the World Bank defended India's rise in Feb 2018. Shanta Devarajan said the improvements "are not an artefact of methodology, or an artefact of data". India Country Director Junaid Ahmad said "all the shifts that you're seeing [are] based on ground realities". Both are quoted in CGD, https://www.cgdev.org/blog/world-banks-misleading-defense-doing-business-index. Devarajan was later named in the WilmerHale findings on China. No Government of India statement specific to the audit was found; not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: India's rank rose partly on real de jure reforms (IBC 2016, GST 2017, Delhi/Mumbai construction-permit and electricity changes) and substantially on World Bank methodology changes that it applied retroactively. Neither involves data manipulation. The 2020 scandal concerned China, Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. India's two appearances in the GIA report were reviewed and not classified as irregularities: the DB16 Mumbai Getting Electricity change, and a DB17 construction-permits methodology concern that "Management reconfirmed that they were not data irregularities".
verdicts.reason: The core facts hold. I confirmed the ranks 142 and 63 in the Wikipedia table I opened. The GIA text I opened (documents1.worldbank.org, Report FY21-2-4-2104615) lists nine irregularities in four countries, none of them India. So the claim is not refuted. But the only listed source (Wikipedia) supports the ranks and not the "no India irregularity in the audit record" clause, which rests on the unlisted GIA report. The subject node is also the wrong ministry. The juxtaposition with "editions later found manipulated" is our own inference; it implies something neither fact states, and the claim's own caveat defuses it. That makes it analytic, not reported. Wikipedia is a tertiary summary, not a credible outlet with named sourcing. Two limits should be recorded. First, GIA verified management's review and "did not assess DEC management's technical judgement". Second, the GIA assurance review separately found that 8 of 25 DB staff admitted manipulating data, without naming the country. So "no India irregularity" is only as strong as management's reconfirmation.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Set tier to "analytic" to match pred "analytic". Or split into a documented rank claim citing the DB2015 and DB2020 reports (URLs in the Wikipedia refs, e.g. openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/32436/9781464814402.pdf) plus an analytic juxtaposition claim. 2) Fix `lab` and entity note line 712: change "130 (DB2017/18)" to "130 (DB2016), 130 (DB2017), 100 (DB2018), 77 (DB2019)". 3) Change the subject s from min:ministry-of-finance to fin:dpiit, the nodal EoDB department, or to the India economy node. Change benefit.who to "Union government (DPIIT/PMO)", with confidence unknown. 4) Reword to "across DB2015–DB2020, a span that includes the DB2018 and DB2020 editions later found to contain irregularities for China, Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE", and mark the ranks as as-published, since there are methodology breaks and DB2015 India was revised to 134. 5) Add the GIA verification report URL to srcs, quoting "Management reconfirmed that they were not data irregularities during GIA's verification", and note that "GIA did not assess DEC management's technical judgement". 6) Add CGD (Sandefur & Wadhwa 2018-02-05, https://www.cgdev.org/blog/change-world-bank-methodology-not-reform-explains-indias-rise-doing-business) to srcs and to innocentReading, since methodology changes, not reform, explain most of the DB2018 jump. 7) Revise killIf to something falsifiable. For example: kill if a DB report shows different as-published India ranks; upgradeIf as it stands.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: AIIB signed a US$500m COVID-19 health loan agreement with the Government of India (DEA, Ministry of Finance) on 2020-05-08. The PIB release confirms it (PRID 1622145, "Posted On: 08 MAY 2020"): "The Government of India and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) signed a US$ 500 million 'COVID-19 Emergency Response and Health Systems Preparedness Project' here today". FPJ (2020-09-16) says the same: "the agreement was signed on May 8, 2020". The AIIB board approved it on 2020-05-07. Review began in April, and the loan co-finances the World Bank's US$1bn project P173836 approved in early April, so preparation started before the standoff. The Ladakh standoff began with the Pangong Tso clash on 5–6 May 2020. "During the border standoff" is technically true, but the signing came within days of the standoff starting and before it was widely public. The Galwan clash (15 June) came five weeks later.
verdicts.identityTest: Parties match. The PIB release names Sameer Kumar Khare, Additional Secretary, DEA, Ministry of Finance, for the Government of India, and Rajat Misra, Director General (Acting), for AIIB. The instrument is AIIB's COVID-19 Crisis Recovery Facility, which matches MoS Finance Anurag Thakur's Lok Sabha reply of 2020-09-16 ("two loan agreements with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank under COVID-19 Crisis Recovery Facility"). The s and t fields (fin:aiib to min:ministry-of-finance) are correct.
verdicts.baseRate: Not discriminating. In March–June 2020 India signed COVID emergency and budget-support loans with every multilateral lender it uses: World Bank US$1bn (P173836, which this AIIB loan co-finances), ADB US$1.5bn (signed 2020-04-28), NDB and AIIB. India was already AIIB's largest borrower, at about US$3.6bn or roughly 25% of AIIB lending (FPJ). So a COVID loan from AIIB in May 2020 fits the usual pattern, and far more than 80% of India's multilateral lenders shared the property. The UPA-versus-NDA symmetry control does not apply to AIIB, which only began lending in 2016.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial: the government confirmed the loan. Its account came in MoS Finance Anurag Thakur's Lok Sabha reply of 2020-09-16. He presented both loans as COVID-19 Crisis Recovery Facility borrowing for health-systems preparedness and PMGKY social protection (Scroll, https://scroll.in/latest/973284/india-took-two-loans-of-over-rs-9000-crore-from-china-backed-bank-union-minister-tells-parliament). The criticism came from Rahul Gandhi (Congress), over "huge loans" from a China-backed bank. FPJ itself writes: "There is nothing wrong with borrowing from the bank in which India (7.6 per cent) is the second-largest shareholder... that does not make it a Chinese agency."
verdicts.innocentReading: This was a routine co-financing tranche. AIIB's US$500m sat alongside the World Bank's US$1bn in a single pandemic health project that was prepared in April under AIIB's COVID-19 Crisis Recovery Facility. It was approved on 7 May, before the standoff was widely known. The borrower is a multilateral bank in which India is the second-largest shareholder (7.6%) and the largest borrower. The timing follows the pandemic, not the border.
verdicts.reason: The core fact survives: US$500m, signed 2020-05-08, Government of India with AIIB. It is confirmed by a primary record (PIB release PRID 1622145, 08 May 2020) and by the MoS Finance Lok Sabha reply of 16 Sep 2020, so it qualifies as documented, not just reported. The single cited source (FPJ) supports the amount, date and purpose. It does not give a rupee figure. The official figure in Thakur's reply is about ₹3,676 crore, not the ≈₹3,785 crore the record computes. The "during the border standoff" framing is literally true but leaves out that approval and preparation came before the standoff and that the loan co-financed a World Bank project.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Set tier to "documented". Add srcs ["PIB 2020-05-08", "https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1622145"] and ["Scroll 2020-09-16 (MoS Finance Lok Sabha reply)", "https://scroll.in/latest/973284/india-took-two-loans-of-over-rs-9000-crore-from-china-backed-bank-union-minister-tells-parliament"]. Also add the AIIB project page https://www.aiib.org/en/projects/details/2020/approved/India-COVID-19-Emergency-Response-and-Health-Systems-Preparedness-Project.html. That clears the upgradeIf.
2. Change a and benefit.amountCr from 3785 to 3676, citing "₹3,676 crore as stated in Lok Sabha reply" (or keep 3785 but note that the official figure is ₹3,676 crore). This also resolves the conflict with adb-aiib.json, which wrongly attributes ₹3,676 crore to FPJ; FPJ gives no crore figure.
3. In d, add: "AIIB board approval 2020-05-07; co-financing of World Bank P173836 (US$1bn); project name 'COVID-19 Emergency Response and Health Systems Preparedness Project'; signatories Sameer Kumar Khare (DEA) and Rajat Misra (AIIB)."
4. Qualify "during the border standoff" as "signed days after the 5–6 May Pangong Tso clash; prepared from April, before the standoff". Add innocentReading: "pandemic co-financing alongside World Bank; India 2nd-largest AIIB shareholder and largest borrower".
5. Add contra: "Government (Thakur, LS 2020-09-16) framed both loans as COVID Crisis Recovery Facility borrowing; FPJ notes AIIB is multilateral, not a Chinese agency."

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: AIIB (lender) agreed a US$750m budget-support loan with the Government of India (DEA, Ministry of Finance), signed 2020-06-19. Primary confirmation from PIB release PRID 1632652, posted 19 JUN 2020 6:20PM: "The Government of India and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) here today signed a $750 million 'COVID-19 Active Response and Expenditure Support Programme'... signed by Shri Sameer Kumar Khare, Additional Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs". The AIIB project page for 000409 gives "APPROVED FUNDING USD750 million ... FINANCING APPROVAL June 16, 2020". The signing date holds. "Three days after Galwan" does not: FPJ itself dates the clash to 15 June ("took place on June 15"), and 15 to 19 June is four days. The approval came the day after the clash. The signing came three days after the AIIB Board approval, not three days after Galwan. Processing began before the clash: ADB approved CARES loans 3915/3916 on 2020-04-28, and FPJ says AIIB review "started in May 2020".
verdicts.identityTest: The parties are right. The lender is AIIB, project 000409 (CARES co-financing with ADB 54182-001). The borrower is the Government of India, signed by DEA Additional Secretary Sameer Kumar Khare and, for AIIB, acting Director General Rajat Misra. So s=fin:aiib and t=min:ministry-of-finance are correct. The ownership attribute is wrong. The 26.5% figure is China's voting power, not its ownership. China subscribes about 30% of AIIB capital and holds about 26-27% of votes (CRS IF10154/R44754; CGD). FPJ calls it "shareholder (26.5 per cent)" and the claim repeats that as "26.5% China-owned". The same mix-up applies to India's 7.6%, which is its vote share; its capital share is about 8.4%.
verdicts.baseRate: This is non-discriminating. India was AIIB's largest borrower both before and after June 2020: FPJ says "around USD 3.6 billion which is around 25 per cent of the AIIB's overall lending". It borrowed from AIIB throughout, e.g. US$500m on 2020-05-08, and more later in 2020-21. Almost all of India's AIIB sovereign loans are signed by DEA. The AIIB loan was one tranche of a US$2.25bn CARES package whose lead financier, ADB, gave US$1.5bn in April. The COVID Crisis Recovery Facility put out similar budget-support loans to many members that year. The Galwan timing is a coincidence of date, not a sign of anything. The control is symmetric: under the UPA, India was a founding-era supporter of AIIB, joining in 2014, and borrowing from it continued unchanged across the border crisis.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed, because the government confirmed the loan itself. The PIB release PRID 1632652 (https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1632652) gives the official reason: "social assistance for compensating economic loss to vulnerable sections including women and social security measures enhanced for affected workers". FPJ also gives the innocent reading ("There is nothing wrong with borrowing from the bank in which India (7.6 per cent) is the second-largest shareholder... that does not make it a Chinese agency"). I found no statement from the government or AIIB about the Galwan timing specifically. None found; not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is the AIIB part of an ADB-led pandemic budget-support package. ADB approved its US$1.5bn on 2020-04-28, and AIIB processing started in May. AIIB Board approval (16 June) and signing (19 June) followed the co-financing schedule set before the clash. India is AIIB's second-largest shareholder and largest borrower, and borrows there for price reasons. The money paid for PMGKY-type cash transfers.
verdicts.reason:
The core fact holds: US$750m signed on 2020-06-19, confirmed by primary records (PIB PRID 1632652 and AIIB 000409). But the claim as written is wrong in three places.
(1) The source chain is misstated. FPJ literally says "two loans proposed during the COVID-19 period — USD 500 million and USD 250 million", while also giving a total of "USD 1,250 million". FPJ is internally inconsistent, and the claim's note that the US$250m was an "extraction error" is false: that figure is in FPJ's own text. The US$750m comes from PIB and AIIB, not FPJ.
(2) "Three days after Galwan" is off by one. The clash was 15 June (per FPJ), so the signing was four days later; three days is the gap from AIIB approval to signing.
(3) "26.5% China-owned" mixes up China's voting power with its capital share, which is about 30%.
The edge also duplicates adb-aiib:c003, which already records the same loan at tier documented.
verdicts.corrections:
1. srcs: add PIB "Government of India & AIIB sign an Agreement for $750 Million for COVID-19 support for India", 2020-06-19, https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1632652. Add AIIB 000409, https://www.aiib.org/en/projects/details/2020/approved/India-COVID-19-Active-Response-and-Expenditure-Support.html. Keep FPJ only as commentary.
2. tier: change to documented.
3. text/d: state US$750m directly from PIB and AIIB. Delete "FPJ total ... implies US$750m" and the "extraction error" sentence. Record instead that FPJ misreports the amount as US$250m, with an inconsistent total of US$1,250m.
4. lab/text: change "three days after Galwan" to "four days after the Galwan clash of 2020-06-15; AIIB Board approval 2020-06-16". Add the signatories: Sameer Kumar Khare (Additional Secretary, DEA) and Rajat Misra (acting Director General, AIIB).
5. Ownership: replace "AIIB 26.5% China-owned" with "China about 26.5% of AIIB voting power (about 30% of subscribed capital); India 7.6% of votes". Apply the same fix to the fin:aiib node and to the China-to-AIIB own edge at literature.json around lines 2096-2111, which have the same FPJ-sourced error.
6. Conversion: ₹76/US$ is fine; the RBI reference rate was about ₹76.2 on 2020-06-19, giving about ₹5,715 crore. Keep a=5700 and mark it approximate.
7. terms.conditions: add "ADB lead cofinancier; ADB policy-based-lending policies applied by AIIB Board decision".

verdicts.identityTest: FAILS. The edge targets fin:government-of-china (ty: state), but the source's subject is "China Inc", meaning Chinese companies. The source also says outright that the growth after 2014 came from private firms and not the state: "with a noticeable shift from state-driven to market-driven investment from the Chinese private sector." verdicts.baseRate: Routing FDI through Singapore or Mauritius is not distinctive. For many years Singapore and Mauritius have together supplied roughly a third or more of India's recorded FDI equity inflows, and investors from the US, Japan and Europe use the same routes. Growth after 2014 was also broad: total FDI into India rose sharply from every major source. By DPIIT's source-country measure, China is small. DPIIT reports about US$2.45bn (0.43% of equity inflows) for April 2000 to December 2021, and about US$2.51bn (0.32%, ranked 23rd) up to March 2026. So the US$8bn MOFCOM figure is itself contested from the Indian side.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; not asked. The PRC government has no reason to respond to a tally of private investment. The contrary data point is DPIIT/Lok Sabha: cumulative Chinese FDI equity of about US$2.45bn (April 2000 to December 2021), far below MOFCOM's US$8bn. The gap comes from different measurement bases (MOFCOM counts by ultimate parent; DPIIT by immediate source country). This should be recorded as a contra/killIf note, not as a denial.
verdicts.innocentReading: This was private Chinese corporate capital (smartphone makers, Alibaba and Tencent stakes in startups, pharma acquisitions) following India's market after 2014, as capital from every other source country did. The source itself describes a shift away from state-driven investment. The US$26bn headline is mostly pledged, unapproved infrastructure bids. Singapore routing is the normal FDI structure for most foreign investors.
verdicts.reason: The figures are faithfully taken from the source: US$1.6bn before 2014, at least US$8bn after, at least 25% undercount, at least US$26bn including announcements, US$4.4bn greenfield, about US$15bn pledged, and Xiaomi US$504m (Rs 3,500 crore) via Singapore.
