(1) It points the money at the Government of China, when the source credits the growth after 2014 to a "shift from state-driven to market-driven investment from the Chinese private sector". (2) It calls the infrastructure pledges "SOE-dominated", when the source uses "predominantly state-owned enterprises" only for the US$1.6bn stock before 2014. Together these turn a source that argues for private capital into support for state capture. The numbers can stay at reported tier (one credible outlet with named data: MOFCOM). The actor attribution and the SOE clause cannot.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: JICA made MAHSR ODA loans, tranches I–V, to the Government of India with NHSRCL as executing agency, from 2017 to 2023-12-21, on tied (STEP) terms. The terms confirm for tranche V. JICA press 2023-12-22: "On December 21, the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) signed loan agreements ... Project for the Construction of Mumbai-Ahmedabad High Speed Rail (V) (loan amount: 400,000 million yen)". The terms table reads "400,000 0.1 0.1 50 15 Tied". The claim's "from": "2018" is wrong. JICA's own India press release of 2023-12-21 says JICA has supported MAHSR "by providing ODA loans with the cumulative commitment amount of JPY 1 trillion and 50 billion (INR 59,396 crore) since 2017", so the start date should be 2017. No tenure-overlap problem otherwise.
verdicts.identityTest:
The entities resolve. The JICA release names the executing agency as "National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited, 2nd FLOOR, ASIA BHAWAN, Road NO-205, Dwarka Sector 9, New Delhi". The fin:nhsrcl node has CIN null (MCA is blocked), which is acceptable for a PSU named by address in the lender's document. The problem is not identity. It is what "Tied" means. The claim reads "Tied" as "the eligible-supplier set is Japanese by design". JICA's STEP Operational Rules (2013) define it more narrowly:
- The prime contractor must be a Japanese company or a JV led by a Japanese company.
- "The procurement condition for sub-contracts is general untied."
- "the bilateral tied condition (i.e. not only Japanese companies but also companies in a recipient country are eligible for a prime contractor) may be applied to a certain bidding package(s) once it becomes evident that no Japanese company is expected to bid".
- Not less than 30% of contract value must be goods or services of Japanese origin.
So "Tied" does not mean a Japanese-only supplier set.
verdicts.baseRate: This part is not discriminating. Tied procurement is a standard feature of every JICA STEP loan: it is a condition of the instrument, set under OECD tied-aid rules, not something specific to India or MAHSR. The SDG programme signed the same day was "Un-tied" at 2.10%/30y, which shows the tie follows the instrument, not the borrower. For the SPEC control (Chinese official finance to Indian private companies, per AidData), the claim runs no comparison at all. It swaps in multilateral procurement as the comparator, and the one cited URL says nothing about multilateral procurement.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; nobody was asked. JICA's own record effectively contradicts the claim. JICA India press release of 2022-01-21 (https://www.jica.go.jp/india/english/office/topics/press220121.html): "National High-Speed Railway Corporation Ltd (NHSRCL) and IRCON International Ltd have concluded the contract for Track Package T-2 ... about 47% of total alignment". The same release says Japan Railway Track Consultants "will work as Nominated Sub Contractor" and that "Track packages offers a unique opportunity for Indian companies". L&T press release of 2022-12-05 (https://www.larsentoubro.com/pressreleases/2022/2022-12-05-lt-construction-awarded-yet-another-contract-large-in-the-bullet-train-project): "L&T is already executing civil viaduct and station packages C4, C5 & C6, special steel bridges packages P4(X) & P4(Y) and Ballastless Trackworks (Package No: T3)".
verdicts.innocentReading: STEP tying is the price of 0.1%/50-year money. It restricts prime contractorship and requires at least 30% Japanese content, but it lets in Indian primes where no Japanese firm bids, and subcontracts are untied. In practice the large civil and track packages went to Indian primes (L&T: C4, C5, C6 and T3; IRCON: T-2), with Japanese firms as nominated subcontractors or as advisers (JRTC, JARTS). The Japanese-restricted segment is mainly systems, rolling stock and consulting, which is the Shinkansen technology India chose to buy.
verdicts.reason: The claim meets its own killIf condition. The record's killIf reads: "Evidence that MAHSR civil packages went to Indian firms ... despite tying". JICA's own 2022-01-21 release names Indian PSU IRCON as prime contractor for track package T-2 (47% of the alignment). L&T's own release lists it as executing C4, C5, C6, P4(X), P4(Y) and T3. JICA's STEP Operational Rules also contradict the claim's gloss that the "eligible-supplier set is Japanese by design": subcontracts are untied, a "bilateral tied" exception admits recipient-country primes, and the Japanese-origin requirement is 30% of contract value, not 100%. The claim is also a conjunction. Its one source (the JICA 2023-12-22 release) supports only "Procurement: Tied" and the 0.1%/50y/15y terms. It says nothing about multilateral procurement, so the "not multilateral procurement" half, and the label "the documented closed club", are not sourced by the cited URL. Finally, it does not run the SPEC control (AidData Chinese finance to Indian private firms). The loan terms are documented; the "closed club" inference as written is refuted.

verdicts.dateTest: Two actions, each checked against who held office. (1) IDA extended a US$250m credit to the Republic of India for Kerala's First Resilient Kerala DPO. The program document PGD77 is dated May 31, 2019, and the World Bank projects API gives a board approval date of 2019-06-27 for P169907 (status Closed, closing date 2021-06-30). At that time the Union was NDA (Modi government from May 2014) and Kerala was LDF (Pinarayi Vijayan from May 2016), so the "opposition state, NDA Centre" framing overlaps correctly. (2) The Union set Kerala's net borrowing ceiling for FY2023-24 at Rs 32,442 crore. This is recorded in the SC order of 2024-04-01 in Kerala v Union of India, and the same governments were in office. The phrase "four years before the same Centre capped its borrowing" in `text` is misleading. Under Art. 293(3) the Union fixes a net borrowing ceiling for every state every year, including FY2019-20. The same order records that the Union deducted Kerala's earlier over-borrowing in FY2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 (Rs 9,197.15 cr, 13,067.78 cr and 4,354.72 cr). The 2023-24 ceiling was an annual figure, not a new cap. from=2019 / to=2024 is acceptable.
verdicts.identityTest: The two parties are the ones the sources name. PGD77 reads: "INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT ASSOCIATION ... PROPOSED CREDIT IN THE AMOUNT OF SDR 115.2 MILLION AND US$ 90.4 MILLION (US$250 MILLION EQUIVALENT) TO THE REPUBLIC OF INDIA FOR THE FIRST RESILIENT KERALA PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT POLICY OPERATION". The financing table lists "IDA Credit 250.00" and "IBRD 0". The legal borrower is the Republic of India through DEA, and Kerala is the program state and ultimate beneficiary, so the edge fin:ida -> fin:state-kerala is a beneficiary edge, which is acceptable for an analytic edge. The blend terms are confirmed: "The proposed operation will be financed by IDA. While India is currently eligible for only IBRD financial terms, IDA Blend financial terms will be applied to the operation under the amendments approved by the Board based on the IDA18 midterm review." The ceiling figure is confirmed by the Indian Kanoon order: "This ceiling was quantified as three percent of the projected Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) for the F.Y. 2023-24, which came to INR 32,442 crores. This Net Borrowing Ceiling covered all sources of borrowings..."
verdicts.baseRate: Every state's external loan is signed by the Union and routed through DEA, so "through an NDA Centre" is true of 100% of state externally aided projects and does not distinguish Kerala. That is acceptable here because the claim is framed as a control, not as evidence of favour. Every state is also subject to an Art. 293(3) net borrowing ceiling every year (100%), so the ceiling does not distinguish Kerala either. What is unusual is the IDA-blend concession for an India operation after India graduated from IDA. That concession came from a World Bank Board decision (the IDA18 MTR amendment), not from the Union, so it is evidence that the Union did not block the loan, not evidence that it favoured Kerala. The World Bank API shows further Kerala lending under the same NDA Centre: P174778 PforR US$125m IBRD (2021-06-24), P168633 solid waste US$105m (2021-03-09), P177980 AF US$150m (2023-06-16), and P178254 KERA US$200m (2024-10-31). This supports the control. One contrary data point: P170521, the Second Resilient Kerala DPO (US$350m IBRD), has no board approval date, meaning it was dropped or converted. I found no document giving the reason, and it should be recorded as a gap.
verdicts.denialFound: The Union's stated position in the suit, per the 2024-04-01 order: Kerala "is apparently a highly debt stressed State that has mismanaged its finances", has "the highest ratio of Pension to Total Revenue Expenditure among all States", and its over-borrowing was deducted under the 14th Finance Commission's Annexure 14.2 rule (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/191833676/). The court prima facie accepted the Union's over-borrowing argument and referred the constitutional questions, including Kerala's Article 14 claim of differential treatment versus other states, to a Constitution Bench. I found no Union statement specifically answering a charge that opposition states are denied external loans, and I could not establish whether the Union was asked about that.
verdicts.innocentReading: External loans to states are routed through DEA and count inside the Art. 293(3) ceiling whichever party runs the state. The 3%-of-GSDP ceiling and the deduction of earlier over-borrowing come from Finance Commission norms that apply to every state. The concessional terms of the 2019 DPO were a World Bank Board decision made because of the 2018 floods, not a political favour from the Union. Kerala's 2023-24 dispute is about how off-budget borrowing (KIIFB, KSSPL) and past over-borrowing are counted, not about being refused external projects. This reading fits the evidence as well as any partisan reading, and the claim already records it.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives as analytic. The load-bearing facts check out against the primary sources: US$250m, IDA credit, blend terms despite India's IBRD-only eligibility, borrower Republic of India, dated May 2019 and Board-approved June 27, 2019; and the FY2023-24 net borrowing ceiling of Rs 32,442 cr. It draws no inference of wrongdoing and carries an innocentReading and upgradeIf/killIf, which is what the analytic tier requires. It is also the state-level symmetry control SPEC.md asks for. It is only partially sourced, for two reasons. First, "capped its borrowing" four years later implies a new cap when ceilings are set every year. Second, the `d` field's statement that the Union "defended it as a rule applying to all states" is not a sentence in the order: the Union's recorded defence is the Finance Commission over-borrowing adjustment plus Kerala's fiscal stress. These are wording faults, not refutations.
verdicts.corrections:
1. text: replace "four years before the same Centre capped its borrowing" with "four years before the same Centre set its FY2023-24 net borrowing ceiling at Rs 32,442 cr (ceilings are fixed annually for every state under Art. 293(3))".
2. d: replace "defended it as a rule applying to all states" with "defended it in the Supreme Court as a Finance Commission over-borrowing adjustment (Rs 9,197.15 / 13,067.78 / 4,354.72 cr deducted in FY22/23/24) and on the ground that Kerala is debt-stressed; the SC (2024-04-01) prima facie accepted the adjustment and referred the federalism and Art. 14 questions to a Constitution Bench".
3. d: add that the legal borrower is the Republic of India (PGD77) and that the IDA-blend terms came from a World Bank Board IDA18 MTR amendment, not from the Union.
4. benefit.amountCr: change 1735 to 1739 (US$250m x INR 69.56, the PGD77 rate as of Apr 30, 2019), or state which rate was used.
5. Add the board approval date 2019-06-27 and project id P169907 to d.
6. Add a gap: P170521, the Second Resilient Kerala DPO (US$350m IBRD), was never Board-approved; find the reason (Union, Bank or state) before the control is treated as complete.
7. Optionally note the later NDA-era Kerala loans (P174778 2021, P177980 2023, P178254 2024) as further evidence for the control.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, restated: the Ministry of Finance (the Union) was eligible for only IBRD terms from the World Bank by 2019. The quote holds. PGD77 (the Resilient Kerala DPO, 2019) says: "The proposed operation will be financed by IDA. While India is currently eligible for only IBRD financial terms, IDA Blend financial terms will be applied to the operation under the amendments approved by the Board based on the IDA18 midterm review." Graduation happened earlier, at the end of FY2014 (30 June 2014), with transitional IDA17 support through FY2017. That is five weeks after the NDA took office on 26 May 2014. Graduation and the change of government therefore coincide almost exactly. This is a confound. It does not show that the coalition had no effect, and a UPA-vs-NDA series cannot separate the two by timing alone. The record's d-field says JICA's 0.1%/50-year yen loans "entered the mix under NDA". That is wrong as a general statement. JICA was India's largest bilateral ODA lender under UPA as well (Delhi Metro, DFC, 2004-14). The 0.1%/50-year/15-year-grace tied terms belong specifically to the Mumbai-Ahmedabad HSR, whose loan tranches started under NDA. The other loan in the same JICA 2023-12-22 release is at 2.10%, 30 years, untied.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match. s=min:ministry-of-finance is the borrower of record for the Union. t=fin:ida is the World Bank's concessional window, which PGD77 names as the financier. The JICA release names the "Project for the Construction of Mumbai-Ahmedabad High Speed Rail (V), 400,000 million yen, 0.1%, 50 yrs, 15 grace, Tied".
verdicts.baseRate: IDA graduation is mechanical: GNI per capita above the operational cutoff plus creditworthiness. Every country crossing the threshold loses IDA terms whoever is in government (for example Vietnam in 2017 and Sri Lanka), so graduation itself does not discriminate between coalitions. Lender mix does not share this property. It partly reflects policy choices: joining AIIB as a founding member in 2015-16 and taking the tied Shinkansen deal in 2015 were government decisions. So "not by governing coalition" is non-discriminating only for the IDA half of the claim.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is an analytic claim that alleges no wrongdoing, and no party was asked. I found no contrary statement.
verdicts.innocentReading: India crossed the IDA income threshold around 2011-13 and graduated at the end of FY2014. Any government from mid-2014 on would have faced a less concessional World Bank window. JICA and AIIB loan terms follow each lender's own pricing rules.
verdicts.reason: The source quote is confirmed, but the claim concludes more than the evidence supports. It asserts a causal negative ("not by governing coalition") while admitting that the series needed to test it was not fetched. It also contradicts itself: it names lender mix as a determinant, yet lender mix (AIIB membership, the tied JICA HSR deal) was partly a choice made by the governing coalition. The source it relies on also weakens the "set by income status" premise, since it records the Board granting IDA Blend terms to India in 2019 as an exception after the Kerala floods. The claim can stay analytic only as a hypothesis that flags the confound.
verdicts.corrections: text/lab: replace with "IDA concessionality ended through income-based graduation (end-FY2014, transitional support to FY2017), which coincides with the May-2014 change of government, a confound. Lender mix (JICA HSR tied 0.1% loans, AIIB from 2016) is partly a policy choice. A UPA-vs-NDA concessionality comparison is untested pending the DEA/RBI external-debt series." d: remove "JICA's ... entered the mix under NDA". JICA was the largest bilateral lender under UPA too. Limit the 0.1%/50yr/tied terms to MAHSR; the co-listed SDG program loan is 2.10%/30yr/untied. Add the PGD77 exception: "IDA Blend terms applied to the 2019 Kerala DPO under IDA18 MTR amendments despite IBRD-only eligibility". Add a srcs entry for the graduation date: IDA India retrospective, https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/9cb5d26ee211a20a9c8beb5baa97d242-0410012020/original/ida-india-retrospective-2018.pdf. Keep tier analytic, keep innocentReading, keep upgradeIf/killIf. In killIf, add that the test must control for graduation timing, for example using the non-IDA share only.

verdicts.dateTest: FAIL on the strongestCase chronology. The claim reduces to "IMF/WB (actor) imposed conditions (did) that produced the 1991-07-24 Budget reforms (thing) after the 1991 package (when)". But the order runs the other way. The 1991 Budget speech (indiabudget.gov.in/doc/bspeech/bs199192.pdf, fetched 200) says only: "despite large borrowings from the International Monetary Fund in July 1990 and January 1991". Those were pre-Rao drawings under earlier governments. The World Bank SAL I (P010389, US$500m) has boardapprovaldate 1991-12-05 in worldbank-projects.json, and its President's report is dated 1991-11-12 (Wikipedia, Economic liberalisation in India). Both come about 4.5 months AFTER the Budget. The IMF stand-by also came after the Budget: autumn 1991, not verifiable here because imf.org is blocked and the search budget is exhausted. So "package was followed within weeks by the Budget" reverses the order. A defensible wording is "the Budget preceded, and was negotiated alongside, the SAL and SBA". The OED quote "Conditionality was used sparingly…" also fails on date. Its source (OED CAE 2001, para 2.5) is a summary of the late-1960s/1970s phase from Kraske's 1997 background paper. It is not a finding about 1991 or DPF-era India. The narrative uses it as a general verdict.
verdicts.identityTest: Mostly passes, with two fixes. (1) The legislature at issue in the Kerala DPO is the Kerala Legislative Assembly, not Parliament. The borrower of record is the Union: under Art. 293(1), states cannot borrow abroad. So the Kerala example cannot show anything about "overriding Parliament". (2) "Bhagwati–Panagariya" as pre-1991 advocates of reform has no source and is likely the wrong pairing. The pre-crisis works are Bhagwati–Desai (1970) and Bhagwati–Srinivasan (1975). The Bhagwati–Panagariya collaboration comes later. Ahluwalia (1985 book; 1990 'M-document') and Rangarajan are also unsourced in srcs. The "IMF Monitor" figure (65,894 conditions, 1980–2019) is confirmed verbatim ("65,894 policy reforms mandated by the IMF between 1980 and 2019"). But it is a global count: the page contains no India rows.
verdicts.baseRate: Non-discriminating. Every DPF operation carries prior actions by construction. The World Bank DPF page says prior actions "present the legal terms defined in the financing agreement". Essentially every IMF programme carries conditions, and 65,894 across all programmes is a global stock. The share of policy-based multilateral loans with policy conditions is about 100%, far above the 80% threshold, so "comes with policy strings" says nothing specific about India or any government. What would discriminate is the share of prior actions or triggers that require an Act of a legislature against a recorded ministry or committee position. That share has not been computed. The DPF prior-actions database (FY2005 onward) exists and could supply the denominator.
verdicts.denialFound: No specific denial from GoI or the Bank about India was located. The search budget is exhausted, and no sansad.in Q&A was opened, so asked/not asked is unknown. What exists is the lender's general institutional position on the DPF page: "The DPF Policy emphasizes country ownership, stakeholder consultation…" and "non-earmarked general budget financing that is subject to the borrower's own implementation processes and systems" (https://www.worldbank.org/en/what-we-do/products-and-services/financing-instruments/development-policy-financing). There is also OED CAE 2001 para 2.13: "the central challenge was to help the newly elected, reform-minded government implement its programs". These are lender self-descriptions, not responses to this claim.
verdicts.innocentReading: Policy-based lending pays out budget support against actions the borrowing executive agreed to, usually drawn from its own programme (Kerala PA1: "The GoK has adopted the Rebuild Kerala Development Program"). If a legislature does not act, the next tranche is not paid; the legislature is not overridden. The Kerala case shows this. Its DPO1 (P169907, 2019-06-27) set triggers for DPO2 that named legislation: "Draft River Basin Conservation and Management Authority Act has been submitted to the State Assembly" (Trigger 4) and "The GoK has amended TCP Act for risk-informed master planning" (Trigger 9). The Second Resilient Kerala DPO (P170521, US$350m) is recorded as "Dropped", and financing continued as a Program-for-Results (P174778, 2021-06-24). The reason for the drop is not documented. In 1991, the Budget and the Finance Bill went through Parliament, and the loans followed. Bypassing Parliament comes from India's own executive treaty and loan-signing design, which applies to every lender, bilateral and domestic-market alike.
verdicts.reason: The claim fails as worded, and the record supporting it has defects on both sides. Nothing on file shows a lender condition overriding Parliament. The strongest documented items are: (a) the 1966 Bell mission, which the OED itself calls "an early attempt to use the leverage of its lending in a major member country… Bank pressure caused resentment" (OED CAE para 2.3–2.4); the narrative omits this even though it cites the same document; and (b) Kerala DPO triggers that explicitly named Assembly legislation, after which the follow-on DPO was dropped. Neither is an override: in 1966 devaluation was an executive act, and in Kerala the Assembly is a state legislature whose refusal or delay simply ended the loan. The weak form ("multilateral loans carry policy conditions") is documented but applies to about 100% of such loans. The strong form ("override Parliament") has no documented instance. The narrative's own text needs fixing: the 1991 sequence is reversed (Budget 1991-07-24 came before SAL I 1991-12-05); the "sparingly" quote is applied to the wrong era; the budget content is sourced to Wikipedia although the primary speech is reachable; and the Bhagwati–Panagariya attribution has no source. Keep the item as a narrative only. Its status should be "unsupported as worded; weak form documented but non-discriminating". It should not appear as an edge.

Cite the primary Budget speech https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/bspeech/bs199192.pdf in place of, or alongside, Wikipedia. The Wikipedia citation of that speech carries a retrieval date of 2026-09-22, so check it for circular sourcing. 2. strongestCase: add OED CAE 2001 para 2.3–2.4 (the 1966 Bell mission: "an early attempt to use the leverage of its lending"; "Bank pressure caused resentment"). Add the Kerala DPO1 legislative triggers (Trigger 4, River Basin Act submitted to the State Assembly; Trigger 9, TCP Act amendment) and the fact that DPO2 P170521 (US$350m) was Dropped. 3. strongestCounter: re-date the "Conditionality was used sparingly" quote as describing the late-1960s–1970s phase (OED para 2.5, summarising Kraske 1997), not India generally. Add the 1991 quote from para 2.13: "help the newly elected, reform-minded government implement its programs". 4. verdicts.dateTest: The claim has no single actor or date. Its actual form is: lenders (JICA; World Bank/ADB) fund contracts, and those contracts go to a closed club, across 2000–2026. The only dated anchor is the JICA press release of 2023-12-22 (loan signed 2023-12-21, MAHSR tranche V, ¥400,000m, 0.1%/50y/15y, NDA era). It is correctly dated. The release says consulting was "already hired" and the initial ICB construction package "already contracted", so it describes terms and says nothing about who won contracts. The OED CAE (2001) covers FY90–00 and its finding is delay, not capture. Fazekas & Kocsis (BJPS 2020) is about the EU and has no India period. No overlap is broken, but no source ties a closed club to any period.
verdicts.identityTest: The JICA source names the right entity: the Project for the Construction of Mumbai-Ahmedabad High Speed Rail (V), executing agency NHSRCL, Asia Bhawan, Dwarka. The procurement column reads "Tied". But the narrative's strongestCase says tying restricts "suppliers to Japanese firms", and the record of winners contradicts that. The MAHSR civil packages went to Indian firms: C1 MEIL–HCC JV, C2 Afcons, C3/C4/C5/C6 L&T, C7 IRCON–DRA JV, C8 SCC–VRS JV, D1 DRA–DMRC JV, and D2 L&T–Sojitz JV (Wikipedia MAHSR construction table). The track contract went to IRCON. The fleet's own contracts.json records JICA-funded WDFC packages going to Sojitz–L&T consortia. A tied loan restricts the eligible nationality of lead contractors or goods under STEP. In practice, Indian majors win most of the value, as sole bidders or as JV partners. So the "club" is not Japanese firms, and the phrase "true by construction" is wrong.
verdicts.baseRate: For MDB loans, the fleet already has the denominator that this narrative says is missing. In contracts.json, 0 of 55 bidder-listed World Bank ICB awards in India (2011–2016) had a single bidder. The mean was 5.64 bidders, and only 12 of 55 had 3 or fewer. 20 of 55 were won by foreign-led firms (Chinese, Korean, UK, Mexican, Saudi), and 18 of 55 had at least one Chinese bidder. L&T took 20.3% of WB value but lost 5 of the 6 bids it entered in the period with published fields. The ADB RRTS Package 4 drew five qualified bidders from three countries and went to a Chinese SOE. That is the opposite of a closed club. For JICA, every STEP/tied loan to every borrower carries the nationality restriction (100%), so it does not discriminate anything about India. The actual winners are mixed Indian and Japanese–Indian JVs.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. NHSRCL, DFCCIL, JICA and the World Bank were not asked. The only party statement in the fleet is NCRTC's "awarded following the set procedure and guidelines" (contracts.json, STEC Package 4), and it concerns a different claim.
verdicts.innocentReading: Tied yen loans restrict eligibility by nationality as the price of 0.1%/50-year money. That is a published bilateral policy choice, not a club. In MAHSR, most civil value still went to Indian contractors, and the Shinkansen-specific systems went to Japanese vendors because the technology choice requires them. MDB-funded ICB in India draws about 5.6 bidders per award with no single-bid awards, and a mix of foreign winners, including Chinese firms before 2020. A few recurring large winners (L&T, Afcons, Tata Projects) is what prequalification thresholds on multi-thousand-crore civil packages produce in any thin market. The same pattern appears in the domestic Union register (Adani/Reliance/PSUs), so the lens detects package size rather than lender capture.
verdicts.reason: Both halves fail. (1) JICA: the source confirms only the label "Tied". It does not say contracts go to a closed club, and the actual MAHSR civil awards (C1–C8, D1) went to Indian firms. "True by construction" conflates a nationality-eligibility rule with a closed set of winners, which is a conjunction the sources do not support. (2) MDB: the claim calls this "undemonstrated", but the fleet's own contracts.json has already tested it and found the reverse (0/55 single-bid, 5.64 mean bidders, 36% foreign winners). By this narrative's own whatWouldChangeThis rule ("rates at or below baseline ⇒ unsupported"), the status should drop to unsupported. Fazekas & Kocsis is an EU study cited as if it described India. The OED source says the Indian problem was delay, not capture. The label "contested" is not a contract tier and overstates the support.
verdicts.corrections: literature.json narratives[1] ("Lender-funded contracts go to a closed club of contractors"): 1) Change status "contested" to "unsupported" and keep it only as a narrative, with no edge. 2) In strongestCase, replace "restricting suppliers to Japanese firms" and "true by construction" with: "JICA MAHSR tranches are 'Tied' (press release 2023-12-22: 0.1%/50y/15y, procurement Tied), i.e. STEP nationality eligibility; the resulting MAHSR civil awards went mainly to Indian firms (L&T C3–C6, Afcons C2, MEIL–HCC C1, IRCON–DRA C7) and Japanese–Indian JVs (L&T–Sojitz D2; WDFC Sojitz–L&T)". Cite NHSRCL award notices or the Wikipedia MAHSR construction table. 3) In strongestCounter, delete "no India single-bidding rate for lender-funded contracts has been computed in this fleet yet" and replace it with the contracts.json base rates: 0/55 single-bid, mean 5.64 bidders, 20/55 foreign-led winners, L&T lost 5 of 6 WB bids (2011–2016). Add the caveat that post-2016 WB notices do not publish losing bidders. 4) Label Fazekas & Kocsis as a method reference (EU data), not evidence about India. 5) In the claim text given to the verifier, drop the parenthetical "true by construction for tied JICA loans"; the accurate wording is "tied JICA loans restrict prime-contractor nationality; the winners are not a closed set".

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the Union government borrowed externally on more concessional terms, or borrowed less, during the NDA years (2014-05-26 onward) than during the UPA years (2004-05-22 to 2014-05-26). The three cited items do fall inside the NDA window. The Kerala IDA-blend DPO was 2019. The JICA MAHSR tranche V at 0.1%, 50 years, 15-year grace and 'Tied' is dated 2023-12. The AIIB press item is dated 2020-09. So the dates hold, but they show only that some individual loans existed. They are not a comparison between the two governments. The denominator that the record says was never opened is available. DEA 'India's External Debt: A Status Report 2013-14', Table 1.1, gives concessional debt as a share of total external debt: 28.4% (end-March 2006), 23.0, 19.7, 18.7, 16.8, 14.9, 13.3, 11.1, and 10.5% (end-March 2014). The DEA 2024-25 Status Report says 'The share of concessional debt in total external debt, however, contracted to 6.9 per cent at end-March 2025 from 7.4 per cent a year earlier'. It also says the concessional stock (USD 51.1 bn) 'has remained broadly range-bound for many years'. That is a steady decline across both governments with no break at 2014: about -17.9 pp over 8 UPA years and about -3.6 pp over 11 NDA years. The volume half of the claim also fails. Total external debt was USD 440.6 bn at end-March 2014 and USD 736.3 bn at end-March 2025 (RBI release). Sovereign external debt was about USD 81.5 bn in 2014 (my calculation: 18.5% sovereign share, i.e. 100 minus the 81.5% non-government share, times 440.6) and USD 168.4 bn in 2025. Only external debt to GDP is lower (23.3% to 19.1%), and that ratio had risen under UPA from 16.8%. It moves with the cycle and with private borrowing, not with which party is in power.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the Union of India as sovereign borrower. The Kerala DPO names 'Borrower: REPUBLIC OF INDIA; Implementing Agency: STATE OF KERALA'. JICA tranche V lends to the Government of India. The FPJ item concerns India's borrowing from the AIIB. Identity matches. One mismatch: the DEA concessional-share series covers all of India's external debt, including private ECBs and NRI deposits. The sovereign-only figure is 28% of government external debt concessional at end-March 2025, and I did not open a 2014 equivalent. The narrative never names who makes the partisan claim. No claimant is identified.
verdicts.baseRate: Among comparable lower-middle-income countries that graduated from IDA, the concessional share of external debt falls after graduation almost regardless of government. For India the decline is continuous from 42.9% (1991-2000 average) to 28.1% (2001-2010) to 10.5% (2014) to 6.9% (2025), according to DEA. The concessional stock has stayed range-bound while the denominator (commercial and private debt) has grown. On this measure every government since 1991 shows 'less concessional than its predecessor'. The trait does not distinguish between the two governments. Symmetry: run the same lens on the UPA control and UPA looks worse on share (bigger fall) and on the debt-to-GDP rise. Run it on NDA and NDA looks worse on the absolute stock of sovereign external debt, which roughly doubled. The lens picks up structure, not party.
verdicts.denialFound: none found, and no one was asked. This is a partisan claim with no named claimant, and there is no allegation of wrongdoing to deny. The closest thing to an official statement is the Ministry of Finance (DEA) Status Report 2024-25 itself. It attributes the falling concessional share to structure: 'range-bound' concessional stock against growing non-concessional debt. The 2013-14 report says the same: 'The share of concessional debt in total debt has declined due to shrinking share of official creditors and the Government debt and the surge in non-concessional private debt' (http://dea.gov.in/files/external_debt_documents/India_External_Debt201314E.pdf).
verdicts.innocentReading: India's income growth led to IDA graduation around FY2014, so new World Bank money after that came on IBRD terms. The Kerala 2019 blend terms were a Board exception under the IDA18 mid-term review, not a choice by the government: 'While India is currently eligible for only IBRD financial terms, IDA Blend financial terms will be applied'. Private and commercial external borrowing grew faster than official credit. JICA soft loans are project-specific and tied. Whichever coalition is in power, the concessional share falls and the stock rises with the size of the economy.
verdicts.reason: The proposition is refuted, and the narrative record is out of date. The series it says was 'not opened' is public, and it answers the question on the narrative's own falsifier ('a smooth trend would move it to debunked'). DEA Status Reports show concessional share falling smoothly: 28.4% (2006) to 10.5% (2014) to 6.9% (2025), with no break at 2014. The volume of external debt (USD 440.6 bn to 736.3 bn) and of sovereign external debt (about 81.5 bn to 168.4 bn) went up under NDA, not down. The cited sources confirm the individual facts: JICA's 0.1%/50y/15y/'Tied'; Kerala's IDA credit of US$250m on blend terms; India's roughly USD 3.6 bn, about 25% of AIIB lending. None of them compares the two governments, so treating these examples as a trend is the error. Keep this as a narrative (it is a mandatory symmetry control) but mark it debunked. The UPA-vs-NDA comparison is our own inference from a documented series, so it goes in as analytic with an innocentReading. It must never become an edge.
verdicts.corrections: 1) status: 'speculative' changes to 'debunked'. 'speculative' is not a valid tier under CONTRACT.md. Set the record's tier to 'analytic' and carry the innocentReading above. 2) strongestCounter: replace 'No consolidated series ... was opened in this sweep, so neither ... has a denominator here' with these figures: concessional/total external debt 28.4% (end-Mar 2006), 10.5% (end-Mar 2014), 6.9% (end-Mar 2025); concessional stock USD 51.1 bn, 'broadly range-bound'; total external debt USD 440.6 bn (2014) and 736.3 bn (2025); sovereign external debt about 81.5 bn (2014, computed from the 18.5% share) and 168.4 bn (2025); 28% of government external debt concessional at end-Mar 2025. 3) Add srcs: ['DEA External Debt Status Report 2013-14','http://dea.gov.in/files/external_debt_documents/India_External_Debt201314E.pdf'], ['DEA External Debt Status Report 2024-25','http://www.dea.gov.in/files/external_debt_documents/Ex%20Debt%20Report%202024-25.pdf'], ['RBI press release, external debt end-March 2025','https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=60729']. 4) strongestCase: remove the unsourced superlative 'most concessional large loan in its history'. The JICA page supports only '0.1%, 50 years, 15-year grace, procurement Tied' for tranche V (2023-12). 5) strongestCounter: 'graduated ... on income grounds' is not in the cited Kerala document, which says only 'currently eligible for only IBRD financial terms'. Either cite a World Bank IDA-graduation source or reword. 'AIIB/NDB lend at near-IBRD terms' is not supported by the FPJ item, which says only that India borrows from AIIB because 'the cost of borrowing ... plays an important role'. Add an AIIB/NDB pricing source or delete the phrase. 6) Add a note that the DEA ratio includes private debt. The sovereign-only concessional share for end-March 2014 is still a gap. 7) Record that no named claimant has been identified for the partisan claim.

verdicts.dateTest: Actor: the Union Ministry of Finance, specifically DEA. Action: refused external loans to opposition-run states. Period: NDA, 2014–2026 (implied). DEA's power over the pipeline covers the whole window, so tenure is not the problem. Timing is. The one dated episode cited is the FY2023-24 Net Borrowing Ceiling in State of Kerala v Union of India, OS 1/2024, order of 2024-04-01 (2024 INSC 253). But the World Bank board approved the US$250m IDA credit for LDF-run Kerala on 2019-05-31 (PGD77, dated May 31 2019), inside the same NDA/LDF overlap. The fleet's own worldbank-projects.json also has NDA-era approvals naming Kerala (10), Tamil Nadu (16), West Bengal (11), Punjab (5), Telangana (3), Karnataka (11), Himachal (8), Jharkhand (4) and Odisha (7). Every loan to a state has to be posed by DEA, so each approval is a dated counter-instance to "denied".
verdicts.identityTest: The record names the wrong authority and the wrong kind of borrowing. The Indian Kanoon order (2024-04-01, Surya Kant J.) says "the Defendant has imposed a 'Net Borrowing Ceiling' on the Plaintiff - State ... quantified as three percent of the projected Gross State Domestic Product ... INR 32,442 crores. This Net Borrowing Ceiling covered all sources of borrowings, including open market borrowings, loans from Financial Institutions, and the liabilities arising out of the Public Account". The order contains 0 hits for "Economic Affairs", "external", "externally" or "foreign". The ceiling is a Union/Ministry of Finance consent under Article 293(3) (in practice set by the Department of Expenditure), not a DEA decision on externally aided projects. Article 293(1) only covers state borrowing "within the territory of India". External loans are borrowed by the Union and passed on to the state, and DEA gates them through its screening and posing to lenders, which the order does not discuss. So "the DEA fixed Kerala's FY2023-24 ceiling" and "all state borrowing including externally aided projects needs Union consent under Article 293(3)" are identity and mechanism errors. The narrative's own counter already concedes that the "denial" Kerala documents is of borrowing room, not of external projects.
verdicts.baseRate: Comparables: states run by opposition parties for long stretches of 2014–2026 (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Punjab, Telangana, Karnataka, Himachal, Jharkhand, Odisha, Delhi). Share with at least one DEA-posed, World Bank-approved state-named operation under NDA: 10 of 10 in worldbank-projects.json. Delhi's only hit is a single pipeline operation, P517479, with an approval date of 2026-11-25. Share with none: 0 of 10. worldbank.json's per-capita lens has Kerala (LDF) at 1.9x, Tamil Nadu at 1.75x and Andhra Pradesh at 1.62x their population share under NDA. BJP-run UP is at 0.61x, MP 0.56x, Haryana 0.55x and Chhattisgarh 0.18x. The sibling adb-aiib.json records AIIB loans to Kerala, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and AP. Nothing in the record shows a gap against opposition states. On the "denied room" part, the Article 293(3) ceiling itself is 3% of GSDP for every state, so the rule does not discriminate by party.
verdicts.denialFound: No accuser is named. The record cites no opposition minister, state or party saying that DEA refused its external projects on partisan grounds. It cites only Kerala's suit, which is about the Net Borrowing Ceiling and never mentions external loans. The Union's response on that issue is in the court record (indiankanoon.org/doc/191833676/). It said Kerala "is apparently a highly debt stressed State that has mismanaged its finances" and "has the highest ratio of Pension to Total Revenue Expenditure among all States", and it pointed to "grave consequences regarding the fiscal health of the country". The Court found "prima facie merit in the submission of the Union of India that ... the State has no unutilized fiscal space". I found no DEA or Union denial on the external-loan allegation itself, because no one has put it to them on the record: none found, not asked. My web-search budget was used up, so I could not search further for contrary or supporting press reports, for example Tamil Nadu on the delay to Chennai Metro Phase 2 (JICA-funded). That gap should be closed before the narrative is re-rated upward on any specific episode.
verdicts.innocentReading: DEA clears state external-aid proposals against a fiscal and priority screen, and the lender's own pipeline adds more filtering. That screen applies to every state: the 3%-of-GSDP ceiling, whether the state can repay, and the state's past record of using up its borrowing limit. Kerala's constraint in FY2023-24 came from its own admitted over-borrowing in FY2017-18 to FY2019-20 plus off-budget liabilities counted within the ceiling, not from its party. Meanwhile the same Union posed a US$250m IDA-blend DPO for Kerala in 2019, and it posed dozens of World Bank, ADB and AIIB operations for DMK/AIADMK Tamil Nadu, TMC West Bengal, Congress/AAP Punjab and Congress Karnataka. Per-capita differences are driven mostly by small hill and north-eastern states and by project pipeline timing, under both UPA and NDA.
verdicts.reason: The claim is refuted on the record the fleet already holds. As a general statement ("opposition-run states are denied external loans"), 10 of 10 opposition-run comparison states received DEA-posed World Bank loans under NDA, and several are above population parity while several BJP-run states are below it. The one cited source, the SC order of 2024-04-01, is about the Article 293(3) Net Borrowing Ceiling on Kerala's total borrowing. It never mentions DEA, external loans or externally aided projects, so it cannot support a "DEA approval bottleneck" on external loans. The claim takes three separately true facts (the Union has consent power, Kerala's ceiling was tightened, and the World Bank chose "reforming states" in the 1990s) and joins them into a partisan motive that none of them states. No named party is recorded making the allegation, so the claim does not even reach the "alleged" tier. The symmetric control run in worldbank.json and adb-aiib.json already put the mirror-image narrative (lending goes to BJP-run states) at "unsupported". "Speculative" in literature.json is therefore inconsistent with the fleet's own evidence. Kill it as a claim or edge, and keep it only as a narrative marked unsupported.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Change status from "speculative" to "unsupported", in line with the matching narratives in worldbank.json and adb-aiib.json. 2) In strongestCase, replace "the DEA fixed Kerala's FY2023-24 ceiling at ₹32,442 crore" with "the Union (Ministry of Finance) fixed Kerala's FY2023-24 Net Borrowing Ceiling at ₹32,442 crore (3% of projected GSDP)". The order never mentions DEA. 3) Delete "all state borrowing including externally aided projects needs Union consent under Article 293(3)". Article 293 governs state borrowing within India; external loans are Union borrowing passed on to the state and gated by DEA's screening and posing, which is a separate mechanism with no court record here. 4) Remove "counted off-budget (KIIFB-type) borrowings" as a quotation from the source. The order says "off budget borrowing" and does not name KIIFB. 5) Add to strongestCounter the fleet's own NDA-era per-capita figures (Kerala 1.9x, TN 1.75x, AP 1.62x vs UP 0.61x, MP 0.56x, Haryana 0.55x, Chhattisgarh 0.18x; worldbank.json) and the count of state-named World Bank approvals for opposition-run states (Kerala 10, TN 16, West Bengal 11, Punjab 5, Karnataka 11; worldbank-projects.json). Also add the AIIB lending to Kerala, West Bengal, TN and Punjab (adb-aiib.json). 6) Add srcs pointing to worldbank.json and adb-aiib.json. The OED 1990s "reforming states" source is off-period and speaks to the Bank's discretion, not the Centre's, so drop it from strongestCase or mark it as context. 7) Record accuser "none named" and denial "none; not asked". 8) Keep whatWouldChangeThis but specify the evidence needed: DEA screening-committee minutes or RTI replies listing proposals a state submitted that DEA did not pose to a lender, 2014–2026, by state and ruling party. The approvals table alone cannot show denials, because refused proposals never reach the lender's database.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as actor/act/object/time: "Chinese state lenders and SOEs (CDB, China Eximbank, ICBC, BOC) took control of Indian infrastructure companies before 2020." Lending window per the AidData rows in bilateral-china.json runs 2008-06 (CDB Facility I to RCom) to 2015-03 (CDB to Aircel). The only coercive acts fall inside the window: CDB's NCLT insolvency petition against RCom (2017-11), withdrawn 2018-01-05, and RCom's insolvency (2019-02). None of these is a transfer of control. The Ambani judgment (UK High Court, 2020-05-22) falls after the "before 2020" cutoff and enforces a personal guarantee. It is not an equity or board step-in. Press Note 3 (2020-04-18) also comes after the window and governs equity, not these loans. On Brookings: the "five-fold to at least US$8 billion" covers the three years after 2014, so roughly 2017. That matches the narrative's "by 2017".
verdicts.identityTest: The named borrowers (RCom, Reliance Power/Sasan, Lanco Infratech, Adani Power Maharashtra, Essar, Aircel) are private Indian companies. The Chinese lenders are named state policy banks and commercial banks, not a nationality acting as one bloc. The claim's actor, "Chinese money", is a nationality-level abstraction. Under CONTRACT rule 1 that belongs only in narratives, never as an edge. Brookings (Ananth Krishnan, 2020-03-30) refers to "official figures", meaning MOFCOM FDI data, not "official finance" in the AidData sense. The narrative's phrase "official Chinese FDI" mixes the two. Banking on Beijing (Dreher, Fuchs, Parks, Strange, Tierney 2022) mentions "corruption, political capture, and conflict" as general risks for low- and middle-income countries. India is not named on the opened page.
verdicts.baseRate: The Chinese banks were never sole lenders. Standard Chartered sat in the Sasan and Tiroda syndicates. US Ex-Im lent US$650m to Sasan. SEK and the Nordic Investment Bank co-financed Aircel. In the RCom insolvency, CDB held about 37% of RCom's secured debt (c039), a large but not controlling creditor position. The bilateral-china.json analytic (c061) finds that 3 of the 4 largest Chinese-bank borrowers went insolvent (RCom, Aircel, Lanco). That default rate matches the wider 2015–19 stress in Indian telecom and thermal power, where Indian public-sector banks carried most of the losses. Default is not a distinguishing feature of Chinese-financed borrowers. On sovereign books China records zero PPG debt, against Japan's 72% of India's PPG bilateral debt (c060). The same capture lens applied to the Japanese control gives a more concentrated picture (tied MAHSR procurement, a 50-year creditor to a Union PSU). The alarm is therefore a property of the lens, as the file's symmetryCheck already says.
verdicts.denialFound: Ambani's spokesperson (The Wire, 2020-05-22, recorded as contra bilateral-china:c042) said the guarantee was "never signed by Ambani" and that the debt was "not a personal loan" but RCom's 2012 corporate refinancing: https://thewire.in/business/uk-court-orders-anil-ambani-to-pay-717-million-to-chinese-banks-within-21-days. No response from CDB, China Eximbank or ICBC was found, and none was asked for. No Indian government statement claiming Chinese control of an infrastructure company before 2020 was found. PN3's stated purpose is "curbing opportunistic takeovers/acquisitions" during COVID-19, which is forward-looking.
verdicts.innocentReading: Between 2008 and 2015, Indian private telecom and power companies borrowed dollar credit from Chinese policy banks. Much of it was buyer's credit tied to Chinese equipment (Shanghai Electric turbines and boilers, Chinese telecom gear) and priced at LIBOR plus 1.8–4.75%. It was ordinary commercial export credit, the same instrument US Ex-Im and the Nordic ECAs gave the same sectors. When the borrowers failed in the 2017–19 telecom and power bust, the Chinese banks acted like any secured creditor: an NCLT petition, which was withdrawn, then a vote in the IBC committee of creditors alongside Indian banks, then a UK guarantee claim. The Chinese equity that did arrive went mostly into technology and pharma stakes and start-ups. The infrastructure figures were pledges and bids "as yet unapproved" (about US$15bn, per Brookings).
verdicts.reason: The claim is refuted as an assertion, and the file's "unsupported" calibration survives. None of the three sources shows a Chinese entity with control, a board seat or step-in rights over an Indian infrastructure company before 2020. Brookings says the opposite for the relevant period: the investment was "predominantly state-owned enterprises (SOEs)" only in the pre-2014 US$1.6bn stock. After that it records "a noticeable shift from state-driven to market-driven investment from the Chinese private sector". It places "controlling stakes" in "the technology sector", and describes the infrastructure money as pledges "in bids for major infrastructure projects that are as yet unapproved". The AidData rows in bilateral-china.json are all debt (c052). The strongestCase is a conjunction of true facts (large Chinese credit, borrower defaults, a 2020 guarantee judgment, PN3) that together suggest "capture" when no single source says it. The status should not move to "debunked" yet. Chinese lenders sat on IBC committees of creditors for RCom, Aircel and Lanco in 2018–19, and those committees legally control a corporate debtor's resolution. The Chinese voting shares have not been verified, and DPIIT equity data was not opened. The narrative should stay a narrative (nationality as actor) at status "unsupported", with the fixes below.
verdicts.corrections: 1) strongestCase misquotes Brookings. "dominated by state-owned enterprises" is not in the source. The text says "Most of the investment was in the infrastructure space, involving major Chinese players in this sector, predominantly state-owned enterprises (SOEs)", and it describes the pre-2014 US$1.6bn stock. Replace the quote and add Brookings' next clause ("a noticeable shift from state-driven to market-driven investment from the Chinese private sector") to strongestCounter. 2) Change "official Chinese FDI rose five-fold to US$8bn by 2017" to "Chinese FDI per MOFCOM data rose five-fold to at least US$8bn in the three years after 2014". "Official" there refers to the statistics, not official finance. 3) The "at least US$26 billion" figure is "current and planned investment" across all sectors, not infrastructure. Say so. 4) Banking on Beijing: say that "political capture" is a general risk listed for low- and middle-income countries and that India is not named on the opened page. 5) The Ambani judgment (2020-05-22) falls after the "before 2020" window and enforces a guarantee that is contested.
